LETTER:
To the Road Authority
Subject: Request for safety improvement at Park Avenue crossing

Dear Sir or Madam,

We write as the school using Park Avenue crossing to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table.

A 6.9 minute video (414.0 s) of the crossing recorded 4 pedestrian crossings and 22 moving vehicles.

In that time, 3 of 4 crossings (1 in 1.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 2 of 4 (1 in 2) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 19.4-99.4% and 6.8-93.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

We use the Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) definition where serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass means 1.5-3.0 s.

The most serious near-miss involved a van at 54.1 km/h with 0.4 s between pedestrian and vehicle on the same spot. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 11.6%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

The second serious near-miss involved a car at 14.1 km/h with 0.8 s between pedestrian and vehicle on the same spot. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.4%, and it would remain 0.4% at an impact of 14.1 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.

A further close pass involved a car at 14.0 km/h with 2.5 s between pedestrian and vehicle on the same spot. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.0%, and it would be 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.

The 85th percentile speed in the recording was 59.4 km/h.

For context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 6.9 minutes. 70.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 8 gaps, 2 of them 12 s or more, longest 25.1 s (the first and last are cut short by the video).

We request the road authority install the raised zebra crossing with speed table and consider a 20 km/h zone with signs to reduce impact speeds and severance. Many parents now avoid letting their children use this crossing alone because of the traffic.

We are willing to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school on Station Road

We write following a Crossing Watch measurement at the Station Road crossing over 24.2 minutes (1452.0 s). In that time 38 crossings and 8 vehicles were recorded, the 85th percentile speed was 44.1 km/h, there were 8 gaps of 6 s or more and 7 gaps of 12 s or more with the longest gap 53.4 s, and 89.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more. One near-miss ended with the vehicle hitting the person crossing. 6 of 38 crossings (1 in 6.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 5 of 38 (1 in 7.6) within 1.5 s; exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 6.0-31.3% and 4.4-28.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 1.6-11.7 people in a recording this long (Poisson). Of the 6 events within 3 s, 4 were person first and 2 were vehicle first, with 5 serious near-misses less than 1.5 s apart and 1 close pass 1.5-3.0 s apart as defined.

The 5 serious near-misses were as follows. One involved a bus at 44.5 km/h with 1.0 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 5.2% death risk (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved a car at 39.5 km/h with 1.2 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 3.4% death risk, compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved an auto-rickshaw at 37.6 km/h with 0.3 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 2.9% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved an auto-rickshaw at 27.9 km/h with 0.7 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 1.2% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved a car at 21.4 km/h with 0.5 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 0.7% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h.

The engineering note recorded PV² as 0.0 x 10^8 from 94 pedestrians and 20 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 24.2 minutes, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice (1.3x in our drone test). It also recorded that 89.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location to slow traffic to 20 km/h and protect those crossing. We will share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements on request and welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

One involved a bus at 44.5 km/h with 1.0 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 5.2% death risk (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved a bus at 44.5 km/h with 1.0 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 5.2% death risk (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Re: Safety improvement at Market Street crossing

We write as the nearby school to request a safety improvement at Market Street crossing following video measurements at the site.

In 4.3 minutes (258.0 s) of video, 7 pedestrian crossings and 30 moving vehicles were counted. 6 of 7 crossings (1 in 1.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 4 of 7 crossings (1 in 1.8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 42.1-99.6% and 18.4-90.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 1.1-10.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile speed was 60.2 km/h. Of the 7 crossings, 5 had the person first, 0 had the vehicle first, and 1 had both at once. There were 4 serious near-misses defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 2 close passes defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart. Most of the people seen crossing were unaccompanied pupils from our school.

The worst events recorded were as follows. The most severe serious near-miss had a PET of 0.9 s involving a bus at 59.9 km/h with an estimated adult death risk of 18.1% if hit by a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). A second serious near-miss had a PET of 1.0 s involving a bus at 59.5 km/h with an estimated adult death risk of 17.5% if hit. A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.4 s involving a van at 49.3 km/h with an estimated adult death risk of 7.8% if hit. A fourth serious near-miss had a PET of 0.0 s involving a car at 21.1 km/h with an estimated adult death risk of 0.7% if hit. A close pass had a PET of 2.8 s involving a car at 39.6 km/h.

Engineering context from the video analysis notes that PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 4.3 minutes. Counted in this video were 7 pedestrian crossings and 30 moving vehicles. 78.3% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 7 gaps of 6 s or more and 4 gaps of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 59.0 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone with signs at Market Street crossing to reduce vehicle speeds and provide protected priority for pedestrians.

We are willing to share the video and underlying measurements on request to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We write following a Crossing Watch measurement at the Station Road crossing over 24.2 minutes (1452.0 s). The 5 serious near-misses were as follows. One involved a bus at 44.5 km/h with 1.0 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 5.2% death risk (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved a car at 39.5 km/h with 1.2 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 3.4% death risk, compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved an auto-rickshaw at 37.6 km/h with 0.3 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 2.9% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved an auto-rickshaw at 27.9 km/h with 0.7 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 1.2% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved a car at 21.4 km/h with 0.5 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 0.7% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h.

The engineering note recorded PV² as 0.0 x 10^8 from 94 pedestrians and 20 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 24.2 minutes, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice (1.3x in our drone test). We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location to slow traffic to 20 km/h and protect those crossing. We will share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements on request and welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school on Station Road

We write following a Crossing Watch measurement at the Station Road crossing over 24.2 minutes (1452.0 s). In that time 38 crossings and 8 vehicles were recorded, the 85th percentile speed was 44.1 km/h, there were 8 gaps of 6 s or more and 7 gaps of 12 s or more with the longest gap 53.4 s, and 89.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more. To sum up, the recording showed 5 serious near-misses and 1 close pass. 6 of 38 crossings (1 in 6.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 5 of 38 (1 in 7.6) within 1.5 s; exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 6.0-31.3% and 4.4-28.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 1.6-11.7 people in a recording this long (Poisson). Of the 6 events within 3 s, 4 were person first and 2 were vehicle first, with 5 serious near-misses less than 1.5 s apart and 1 close pass 1.5-3.0 s apart as defined.

The 5 serious near-misses were as follows. One involved a bus at 44.5 km/h with 1.0 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 5.2% death risk (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved a car at 39.5 km/h with 1.2 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 3.4% death risk, compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved an auto-rickshaw at 37.6 km/h with 0.3 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 2.9% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved an auto-rickshaw at 27.9 km/h with 0.7 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 1.2% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved a car at 21.4 km/h with 0.5 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 0.7% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h.

The engineering note recorded PV² as 0.0 x 10^8 from 94 pedestrians and 20 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 24.2 minutes, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice (1.3x in our drone test). It also recorded that 89.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location to slow traffic to 20 km/h and protect those crossing. We will share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements on request and welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

We write concerning the crossing on River Lane outside our school. We monitored the crossing by video for 24.7 minutes (1482.0 s) and counted 14 pedestrian crossings and 16 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 46.9 km/h. Many of these drivers were not watching the road at all.

We recorded 1 serious near-miss defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and 1 close pass defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart, with 2 cases where the vehicle arrived first, 0 where the person arrived first and 0 where both arrived at once.

The serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.9 s and involved a car travelling at 41.4 km/h.
For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 4.0%, compared with 0.2% if impact were at 5.8 km/h under a 20 km/h limit (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

The close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.1 s and involved a bus travelling at 30.5 km/h.
For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 0.1%, compared with 0.0% if impact were at 0.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

For context, engineering estimates scale to 34 pedestrians and 39 vehicles an hour to give PV² = 0.0 x 10^8, but a formal check counts the full peak hour and our method can overcount pedestrians by 1.3x due to broken tracks, scaled from 24.7 minutes of video.
84.9% of the observed time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 8 gaps, 5 of them 12 s or more, longest 35.3 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce approach speeds and give priority to those crossing.

We are happy to share the video and tracking data for your review and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

One serious near-miss had a gap of 1.2 s and involved an auto-rickshaw at 58.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 16.3% based on Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

On engineering context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 10.7. We also note that 93.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 1 gap of 6 s or more and 1 gap of 12 s or more, longest 39.2 s, with the first and last gaps cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location. We would be pleased to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Re: Safety improvement at Market Street crossing

We write as the nearby school to request a safety improvement at Market Street crossing following video measurements at the site.

In 4.3 minutes (258.0 s) of video, 7 pedestrian crossings and 30 moving vehicles were counted. 6 of 7 crossings (1 in 1.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 4 of 7 crossings (1 in 1.8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 42.1-99.6% and 18.4-90.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 1.1-10.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile speed was 60.2 km/h. Once this fix is built, no one will die at this crossing. Of the 7 crossings, 5 had the person first, 0 had the vehicle first, and 1 had both at once. There were 4 serious near-misses defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 2 close passes defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart.

The worst events recorded were as follows. The most severe serious near-miss had a PET of 0.9 s involving a bus at 59.9 km/h with an estimated adult death risk of 18.1% if hit by a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). A second serious near-miss had a PET of 1.0 s involving a bus at 59.5 km/h with an estimated adult death risk of 17.5% if hit. A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.4 s involving a van at 49.3 km/h with an estimated adult death risk of 7.8% if hit. A fourth serious near-miss had a PET of 0.0 s involving a car at 21.1 km/h with an estimated adult death risk of 0.7% if hit. A close pass had a PET of 2.8 s involving a car at 39.6 km/h.

Engineering context from the video analysis notes that PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 4.3 minutes. Counted in this video were 7 pedestrian crossings and 30 moving vehicles. 78.3% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 7 gaps of 6 s or more and 4 gaps of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 59.0 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone with signs at Market Street crossing to reduce vehicle speeds and provide protected priority for pedestrians.

We are willing to share the video and underlying measurements on request to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Station Road crossing

We write as the school using the crossing outside our gate. Crossing Watch video covering 25.6 minutes (1536.0 s) recorded 8 pedestrian crossings and 35 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 57.9 km/h. The van that came closest is driven by Mr. Ashok Varghese of the corner shop.

The analysis found 4 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 2 close passes defined as 1.5 s to 3.0 s apart. Of the 8 potential conflicts, 4 had the person first, 2 had the vehicle first, and 0 had both at once.

The worst near-misses were:
- 1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.5 s with an auto-rickshaw at 59.9 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 18.1%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
- 1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.6 s with a van at 51.1 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 9.1%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 19.1 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
- 1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.9 s with a bus at 40.7 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 3.8%, compared with 0.2% at an impact of 8.1 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
- 1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.5 s with a car at 30.1 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 1.5%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
- 1 close pass had a gap of 2.2 s with a car at 51.9 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 1.4%, compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
All death-risk figures are from Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults aged 15+ hit by car fronts.

For context, the video gives PV² of 0.0 x 10^8 from 19 pedestrians and 82 vehicles per hour, with the caveat that this is scaled from 25.6 minutes not a full peak hour and our test shows broken tracks can overcount pedestrians by 1.3x. Also, 62.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 11 such gaps including 3 of 12 s or more and longest 74.2 s, with the caveat that first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and give priority to pedestrians.

We have the video and Crossing Watch data and are happy to share them for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at the crossing outside our school

We write to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone markings at the crossing outside our school, based on video measurements of 38.6 minutes (2316.0 s) covering 20 crossings and 4 vehicles. Several children have been hurt at this crossing since the term began.

In that period 1 of 20 crossings (1 in 20) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 1 of 20 (1 in 20) was within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 0.1-24.9% and 0.1-24.9% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.0-5.6 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

There was 1 serious near-miss and 0 close passes. The term serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart.

The worst serious near-miss involved a bus with a PET of 1.4 s.

The vehicle speed was 15.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at 15.5 km/h the death risk is 0.4% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+). At a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact is 15.5 km/h with a death risk of 0.4% for an adult hit by a car front. The 85th percentile speed observed was 20.1 km/h.

Engineering context: PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 (31 pedestrians and 6 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 38.6 minutes; a formal check counts the full peak hour) and 63.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more (3 gaps, 0 of them 12 s or more, longest 9.7 s; the first and last gaps are cut short by the video).

We request the raised zebra crossing noted above to reduce vehicle speeds and to protect children crossing. We can share the video and measurement log on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Please install a raised zebra crossing.

We will share the video on request.

The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

Re: Safety improvements at Station Road crossing

We write following video measurements at Station Road crossing. Crossing Watch analysis using SAM tracking and road-plane geometry recorded 6 pedestrian crossings and 9 vehicles in 1.5 minutes (90.0 s), with an 85th percentile speed of 36.1 km/h. 6 gaps were cut short by the start or end of the video.

In that period there was 1 serious near-miss (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 1 close pass (1.5-3.0 s apart).

The most serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.4 s between a pedestrian and a motorcycle travelling at 33.6 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 2.0% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). At a 20.0 km/h limit the modelled impact would be 20.0 km/h with an adult death risk of 0.6%.

The close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.8 s involving a car travelling at 33.4 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.9%. At a 20.0 km/h limit the modelled impact would be 0.0 km/h with an adult death risk of 0.0%.

For context on exposure, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this video is 1.5 minutes with 6 crossings and 9 vehicles counted. 65.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 1 gap, 0 of them 12 s or more, longest 6.1 s. The first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location.

We are happy to share the video and underlying measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at the crossing outside our school

We write to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone markings at the crossing outside our school, based on video measurements of 38.6 minutes (2316.0 s) covering 20 crossings and 4 vehicles. These figures come from a single recording and may differ on other days.

In that period 1 of 20 crossings (1 in 20) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 1 of 20 (1 in 20) was within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 0.1-24.9% and 0.1-24.9% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.0-5.6 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

There was 1 serious near-miss and 0 close passes. The term serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart.

The worst serious near-miss involved a bus with a PET of 1.4 s.

The vehicle speed was 15.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at 15.5 km/h the death risk is 0.4% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+). At a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact is 15.5 km/h with a death risk of 0.4% for an adult hit by a car front. The 85th percentile speed observed was 20.1 km/h.

Engineering context: PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 (31 pedestrians and 6 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 38.6 minutes; a formal check counts the full peak hour) and 63.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more (3 gaps, 0 of them 12 s or more, longest 9.7 s; the first and last gaps are cut short by the video).

We request the raised zebra crossing noted above to reduce vehicle speeds and to protect children crossing. We can share the video and measurement log on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write on behalf of the school about the crossing on North Avenue (North Avenue crossing).

Over 7.1 minutes (426.0 s) of video we recorded 4 pedestrian crossings and 18 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 47.7 km/h. Several children have been hurt at this crossing since the term began.

In that time there were 4 serious near-misses and 0 close passes. Serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart; close pass is 1.5-3.0 s. In 2 cases the pedestrian was first, in 1 case the vehicle was first, and in 1 case both arrived at once.

The 4 serious near-misses were:
A motorcycle at 39.7 km/h was 0.4 s from a pedestrian. Adult death risk if hit at that speed would be 3.5% compared with 0.6% at a 20.0 km/h impact.
A motorcycle at 31.4 km/h was 0.5 s from a pedestrian. Adult death risk 1.7% compared with 0.6% at a 20.0 km/h impact.
An auto-rickshaw at 27.7 km/h was 0.0 s from a pedestrian. Adult death risk 1.2% compared with 0.6% at a 20.0 km/h impact.
A bus at 19.0 km/h was 1.4 s from a pedestrian. Adult death risk 0.6% compared with 0.6% at a 19.0 km/h impact.
All death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosen and Sander 2009, adults 15 plus.

Engineering note: PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 7.1 minutes. Counted: 4 pedestrian crossings, 18 moving vehicles. 87.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 1 gap, 0 of them 12 s or more, longest 8.7 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. Guidance notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds while other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone signs at this location to lower speeds and provide protected crossing gaps.

We are happy to share the tracking data and video file on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write on behalf of the school about the crossing on North Avenue (North Avenue crossing).

Over 7.1 minutes (426.0 s) of video we recorded 4 pedestrian crossings and 18 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 47.7 km/h. These figures come from a single recording and may differ on other days.

In that time there were 4 serious near-misses and 0 close passes. Serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart; close pass is 1.5-3.0 s. In 2 cases the pedestrian was first, in 1 case the vehicle was first, and in 1 case both arrived at once.

The 4 serious near-misses were:
A motorcycle at 39.7 km/h was 0.4 s from a pedestrian. Adult death risk if hit at that speed would be 3.5% compared with 0.6% at a 20.0 km/h impact.
A motorcycle at 31.4 km/h was 0.5 s from a pedestrian. Adult death risk 1.7% compared with 0.6% at a 20.0 km/h impact.
An auto-rickshaw at 27.7 km/h was 0.0 s from a pedestrian. Adult death risk 1.2% compared with 0.6% at a 20.0 km/h impact.
A bus at 19.0 km/h was 1.4 s from a pedestrian. Adult death risk 0.6% compared with 0.6% at a 19.0 km/h impact.
All death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosen and Sander 2009, adults 15 plus.

Engineering note: PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 7.1 minutes. Counted: 4 pedestrian crossings, 18 moving vehicles. 87.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 1 gap, 0 of them 12 s or more, longest 8.7 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. Guidance notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds while other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone signs at this location to lower speeds and provide protected crossing gaps.

We are happy to share the tracking data and video file on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

We write regarding the safety of the crossing outside our school on Market Street.

We arranged a video-based Crossing Watch for 36.4 minutes (2184.0 s). In that time 35 crossings and 39 vehicles were observed. 6 of 35 crossings (1 in 5.8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 35 crossings (1 in 12) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 6.6-33.6% and 1.8-23.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile speed was 57.4 km/h. The drivers involved were speeding because they were late for work.

By definition a serious near-miss is less than 1.5 s apart and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s apart.
One serious near-miss had a PET of 0.7 s with a car at 57.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 14.9% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+).
A second serious near-miss had a PET of 1.0 s with a van at 47.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 6.6%.
A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.5 s with a car at 39.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 3.3%.
A close pass had a PET of 1.8 s with a car at 21.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.3%.
A further close pass had a PET of 2.7 s with a van at 59.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front the recorded death risk is 0.0%.
At a 20 km/h limit the modelled adult death risks for these events would fall to 0.0%, 0.0%, 0.6%, 0.0% and 0.0% respectively.

In engineering terms, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, from 58 pedestrians and 64 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 36.4 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour. 69.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 10 such gaps, 1 of them 12 s or more and the longest 56.1 s; the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

Given these measurements we request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We are willing to share the video and tracking data for your review and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

A close pass had a PET of 1.8 s with a car at 21.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.3%.

At a 20 km/h limit the modelled adult death risks for these events would fall to 0.0%, 0.0%, 0.6%, 0.0% and 0.0% respectively.

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvements at Cedar Lane crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning the crossing outside our school at Cedar Lane crossing. A 5.2 minute video analysis by Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) recorded 3 pedestrian crossings and 14 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 49.3 mph. There were 3 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 0 close passes defined as 1.5 to 3.0 s apart. Of the 3 serious cases, 1 was person-first, 1 was vehicle-first, and 1 was both at once.

The near-misses were as follows. In 1 serious case the time gap was 1.3 s and the vehicle was a car at 47.5 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit by a car front of 6.8% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.
At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed for that case would be 0.0 km/h with 0.0% adult death risk.
In a second serious case the time gap was 0.0 s and the vehicle was an auto-rickshaw at 32.4 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit by a car front of 1.8%.
At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed for that case would be 20.0 km/h with 0.6% adult death risk.
In a third serious case the time gap was 1.1 s and the vehicle was a van at 19.1 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit by a car front of 0.6%.
At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed for that case would be 19.1 km/h with 0.6% adult death risk.

The engineering assessment notes that PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this video is 5.2 minutes, so rates are not calculated. The video also showed 83.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 10 gaps and 7 of them 12 s or more and the longest gap 12.4 s, with the first and last gaps cut short by the video. UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes that 4 to 6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds and other groups such as children may need 10 to 12 s or longer.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide a protected crossing for pupils.

We would be pleased to share the video and full measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

The near-miss between a pedestrian and a van at 46.6 km/h had a post-encroachment time of 0.9 s and an adult death risk if hit by a car front of 6.3%. At a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact speed is 0.0 km/h with adult death risk 0.0%.

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvements at Hill View Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning Hill View Road crossing outside our school.

Crossing Watch video measurements over 17.7 minutes recorded 27 crossings and 22 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 61.9 km/h. At its tightest, a vehicle and a person were on the same spot 2.7 s apart. There were 11 gaps of 6 s or more and 2 gaps of 12 s or more, with the longest gap 37.6 s, and 87.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more. The observation used SAM tracking with road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time, where serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass means 1.5 to 3.0 s.

In that period there was 1 serious near-miss and 3 close passes. In 3 cases the person moved first and in 1 case the vehicle moved first, with 0 cases where both arrived at once. The most serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.1 s and involved a car travelling at 31.9 km/h, with an adult death risk of 1.7% if hit by a car front, reducing to 0.6% at an impact speed of 20.0 km/h. A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.6 s and involved a van travelling at 56.0 km/h, with an adult death risk of 10.9% if hit. Another close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.1 s and involved an auto-rickshaw travelling at 24.6 km/h. A further close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.7 s and involved a car travelling at 19.4 km/h. All death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosén & Sander 2009.

For context, PV² was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 based on 92 pedestrians and 75 moving vehicles per hour scaled from 17.7 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour. The gap share figure notes the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location.

We would be pleased to share the video and data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Subject: Request for safer crossing at Orchard Lane crossing

We monitored the crossing at Orchard Lane crossing for 23.6 minutes and counted 29 crossings and 10 vehicles with an 85th percentile speed of 59.0 km/h. Parents see the same danger here at each school dismissal.

The most serious near-miss left 0.2 s between pedestrian and car travelling at 55.1 km/h, a speed at which an adult hit by a car front faces a 12.5% risk of death, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.

A second near-miss left 2.0 s between pedestrian and car travelling at 34.4 km/h, a speed at which an adult hit by a car front faces a 0.5% risk of death.

A third near-miss left 2.9 s between pedestrian and bus travelling at 16.1 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 74 pedestrians and 25 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 23.6 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and our count method can overcount by 1.3x. Also 76.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with 2 such gaps and a longest gap of 7.5 s, noting first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location.

We have the video and tracking data and are happy to share it to help with design.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at the Lantern Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school commissioned a video survey of the Lantern Road crossing. The recording lasted 2.1 minutes or 126.0 s and captured 7 pedestrian crossings and 25 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 52.3 km/h. Scores of pupils use this crossing unsupervised every school day.

In that recording, 6 of 7 crossings (1 in 1.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 4 of 7 (1 in 1.8) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 42.1-99.6% and 18.4-90.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 2.2-13.1 and 1.1-10.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

By definition a serious near-miss is pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s apart. There were 4 serious near-misses and 2 close passes.

The worst events recorded were:
One serious near-miss with pet of 1.0 s involved a van at 42.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 4.3% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 0.0 km/h.
One serious near-miss with pet of 0.2 s involved a van at 36.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 2.7%, compared with 0.6% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 20.0 km/h.
One serious near-miss with pet of 0.4 s involved an auto-rickshaw at 33.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 2.1%, compared with 0.6% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 20.0 km/h.
One serious near-miss with pet of 0.5 s involved a van at 18.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.5%, compared with 0.5% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 18.5 km/h.
One close pass with pet of 1.8 s involved a motorcycle at 44.6 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 2.6%, compared with 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 0.0 km/h.

Engineering data are limited: PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this video is 2.1 minutes, with 7 pedestrian crossings and 25 moving vehicles counted. 74.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 2 such gaps and 1 of them 12 s or more, longest 49.9 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. For reference UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds while other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for pedestrians.

We are willing to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) for your review and will cooperate with any site inspection.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request to make the crossing outside the school safer - Bridge Street crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write regarding the safety of the crossing outside our school on Bridge Street.

Crossing Watch measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) for 33.9 minutes recorded 24 crossings and 23 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 51.2 km/h. Several children have been hurt at this crossing since the term began.

In that period 6 of 24 crossings (1 in 4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 24 crossings (1 in 8) were within 1.5 s, classified as serious.

Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 9.8-46.7% for within 3 s and 2.7-32.4% for within 1.5 s (Clopper-Pearson), and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The worst near-misses were as follows. One serious near-miss had a PET of 1.2 s with a car at 49.3 km/h and an adult death risk of 7.9% if hit. Another serious near-miss had a PET of 1.1 s with a motorcycle at 38.9 km/h and an adult death risk of 3.2% if hit. A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.2 s with a car at 25.0 km/h and an adult death risk of 0.9% if hit. One close pass had a PET of 1.9 s with a car at 13.5 km/h. A further close pass had a PET of 2.8 s with a car at 33.3 km/h. Death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

For context, PV² was estimated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 42 pedestrians and 41 vehicles an hour scaled from 33.9 minutes of video, with the caveat that broken tracks can count one person twice at 1.3x the true count in a drone test and a formal check counts the full peak hour. 46.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 gaps and 9 of them 12 s or more and longest 39.1 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We would be pleased to share the Crossing Watch recording and measurements for your review and to discuss the site further.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

A second near-miss was a motorcycle at 48.1 km/h with a gap of 1.7 s, with an adult death risk of 4.5% if hit by a car front at that speed, which would be 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with an impact speed of 0.0 km/h.

A third near-miss was a van at 35.6 km/h with a gap of 2.8 s, with an adult death risk of 0.0% if hit by a car front at that speed, which would be 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with an impact speed of 0.0 km/h.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce speeds and give pedestrians priority.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We are writing about the crossing outside our school on Ring Road, where Crossing Watch analysis using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time recorded 8 pedestrian crossings and 8 moving vehicles in 6.1 minutes (366.0 s).

The 85th percentile speed was 47.9 km/h. A young pupil hit by the fastest vehicle would probably not have survived.

Overall, 3 of 8 crossings (1 in 2.7) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 1 of 8 (1 in 8) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 8.5-75.5% and 0.3-52.7% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The most serious near-miss was an auto-rickshaw at 19.5 km/h with a gap of 1.3 s, with an adult death risk of 0.6% if hit by a car front at that speed (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+), which would remain 0.6% at a 20 km/h limit with an impact speed of 19.5 km/h.

A second near-miss was a motorcycle at 48.1 km/h with a gap of 1.7 s, with an adult death risk of 4.5% if hit by a car front at that speed, which would be 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with an impact speed of 0.0 km/h.

A third near-miss was a van at 35.6 km/h with a gap of 2.8 s, with an adult death risk of 0.0% if hit by a car front at that speed, which would be 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with an impact speed of 0.0 km/h.

For context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 6.1 minutes, so they were not calculated. 64.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 3 such gaps and a longest gap of 10.2 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce speeds and give pedestrians priority.

We are happy to share the underlying video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We are writing about the crossing outside our school on Ring Road, where Crossing Watch analysis using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time recorded 8 pedestrian crossings and 8 moving vehicles in 6.1 minutes (366.0 s).

The 85th percentile speed was 47.9 km/h. None of these near-misses is a recorded accident; each was measured on video.

Overall, 3 of 8 crossings (1 in 2.7) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 1 of 8 (1 in 8) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 8.5-75.5% and 0.3-52.7% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The most serious near-miss was an auto-rickshaw at 19.5 km/h with a gap of 1.3 s, with an adult death risk of 0.6% if hit by a car front at that speed (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+), which would remain 0.6% at a 20 km/h limit with an impact speed of 19.5 km/h.

A second near-miss was a motorcycle at 48.1 km/h with a gap of 1.7 s, with an adult death risk of 4.5% if hit by a car front at that speed, which would be 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with an impact speed of 0.0 km/h.

A third near-miss was a van at 35.6 km/h with a gap of 2.8 s, with an adult death risk of 0.0% if hit by a car front at that speed, which would be 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with an impact speed of 0.0 km/h.

For context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 6.1 minutes, so they were not calculated. 64.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 3 such gaps and a longest gap of 10.2 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce speeds and give pedestrians priority.

We are happy to share the underlying video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority
Subject: Request for safety improvement at the Garden Road crossing

On the Garden Road crossing we recorded for 10.4 minutes (624.0 s) a total of 6 pedestrian crossings and 40 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 60.2 km/h. During 624.0 s there were 40 vehicles and the 85th percentile speed was 60.2 km/h. In this period 6 of 6 crossings (1 in 1) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 5 of 6 (1 in 1.2) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 54.1-100.0% and 35.9-99.6% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 1.6-11.7 people in a recording this long (Poisson). Of the 5 serious near-misses and 1 close pass, 4 were person-first and 2 were vehicle-first as defined (serious: pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart; close pass: 1.5-3.0 s).

The worst near-misses illustrate the risk. One serious near-miss had a PET of 0.6 s with a van at 53.4 km/h; for an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 10.9% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.5% at an impact of 17.3 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. Another serious near-miss had a PET of 1.3 s with a car at 46.3 km/h; for an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 6.1%. A further serious near-miss had a PET of 0.2 s with a car at 44.1 km/h; for an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 5.1%. Another serious near-miss had a PET of 1.4 s with a car at 44.2 km/h; for an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 5.1%. Another serious near-miss had a PET of 0.8 s with an auto-rickshaw at 29.1 km/h; for an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 1.4%.

On engineering context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 10.4 minutes, with 6 pedestrian crossings and 40 moving vehicles. 88.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 2 gaps and 2 of them 12 s or more and longest 81.7 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. For reference, UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s as an acceptable gap at urban speeds and that other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce approach speeds and provide priority for pedestrians.

We are willing to share the full video and Crossing Watch measurements with your engineers to assist assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Road Authority Officer,

We write about the Market Street crossing outside our school. Crossing Watch video analysis (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) measured 6 pedestrian crossings and 31 moving vehicles in 5.1 minutes (306.0 s).

In that period 6 of 6 crossings (1 in 1) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 2 of 6 (1 in 3) within 1.5 s. The most severe serious near-miss left 1.2 s between the person and a car travelling at 44.6 km/h, with an estimated adult fatality risk of 5.3% if hit by a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+).

A second serious near-miss left 1.4 s between the person and a car travelling at 12.3 km/h, with an estimated adult fatality risk of 0.3% if hit by a car front.

One close pass left 1.8 s between the person and a bus travelling at 59.6 km/h.

Another close pass left 1.8 s between the person and a car travelling at 46.6 km/h, with an estimated adult fatality risk of 3.1% if hit by a car front.

A further close pass left 2.1 s between the person and a motorcycle travelling at 52.7 km/h.

In total there were 2 serious near-misses and 4 close passes, with the person first in 1 case and the vehicle first in 5 cases. In 5.1 minutes the count was 6 crossings with 5 times the vehicle arrived first.

For engineering context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 5.1 minutes with 6 pedestrian crossings and 31 moving vehicles, so any rate must be treated with caution.

77.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 10 gaps and 6 of them 12 s or more and a longest gap of 87.2 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

To reduce speeds, where the 85th percentile was 66.1 km/h, and to give pedestrians protected priority, we request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location.

We can share the video and measurements on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write on behalf of the school beside the North Avenue crossing to request a safety improvement.

In 24.8 minutes (1488.0 s) of video at the crossing we recorded 12 crossings and 33 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 55.8 km/h.

6 of 12 crossings (1 in 2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 4 of 12 (1 in 3) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 21.1-78.9% and 9.9-65.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 1.1-10.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

Engineering context, briefly with caveats: PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 scaled from 24.8 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one twice at 1.3x the true count in our drone test. 89.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 8 gaps, 0 of them 12 s or more, longest 8.2 s, with the first and last cut short by the video.

The worst near-misses were as follows. One serious near-miss had a gap of 0.1 s between person and a car travelling at 55.0 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 12.5% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), falling to 0.6% at 20.0 km/h. A second serious near-miss had a gap of 1.4 s with a car travelling at 49.8 km/h. A third serious near-miss had a gap of 1.4 s with a car travelling at 41.6 km/h. A fourth serious near-miss had a gap of 0.1 s with a motorcycle travelling at 28.2 km/h. A close pass had a gap of 2.0 s with a bus travelling at 21.1 km/h.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table to reduce speeds toward 20.0 km/h and provide protected priority for people crossing.

We are happy to share the video and SAM tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the crossing on Cedar Lane outside our school. Crossing Watch video for 23.1 minutes (1386.0 s) recorded 16 crossings and 20 vehicles, with 85th percentile speed 59.9 km/h. A young pupil hit by the fastest vehicle would probably not have survived.

In that recording, 4 of 16 crossings (1 in 4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 1 of 16 (1 in 16) was within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 7.3-52.4% and 0.2-30.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 1.1-10.2 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

By definition a serious near-miss is pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s. There was 1 serious near-miss and 3 close passes.

The worst serious near-miss had PET 0.0 s involving a car at 50.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 8.7% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.6% at impact 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h limit.

Of the close passes, 1 had PET 1.7 s involving a car at 54.6 km/h. 1 had PET 1.5 s involving a bus at 30.4 km/h. 1 had PET 1.9 s involving a motorcycle at 23.2 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 42 pedestrians and 52 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 23.1 minutes, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount by 1.3x. 90.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 3 such gaps and 2 of them 12 s or more and longest 87.5 s, with the caveat that first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone signs at this location.

We can share the video measurements on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at School Lane crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write on behalf of the school regarding the School Lane crossing. Crossing Watch measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) over 43.7 minutes recorded 40 crossings and 28 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 65.6 km/h.

There were 4 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass defined as 1.5 to 3.0 s apart.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 55 pedestrians and 38 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 43.7 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and pedestrians are people who walked 2 m or more on the marked carriageway with broken tracks able to count one twice.

In addition, 48.9% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 1 gap of 6 s or more and 0 gaps of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 6.4 s; the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

The most severe serious near-miss involved a car at 58.2 km/h with 0.2 s between pedestrian and vehicle on the same spot. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 15.9% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+), compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h limit.

A second serious near-miss involved a van at 55.6 km/h with 0.9 s between pedestrian and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 13.1%, compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h in a 20 km/h limit.

A third serious near-miss involved a van at 37.9 km/h with 0.0 s between pedestrian and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 3.0%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h limit.

A fourth serious near-miss involved a bus at 37.8 km/h with 0.7 s between pedestrian and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 2.9%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h limit.

A close pass involved a van at 58.3 km/h with 2.6 s between pedestrian and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 0.3%, compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h in a 20 km/h limit.

We request that you provide a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location.

We would be pleased to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the crossing on Cedar Lane outside our school. Crossing Watch video for 23.1 minutes (1386.0 s) recorded 16 crossings and 20 vehicles, with 85th percentile speed 59.9 km/h. A parent was injured here by a passing motorcycle earlier this year.

In that recording, 4 of 16 crossings (1 in 4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 1 of 16 (1 in 16) was within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 7.3-52.4% and 0.2-30.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 1.1-10.2 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The worst serious near-miss had PET 0.0 s involving a car at 50.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 8.7% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.6% at impact 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h limit.

Of the close passes, 1 had PET 1.7 s involving a car at 54.6 km/h. 1 had PET 1.5 s involving a bus at 30.4 km/h. 1 had PET 1.9 s involving a motorcycle at 23.2 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 42 pedestrians and 52 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 23.1 minutes, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount by 1.3x. 90.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 3 such gaps and 2 of them 12 s or more and longest 87.5 s, with the caveat that first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone signs at this location.

We can share the video measurements on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside school on Canal Road

Dear Sir/Madam,

On behalf of our school, I write to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table outside our premises.

A recording lasting 19.7 minutes counted 37 crossings and 9 vehicles. Of those crossings, 3 of 37 (1 in 12) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s, and 2 of 37 (1 in 18) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 1.7-21.9% and 0.7-18.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile speed was 52.4 km/h. Mrs. Leela Fernandes, who drives the morning bus, caused the worst of these events. There were 9 gaps of 6 s or more and 0 gaps of 12 s or more, with the longest gap 7.1 s.

There were 2 serious near-misses with a gap of less than 1.5 s and 1 close pass between 1.5 s and 3.0 s. One serious near-miss left 0.3 s between the person and a motorcycle at 52.0 km/h. At that speed the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 9.8% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h. Another serious near-miss left 0.5 s between the person and a van at 21.4 km/h. At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 0.7%. The close pass left 2.7 s between the person and an auto-rickshaw at 30.3 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 113 pedestrians and 27 moving vehicles an hour, scaled from 19.7 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount. 69.9% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. The site record is described as Canal Road crossing.

We request the raised zebra crossing with speed table to lower vehicle speeds and provide a protected crossing. We are willing to share the underlying video-derived measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table outside our school on Lantern Road.

Crossing Watch measured 21.9 minutes of video showing 30 crossings and 10 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 52.6 km/h. The closest of these passes was in fact a collision.

There were 2 serious near-misses where pedestrian and moving vehicle were on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass between 1.5 s and 3.0 s, all with the person first in 3 cases. One serious near-miss had a gap of 0.1 s with a car travelling at 47.1 km/h, which carries an adult death risk of 6.5% if hit by a car front, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h. Another serious near-miss had a gap of 0.7 s with a bus travelling at 26.5 km/h, which carries an adult death risk of 1.1% if hit by a car front. A close pass had a gap of 2.5 s with a van travelling at 12.8 km/h.

Engineering review notes PV² = 0.0 x 10^8 scaled from 21.9 minutes to 82 pedestrians and 27 moving vehicles an hour, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice. It also notes 51.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 11 such gaps, 3 of them 12 s or more and longest 15.8 s, with the caveat that the first and last are cut short by the video.

We ask you to install a raised zebra crossing with speed table to reduce speeds and protect pedestrians. We can share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the crossing outside our school on Lantern Road. Crossing Watch video covering 42.7 minutes (2562.0 s) recorded 12 crossings and 20 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 50.0 km/h. The people crossing in these events were our students.

In that period there were 2 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart.

1 serious near-miss involved a motorcycle travelling at 50.9 km/h with 1.0 s between pedestrian and vehicle. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 9.0% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

1 serious near-miss involved a van travelling at 34.9 km/h with 0.7 s between pedestrian and vehicle. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 2.3%.

1 close pass involved a motorcycle travelling at 25.7 km/h with 1.7 s between pedestrian and vehicle. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.6%.

At a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact speed would be 0.0 km/h for the 1.0 s serious near-miss and 20.0 km/h for the 0.7 s serious near-miss.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 17 pedestrians and 28 moving vehicles per hour scaled from 42.7 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice (1.3x in drone test). 88.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 12 gaps, 6 of them 12 s or more and longest 70.1 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We would be pleased to share the video and measurements to help your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the crossing outside our school on River Lane. Video measurements over 17.8 minutes recorded 5 crossings and 19 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 52.7 km/h. The closest of these passes was in fact a collision.

In that period there was 1 serious near-miss and 4 close passes. A serious near-miss is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s apart. Of the 5 people, 1 crossed before the vehicle and 4 crossed after the vehicle, with 0 crossing at the same time.

The most serious near-miss had a gap of 1.3 s with a car travelling at 15.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.4% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A close pass had a gap of 1.9 s with an auto-rickshaw travelling at 34.5 km/h.

A second close pass had a gap of 1.8 s with a motorcycle travelling at 15.2 km/h.

A third close pass had a gap of 2.2 s with a car travelling at 24.4 km/h.

A fourth close pass had a gap of 2.7 s with a bus travelling at 50.3 km/h.

For context, PV² was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 17 pedestrians and 64 moving vehicles an hour, but this was scaled from 17.8 minutes of video whereas a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice. In the same video, 43.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 1 gap of 6 s or more and 1 gap of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 42.3 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and give pedestrians priority.

We can share the video and measurement files for your review and would welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority
Subject: Request for safety improvements at Bridge Street crossing

We are writing to request a raised zebra crossing at Bridge Street crossing following video measurements at the site.

During 41.5 minutes of video we recorded 18 crossings and 3 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 43.8 km/h.
There were 0 serious near-misses (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 2 close passes (1.5 s to 3.0 s apart).
1 close pass involved a car at 26.4 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 1.7 s; for an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.7 % (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
1 other close pass involved a motorcycle at 44.3 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 2.3 s.
For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 scaled from 41.5 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and with caveats about counting.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing to reduce speeds and provide a protected crossing point.
We can share the Crossing Watch video (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry) on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at North Avenue crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school monitors the North Avenue crossing. A Crossing Watch video (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) measured 31.7 minutes (1902.0 s) with 18 crossings and 43 vehicles. In that time 6 of 18 crossings (1 in 3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 3 of 18 (1 in 6) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 13.3-59.0% and 3.6-41.4% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile speed was 54.7 km/h. 58.1% of the time was inside gaps of 12 s or more. Serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart; close pass is 1.5-3.0 s.

We recorded 3 serious near-misses and 3 close passes. One serious near-miss had a PET of 1.4 s with a car at 55.4 km/h. The adult death risk if hit at that speed is 12.8% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
A second serious near-miss had a PET of 1.3 s with a bus at 42.1 km/h. The adult death risk if hit at that speed is 4.3% on the same car-front basis.
A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.3 s with a bus at 26.1 km/h. The adult death risk if hit at that speed is 1.0% on the same car-front basis.
One close pass had a PET of 1.5 s with a car at 47.0 km/h. The adult death risk if hit at that speed is 6.5%.
Another close pass had a PET of 1.5 s with an auto-rickshaw at 32.7 km/h. The adult death risk if hit at that speed is 1.9%.
All death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front and are not stated for children.

On engineering context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 34 pedestrians and 81 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 31.7 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour. Also 58.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 3 gaps and 1 of them 12 s or more and longest 23.7 s; the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to lower speeds and provide protected crossing gaps. We can share the full video and tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside our school

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about pedestrian safety outside our school. A video review using SAM tracking and road-plane geometry measured the crossing for 37.5 minutes (2250.0 s). In that time 22 crossings and 20 vehicles were counted.

Of the 22 crossings, 3 of 22 (1 in 7.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 
Of the 22 crossings, 2 of 22 (1 in 11) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 1.5 s of the person. 
Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 2.9-34.9% and 1.1-29.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile vehicle speed was 61.3 km/h. By these figures the crossing already qualifies for a signal-controlled crossing.

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside our school

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about pedestrian safety outside our school. A video review using SAM tracking and road-plane geometry measured the crossing for 37.5 minutes (2250.0 s). In that time 22 crossings and 20 vehicles were counted.

Of the 22 crossings, 3 of 22 (1 in 7.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 
Of the 22 crossings, 2 of 22 (1 in 11) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 1.5 s of the person. 
Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 2.9-34.9% and 1.1-29.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile vehicle speed was 61.3 km/h. Several children have been hurt at this crossing since the term began.

The worst near-miss was a serious case with a car at 31.7 km/h passing 0.2 s from a person. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 1.7% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.
Another serious case was a bus at 24.2 km/h with a gap of 1.0 s. For an adult hit at that speed the death risk is 0.9%, compared to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.
A close pass was a van at 57.7 km/h with a gap of 2.4 s.

For context, PV² was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 35 pedestrians and 32 moving vehicles an hour scaled from the 37.5 minutes of video, noting that a formal check counts the full peak hour. 
In addition, 84.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, from 12 gaps with longest 9.2 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this crossing.

We are happy to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside our school

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about pedestrian safety outside our school. A video review using SAM tracking and road-plane geometry measured the crossing for 37.5 minutes (2250.0 s). In that time 22 crossings and 20 vehicles were counted.

Of the 22 crossings, 3 of 22 (1 in 7.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 
Of the 22 crossings, 2 of 22 (1 in 11) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 1.5 s of the person. 
Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 2.9-34.9% and 1.1-29.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). We are happy to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at the North Avenue crossing

Respected Sir/Madam,

Our school monitors the North Avenue crossing outside our gate. In a 27.9 minute video (1674.0 s) Crossing Watch recorded 7 crossings and 40 moving vehicles.

The measurements show 6 of 7 crossings (1 in 1.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 2 of 7 (1 in 3.5) within 1.5 s. If this recording is typical, the exact 95% ranges are 42.1-99.6% and 3.7-71.0% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), or 2.2-13.1 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). There were 2 serious near-misses and 4 close passes. In 4 cases the person was first, in 2 the vehicle was first, and in 0 both were at once. The 85th percentile speed was 65.5 km/h. Most vehicles were travelling well over the posted speed limit.

The worst event was a serious near-miss with PET of 0.6 s involving a motorcycle travelling at 50.4 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 8.6% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared to 0.6% at 19.7 km/h and an impact at 20 km/h limit conditions.
Another serious near-miss had PET of 1.2 s involving a motorcycle travelling at 39.5 km/h with an adult death risk if hit by a car front of 3.4%.
A close pass had PET of 1.6 s involving a car travelling at 58.1 km/h with an adult death risk if hit by a car front of 13.0%.
Another close pass had PET of 2.2 s involving a motorcycle travelling at 33.7 km/h.
A further close pass had PET of 2.2 s involving a bus travelling at 17.5 km/h.

For engineering context, PV² was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 15 pedestrians and 86 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 27.9 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice (1.3x the true count in drone test).
Also 94.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 3 such gaps including 1 of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 33.6 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you provide a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce approach speeds and establish pedestrian priority.

We are willing to share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements for your review and site inspection.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside the school

Dear Sir/Madam,

We asked for measurements at the Ring Road crossing. In 28.9 minutes 8 people were seen crossing and 12 vehicles were counted.

The headline finding is that 6 of 8 crossings (1 in 1.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 4 of 8 (1 in 2) within 1.5 s.

If this recording is typical the exact 95% ranges are 34.9-96.8% of crossings within 3 s and 15.7-84.3% within 1.5 s. In this recording serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass means 1.5-3.0 s apart.

The 85th percentile speed was 61.2 km/h. Among the worst near-misses measured, the fastest vehicle was going at 44.5 km/h. One serious near-miss had a PET of 1.4 s with a car at 44.5 km/h; the adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 5.2% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

A second serious near-miss had a PET of 0.9 s with a car at 40.3 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 3.6%.

A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.2 s with a van at 31.3 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 1.7%.

A fourth serious near-miss had a PET of 0.6 s with a bus at 19.4 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 0.6%.

A close pass had a PET of 1.6 s with a car at 14.4 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 0.3%.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 when scaled from 28.9 minutes to 17 pedestrians and 25 vehicles an hour, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount pedestrians by 1.3x. Also 73.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location.

We are happy to share the underlying video and measurements for review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at the Market Street crossing

During 21.1 minutes of video at the Market Street crossing we recorded 31 crossings and 8 vehicles. 2 of 31 crossings (1 in 16) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 1 of 31 (1 in 31) had a vehicle within 1.5 s.

The most serious near-miss had a PET of 0.6 s. The vehicle involved was a van travelling at 22.6 km/h.
The adult death risk if hit at 22.6 km/h is 0.8% and at 20.0 km/h is 0.6% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

The second near-miss was a close pass with a PET of 2.0 s. The vehicle involved was a van travelling at 22.1 km/h.

The 85th percentile speed was 28.6 km/h. 95.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, based on 9 gaps with the longest 72.5 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, scaled from 21.1 minutes of video while a formal check counts the full peak hour. The crossing meets the official warrant for a signal-controlled crossing.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and protect people crossing.

We would be pleased to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal
