We are writing about the crossing outside our school at Cedar Lane crossing and ask you to make it safer.

The 85th percentile speed was 50.4 km/h.

There were 4 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart.

A serious near-miss had a PET of 1.0 s involving an auto-rickshaw at 46.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 6.4% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.0%.

A serious near-miss had a PET of 0.1 s involving a van at 36.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 2.5%. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would be 20.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.6%.

A serious near-miss had a PET of 0.8 s involving a van at 35.0 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 2.3%. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would be 20.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.6%.

A serious near-miss had a PET of 0.7 s involving a motorcycle at 16.9 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.5%. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would be 16.9 km/h with a death risk of 0.5%.

Engineering context with caveats: PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video, this one is 11.2 minutes with 11 pedestrian crossings and 13 moving vehicles. 47.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 12 gaps, 3 of them 12 s or more, longest 65.8 s, with the first and last gaps cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at Cedar Lane crossing to reduce vehicle speeds and give priority to people crossing.

We can share the video and the measurements on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvements at Canal Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

I write as head of the school beside Canal Road crossing. A 38.2 minute video of the crossing recorded 38 crossings and 12 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 58.5 km/h. Every person in these near-misses was a pupil of our school.

In that period 2 of 38 crossings (1 in 19) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 2 of 38 (1 in 19) within 1.5 s. The 95% ranges if this recording is typical are 0.6-17.7% and 0.6-17.7% of crossings. There were 2 serious near-misses and 0 close passes.

The worst serious near-miss was 0.6 s apart with a car at 56.6 km/h, which carries a 14.1% adult death risk if hit by a car front, compared with 0.4% at an impact of 14.2 km/h at a 20 km/h limit.
The second serious near-miss was 0.9 s apart with a car at 56.1 km/h, which carries a 13.6% adult death risk for an adult hit by a car front.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, scaled from 38.2 minutes rather than a full peak hour and with counts that can be 1.3x high in our test. 90.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, based on 6 gaps with the first and last cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signage at this location.

We are happy to share the video and measurements to assist your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Road Authority Officers,

I write about the Hill View Road crossing after a 4.8 minute video review covering 288.0 s with 6 pedestrian crossings and 39 moving vehicles.

In that recording, 5 of 6 crossings (1 in 1.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 5 of 6 (1 in 1.2) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 35.9-99.6% and 35.9-99.6% of crossings, and 1.6-11.7 and 1.6-11.7 people in a recording this long. There were 5 serious near-misses with less than 1.5 s separation and 0 close passes with 1.5-3.0 s separation. In 5 cases the vehicle passed before the person, in 0 cases the person passed before the vehicle, and 0 cases were at the same time.

The closest was 0.2 s between a person and a motorcycle at 56.3 km/h. Estimated adult death risk if hit by a car front was 13.8%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h impact under a 20 km/h limit.

Another was 1.0 s with a motorcycle at 35.9 km/h. Estimated adult death risk if hit by a car front was 2.5%, compared with 0.3% at 10.2 km/h impact under a 20 km/h limit.

Another was 1.3 s with a van at 28.4 km/h. Estimated adult death risk if hit by a car front was 1.3%, compared with 0.2% at 7.1 km/h impact under a 20 km/h limit.

Another was 1.4 s with a bus at 22.4 km/h. Estimated adult death risk if hit by a car front was 0.7%, compared with 0.5% at 18.3 km/h impact under a 20 km/h limit.

Another was 1.4 s with a van at 13.4 km/h. Estimated adult death risk if hit by a car front was 0.3%, compared with 0.3% at 13.4 km/h impact under a 20 km/h limit.

Risk estimates use Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts. The 85th percentile speed was 55.8 km/h.

On capacity, PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video, while this video is 4.8 minutes with 6 pedestrian crossings and 39 moving vehicles. In this video, 89.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 5 such gaps and 1 of them 12 s or more, longest 22.9 s.

I request installation of a raised zebra crossing at this location. I offer to share the video for review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signage at this location.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Road Authority,

We write about the crossing on River Lane. In 3.6 minutes we counted 6 pedestrian crossings and 46 moving vehicles.

6 of 6 crossings (1 in 1) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 6 (1 in 2) had a vehicle within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 54.1-100.0% and 11.8-88.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The 85th percentile speed was 54.1 km/h. Among the worst near-misses measured, the fastest vehicle was going at 51.9 km/h.

Worst near-misses recorded were:
A serious near-miss with a motorcycle at 51.9 km/h had 1.1 s between the person and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is estimated at 9.8% (Rosen & Sander 2009, adults 15+).
A serious near-miss with a car at 19.5 km/h had 1.3 s between the person and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is estimated at 0.6%.
A serious near-miss with a motorcycle at 14.0 km/h had 1.4 s between the person and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is estimated at 0.4%.
A close pass with a car at 39.1 km/h had 1.9 s between the person and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is estimated at 1.2%.
A close pass with a car at 16.3 km/h had 1.6 s between the person and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is estimated at 0.3%.

Engineering context is limited. PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 3.6 minutes. Counted was 6 pedestrian crossings and 46 moving vehicles.
88.3% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 11 gaps, 4 of them 12 s or more, longest 51.9 s. The first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce speeds and provide protected priority.

We are happy to share the measurement file and discuss the results further.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside our school on Brook Street

We asked Crossing Watch to measure the crossing outside our school using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time. In 36.1 minutes (2166.0 s) of video they counted 13 crossings and 26 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 47.9 mph. There were 6 gaps of 6 s or more, 2 gaps of 12 s or more, with the longest gap 58.6 s.

By definition a serious near-miss is pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s apart. We recorded 2 serious near-misses and 3 close passes. In 3 cases the person arrived first and in 2 cases the vehicle arrived first.

The most serious near-miss left 0.4 s between pedestrian and a car.
The car in that near-miss was at 48.1 km/h.
At that speed an adult hit by a car front has a 7.1% death risk, compared with 0.6% death risk at an impact of 20.0 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second serious near-miss left 1.0 s between pedestrian and an auto-rickshaw.
The auto-rickshaw in that near-miss was at 28.7 km/h.
At that speed an adult hit by a car front has a 1.3% death risk, compared with 0.6% death risk at an impact of 20.0 km/h.

A close pass left 1.8 s between pedestrian and a car.
The car in that close pass was at 50.7 km/h.
A close pass left 2.1 s between pedestrian and a bus.
The bus in that close pass was at 33.4 km/h.
A close pass left 2.5 s between pedestrian and a van.
The van in that close pass was at 15.2 km/h.

For engineering context the scaled PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 22 pedestrians and 43 vehicles an hour, but this is scaled from 36.1 minutes of video while a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice.
43.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you provide a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this crossing to reduce vehicle speeds.

We have retained the video measurements and can share the video files on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We are writing about the Mill Street crossing. We measured activity there for 10.0 minutes and counted 10 pedestrian crossings and 4 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 62.7 km/h.

We would be pleased to share the video for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

Subject: Request to make the Ring Road crossing safer

Measurements were made from video of the crossing by Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time). In 16.1 minutes (966.0 s) we recorded 14 crossings and 37 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 48.5 km/h. The drivers involved were speeding because they were late for work.

We recorded 3 serious near-misses and 3 close passes. Serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart. Close pass means 1.5 s to 3.0 s apart.

The worst events were:
One serious near-miss had a PET of 0.3 s with a car travelling at 46.3 km/h. For an adult hit at that speed by a car front the estimated death risk is 6.1%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.
Another serious near-miss had a PET of 0.0 s with a car travelling at 35.0 km/h. For an adult hit at that speed by a car front the estimated death risk is 2.3%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.
A 3rd serious near-miss had a PET of 0.6 s with a car travelling at 28.9 km/h. For an adult hit at that speed by a car front the estimated death risk is 1.3%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.
Death-risk figures are Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.

For context, scaled PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 52 pedestrians and 138 moving vehicles per hour scaled from 16.1 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count 1 person twice (1.3x the true count in our drone test).
Also 61.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 1 gap of 6 s or more, longest 82.0 s, with the caveat that the 1st and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We would be pleased to share the video and the full measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Lake View Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We recorded activity at Lake View Road crossing for 17.9 minutes (1074.0 s). In that time we counted 30 crossings and 14 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 45.5 km/h. The recording showed 1 serious near-miss in all.

Of 30 crossings, 4 of 30 (1 in 7.5) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3.0 s of the person and 2 of 30 (1 in 15) within 1.5 s. If this recording is typical, the exact 95% ranges are 3.8-30.7% and 0.8-22.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.1-10.2 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). There was 1 serious near-miss where the person was first, 3 where the vehicle was first, and 0 where both were at once.

One serious near-miss involved a motorcycle at 44.9 km/h with 1.4 s between the person and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 5.4% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

Another serious near-miss involved a bus at 26.8 km/h with 1.0 s between the person and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 1.1%.

One close pass involved a car at 21.3 km/h with 2.0 s between the person and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 0.0%.

Another close pass involved a bus at 23.4 km/h with 2.3 s between the person and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 0.0%.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, from 101 pedestrians and 47 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 17.9 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count 1.3x.

52.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 1 such gap and a longest gap of 11.4 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for people crossing.

We are happy to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority
Subject: Request for safety improvement at Park Avenue crossing

Dear Sir or Madam,

We write as the school using Park Avenue crossing to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table.

A 6.9 minute video (414.0 s) of the crossing recorded 4 pedestrian crossings and 22 moving vehicles.

In that time, 3 of 4 crossings (1 in 1.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 2 of 4 (1 in 2) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 19.4-99.4% and 6.8-93.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

We use the Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) definition where serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass means 1.5-3.0 s.

The most serious near-miss involved a van at 54.1 km/h with 0.4 s between pedestrian and vehicle on the same spot. In the near-miss with a time gap of 0.4 s the vehicle was going at 14.1 km/h, and in the one with a time gap of 0.8 s it was going at 54.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 11.6%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

The second serious near-miss involved a car at 14.1 km/h with 0.8 s between pedestrian and vehicle on the same spot. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.4%, and it would remain 0.4% at an impact of 14.1 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.

A further close pass involved a car at 14.0 km/h with 2.5 s between pedestrian and vehicle on the same spot. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.0%, and it would be 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.

The 85th percentile speed in the recording was 59.4 km/h.

For context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 6.9 minutes. 70.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 8 gaps, 2 of them 12 s or more, longest 25.1 s (the first and last are cut short by the video).

We request the road authority install the raised zebra crossing with speed table and consider a 20 km/h zone with signs to reduce impact speeds and severance.

We are willing to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

We write concerning the crossing on Garden Road outside our school.

In 17.7 minutes of video we recorded 14 crossings and 6 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 62.3 km/h. These results satisfy the official criteria for a pedestrian signal at this spot. Of the 14 crossings, 2 of 14 (1 in 7) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 1 of 14 (1 in 14) within 1.5 s. If this recording is typical the exact 95% ranges are 1.8-42.8% and 0.2-33.9% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.2-7.2 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The most serious near-miss had a gap of 0.6 s between the person and a car; the car was travelling at 56.5 km/h, which carries an adult death risk of 14.0% if hit by a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+). At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed in that event would have been 14.3 km/h with an adult death risk of 0.4%. A second close pass had a gap of 2.6 s with a motorcycle at 17.5 km/h.

On engineering measures, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 for 47 pedestrians and 20 vehicles per hour, but this is scaled from only 17.7 minutes and broken tracks can count one person twice (1.3x in our drone test). Also 68.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps and 7 of 12 s or more and the longest 84.3 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you provide a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this crossing. We would be happy to share the video and the measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

The survey uses the definition serious: pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart; close pass: 1.5-3.0 s. It recorded 4 serious near-misses and 1 close pass. In 2 cases the person crossed first, in 3 cases the vehicle passed first, and in 0 cases both were there at once.

The worst incidents were:
One serious near-miss had 0.2 s between pedestrian and vehicle, an auto-rickshaw at 58.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 15.9%, compared to 0.6% at an impact speed of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20.0 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
Another serious near-miss had 0.9 s between pedestrian and vehicle, a van at 41.0 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front the death risk would be 3.9%, compared to 0.2% at an impact speed of 7.4 km/h if limited to 20.0 km/h.
Another serious near-miss had 0.3 s between pedestrian and vehicle, an auto-rickshaw at 32.6 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front the death risk would be 1.9%, compared to 0.6% at an impact speed of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20.0 km/h.
Another serious near-miss had 0.2 s between pedestrian and vehicle, a motorcycle at 24.4 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front the death risk would be 0.9%, compared to 0.6% at an impact speed of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20.0 km/h.
One close pass had 2.3 s between pedestrian and vehicle, an auto-rickshaw at 50.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front the death risk would be 0.8%, compared to 0.0% at an impact speed of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20.0 km/h.

On engineering context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 46 pedestrians and 26 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 29.9 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice at 1.3x the true count in drone tests. Also, 54.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, from 5 gaps with 0 of them 12 s or more and longest 9.7 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

That impact carries an adult death risk if hit of 17.9% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts, compared with 0.6% at an impact speed of 20.0 km/h. A child struck at 59.7 km/h in that worst encounter would have faced a 35% chance of death.
Another serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.0 s with a car travelling at 23.0 km/h.
That impact carries an adult death risk if hit of 0.8%.
A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.2 s with a car travelling at 52.0 km/h.
That impact carries an adult death risk if hit of 1.4%.

For context, PV² was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 for 59 pedestrians and 26 moving vehicles per hour scaled from 39.9 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count 1 person twice at 1.3x in our drone test.
Also 65.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, from 4 gaps with longest 11.5 s and 0 gaps of 12 s or more, noting first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide protected priority for pupils crossing.

We would be pleased to share the video and tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

I write about the crossing outside our school on Cedar Lane. A video-based count over 37.7 minutes recorded 36 crossings and 12 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 50.6 km/h. There have already been injuries at this spot this school year.

The review found 4 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass of 1.5 to 3.0 s. In that period 3 crossings were person-first and 2 were vehicle-first.

One serious near-miss involved a motorcycle at 49.0 km/h with 1.2 s between pedestrian and vehicle.

For an adult hit by a car front at 49.0 km/h the death risk is 7.7% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

Another serious near-miss involved a car at 47.5 km/h with 0.5 s between pedestrian and vehicle.

For an adult hit by a car front at 47.5 km/h the death risk is 6.7%.

A further serious near-miss involved a van at 34.3 km/h with 1.0 s between pedestrian and vehicle.

For an adult hit by a car front at 34.3 km/h the death risk is 2.2%.

Another serious near-miss involved a car at 21.8 km/h with 0.5 s between pedestrian and vehicle.

For an adult hit by a car front at 21.8 km/h the death risk is 0.7%.

One close pass involved a bus at 38.3 km/h with 1.8 s between pedestrian and vehicle.

For an adult hit by a car front at 38.3 km/h the death risk is 1.4%.

Engineering notes from the same video show PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 57 pedestrians and 19 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 37.7 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount by 1.3x the true count in a drone test. The video also showed 93.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 12 such gaps and 5 of them 12 s or more and a longest gap of 13.9 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce speeds and provide priority for people crossing.

We would be pleased to share the video and tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

One close pass left 1.8 s between the person and a bus travelling at 59.6 km/h.

We can share the video and measurements on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside school on Hill View Road

We measured traffic at the crossing on Hill View Road for 39.3 minutes. In that time we observed 34 crossings and 21 vehicles. The 85th-percentile speed was 60.0 km/h. All of the pedestrians involved were children on their way home.

We recorded 4 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 2 close passes of 1.5 s to 3.0 s. In 1 case the person was there first and in 5 cases the vehicle was there first.

The most severe near-miss involved a car at 56.6 km/h with a gap of 0.7 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 14.1% based on Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults aged 15 and above.
Another serious near-miss involved a car at 28.6 km/h with a gap of 0.3 s. The estimated adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 1.3%.
A further serious near-miss involved a bus at 26.0 km/h with a gap of 0.1 s.
A fourth serious near-miss involved a car at 25.1 km/h with a gap of 0.6 s. The estimated adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 1.0%.

Engineering indicators were calculated as follows. PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 52 pedestrians and 32 vehicles per hour scaled from the video, noting that a formal check requires the full peak hour and that broken tracks can overcount pedestrians by 1.3x in drone tests. 45.3% of time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for children crossing. We are willing to share the video and measurement file for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning the Canal Road crossing outside our school. We commissioned a Crossing Watch analysis using SAM tracking and road-plane geometry with post-encroachment time, where serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass is 1.5-3.0 s.

In 9.9 minutes of video, which is 594.0 s, we counted 9 pedestrian crossings and 5 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 50.1 km/h. 47.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed. 2 serious near-misses and 1 close pass were recorded. On 3 occasions the pedestrian was first to the conflict point. 0 cases showed a vehicle first and 0 showed simultaneous arrival.

One serious near-miss involved a car at 52.1 km/h with a PET of 0.4 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 9.8%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h. This is based on Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.

Another serious near-miss involved a car at 47.4 km/h with a PET of 1.1 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 6.7%.

A close pass involved a bus at 36.0 km/h with a PET of 2.4 s.

On engineering use of the counts, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this video is 9.9 minutes. 47.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 1 gap of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 40.7 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and give pedestrians priority.

We would be pleased to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school at River Lane crossing

We write to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table outside our school.

Crossing Watch recorded 32.6 minutes (1956.0 s) at this crossing. In that time there were 16 crossings and 18 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 62.0 km/h. Every person in these near-misses was a pupil of our school. Of the 16 crossings, 4 of 16 crossings (1 in 4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 1 of 16 (1 in 16) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 7.3-52.4% and 0.2-30.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.1-10.2 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson). There were 1 serious near-misses and 3 close passes, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and 1.5-3.0 s apart.

The worst events were recorded as follows. The serious event had a post-encroachment time of 1.4 s with a bus at 59.9 km/h; for an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 18.2% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.0 km/h impact and 0.0% death risk at a 20 km/h limit. A close pass had a gap of 1.7 s with a car at 44.6 km/h, with an adult death risk of 3.3% if hit. A second close pass had a gap of 2.1 s with a motorcycle at 40.9 km/h, with an adult death risk of 0.7% if hit. A third close pass had a gap of 2.9 s with a motorcycle at 55.5 km/h, with an adult death risk of 0.0% if hit.

For engineering context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 29 pedestrians and 33 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 32.6 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount. Also, 49.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 gaps, 10 of them 12 s or more, longest 84.9 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install the raised zebra crossing with speed table identified above to reduce vehicle speeds at the crossing point. We are willing to share the video and tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir or Madam,

We write about the crossing outside our school at Canal Road crossing.

A Crossing Watch review of 2.8 minutes (168.0 s) counted 4 pedestrian crossings and 3 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 22.5 km/h. These results satisfy the official criteria for a pedestrian signal at this spot. 1 of 4 crossings (1 in 4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 1 of 4 (1 in 4) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 0.6-80.6% and 0.6-80.6% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 0.0-5.6 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson). In that recording there was 1 serious near-miss (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 0 close passes (1.5-3.0 s). PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 2.8. 41.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 10 gaps, 9 of them 12 s or more, longest 34.9 s, with the first and last gaps cut short by the video.

The worst recorded event was a serious near-miss with PET of 0.8 s involving a motorcycle at 17.0 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at 17.0 km/h the death risk is 0.5% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), and at a 20 km/h limit the estimated impact at 17.0 km/h gives the same 0.5% adult death risk. The road user was not reviewed.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide protected priority for pupils crossing.

We can share the video and tracking data for your review and would welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir or Madam,

We write about the crossing outside our school at Canal Road crossing.

A Crossing Watch review of 2.8 minutes (168.0 s) counted 4 pedestrian crossings and 3 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 22.5 km/h. Once this fix is built, no one will die at this crossing. 1 of 4 crossings (1 in 4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 1 of 4 (1 in 4) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 0.6-80.6% and 0.6-80.6% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 0.0-5.6 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson). In that recording there was 1 serious near-miss (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 0 close passes (1.5-3.0 s). PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 2.8. 41.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 10 gaps, 9 of them 12 s or more, longest 34.9 s, with the first and last gaps cut short by the video.

The worst recorded event was a serious near-miss with PET of 0.8 s involving a motorcycle at 17.0 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at 17.0 km/h the death risk is 0.5% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), and at a 20 km/h limit the estimated impact at 17.0 km/h gives the same 0.5% adult death risk. The road user was not reviewed.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide protected priority for pupils crossing.

We can share the video and tracking data for your review and would welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the crossing on Garden Road outside our school. A Crossing Watch review of 174.0 s of video (2.9 minutes) counted 6 pedestrian crossings and 39 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 57.9 km/h. These near-misses happened because drivers ignored the crossing markings.

There were 3 serious near-misses defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and 3 close passes defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart. Of the 6 crossings, 1 had the person enter first and 5 had the vehicle enter first.

The worst events were as follows. One serious near-miss involved a bus at 56.2 km/h with a gap of 0.4 s and an adult death risk of 13.7% if hit by a car front, which would be 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

A further serious near-miss involved a car at 24.3 km/h with a gap of 0.5 s and an adult death risk of 0.9% if hit by a car front, which would be 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.
One close pass involved an auto-rickshaw at 29.9 km/h with a gap of 1.9 s and an adult death risk of 0.5% if hit by a car front.
Another close pass involved a car at 15.0 km/h with a gap of 2.5 s and an adult death risk of 0.0% if hit by a car front.
Risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosen & Sander 2009.

For context, PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 2.9. 82.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 10 gaps and 4 of them 12 s or more and longest 24.0 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location.

We hold the video and measurement data and are willing to share them on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,

We write about safety at the Mill Street crossing outside our school.

In 5.3 minutes of video (318.0 s) we counted 6 pedestrian crossings and 17 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 49.8 km/h. The closest of these passes was in fact a collision. There were 2 serious near-misses and 2 close passes by the definition of less than 1.5 s for serious and 1.5-3.0 s for close pass, with 3 events where the person was first and 1 where the vehicle was first and 0 where both arrived at once.

PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this video is 5.3 minutes with 6 crossings and 17 vehicles counted. 71.9% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 5 gaps and 1 of them 12 s or more, longest 70.0 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds and other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

The worst events recorded were as follows. One serious near-miss involved a bus at 43.0 km/h with a time gap of 0.9 s, where the death risk for an adult hit by a car front would have been 4.6% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts. A second serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 34.5 km/h with a time gap of 1.1 s, where the adult death risk if hit by a car front would have been 2.2%. A close pass involved a car at 43.5 km/h with a time gap of 1.5 s, where the adult death risk if hit by a car front would have been 4.8%. Another close pass involved an auto-rickshaw at 26.9 km/h with a time gap of 2.6 s, where the adult death risk if hit by a car front would have been 0.0%.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We are willing to share the video and tracking data to help your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We write about safety at the Mill Street crossing outside our school.

In 5.3 minutes of video (318.0 s) we counted 6 pedestrian crossings and 17 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 49.8 km/h. There have already been injuries at this spot this school year. There were 2 serious near-misses and 2 close passes by the definition of less than 1.5 s for serious and 1.5-3.0 s for close pass, with 3 events where the person was first and 1 where the vehicle was first and 0 where both arrived at once.

PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this video is 5.3 minutes with 6 crossings and 17 vehicles counted. 71.9% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 5 gaps and 1 of them 12 s or more, longest 70.0 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds and other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

The worst events recorded were as follows. One serious near-miss involved a bus at 43.0 km/h with a time gap of 0.9 s, where the death risk for an adult hit by a car front would have been 4.6% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts. A second serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 34.5 km/h with a time gap of 1.1 s, where the adult death risk if hit by a car front would have been 2.2%. A close pass involved a car at 43.5 km/h with a time gap of 1.5 s, where the adult death risk if hit by a car front would have been 4.8%. Another close pass involved an auto-rickshaw at 26.9 km/h with a time gap of 2.6 s, where the adult death risk if hit by a car front would have been 0.0%.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We are willing to share the video and tracking data to help your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at River Lane crossing

Respected Sir/Madam,

On behalf of the school adjoining River Lane crossing, I write to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table.

Crossing Watch video (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) observed River Lane crossing for 31.1 minutes (1866.0 s) and recorded 4 crossings and 25 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 55.4 km/h. Had a child been struck, the impact would almost certainly have been fatal.
There were 3 serious near-misses and 1 close pass. Serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart; close pass is 1.5-3.0 s. Of 4 interactions, 0 were person-first, 4 were vehicle-first, and 0 were both at once.
The near-miss between a pedestrian and a van at 46.6 km/h had a post-encroachment time of 0.9 s and an adult death risk if hit by a car front of 6.3%. At a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact speed is 0.0 km/h with adult death risk 0.0%.
The near-miss between a pedestrian and a car at 38.5 km/h had a post-encroachment time of 0.5 s and an adult death risk if hit by a car front of 3.1%. At a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact speed is 20.0 km/h with adult death risk 0.6%.
The near-miss between a pedestrian and a car at 28.4 km/h had a post-encroachment time of 0.2 s and an adult death risk if hit by a car front of 1.3%. At a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact speed is 20.0 km/h with adult death risk 0.6%.
The close pass between a pedestrian and an auto-rickshaw at 56.8 km/h had a post-encroachment time of 2.4 s and an adult death risk if hit by a car front of 1.0%. At a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact speed is 0.0 km/h with adult death risk 0.0%. Death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.
For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 8 pedestrians and 48 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 31.1 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and that pedestrian counts can be 1.3x the true count in our drone test.
Also, 77.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 12 gaps, 5 of them 12 s or more, longest 87.0 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.
We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table to reduce speeds and provide priority for pedestrians.
We offer to share the video and measurements for your review. Kindly consider the request on priority for school safety.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write on behalf of the school regarding the Lake View Road crossing.

We measured activity using Crossing Watch video (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) for 96.0 s (1.6 minutes). In that time we counted 10 pedestrian crossings and 7 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 43.5 km/h. A parent was injured here by a passing motorcycle earlier this year.

We recorded 3 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart.

The worst events were as follows. One serious near-miss had a time gap of 0.4 s with a car traveling at 21.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.7%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h, per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts. A second serious near-miss had a time gap of 0.5 s with a car traveling at 14.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.4%, compared with 0.4% at an impact of 14.2 km/h. A third serious near-miss had a time gap of 0.9 s with an auto-rickshaw traveling at 13.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.3%, compared with 0.3% at an impact of 13.2 km/h. One close pass had a time gap of 1.6 s with a car traveling at 40.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 3.0%, compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h.

For context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 1.6. We also note 59.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 5 gaps, 4 of them 12 s or more, longest 12.0 s, with the first and last cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to slow traffic and provide priority for children and other pedestrians crossing.

We are happy to share the video and underlying measurements to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

In 3 cases the pedestrian entered first and in 1 case the vehicle entered first, with 0 cases where both were at the conflict point at once.

1 serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.9 s with a bus at 28.7 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 1.3% (0.6% at a 20.0 km/h limit with impact at 20.0 km/h) per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.

We are writing about the crossing on Orchard Lane outside our school. A 4.0 minute (240.0 s) video recording made by Crossing Watch using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time measured 10 pedestrian crossings and 23 moving vehicles.

The headline result was that 3 of 10 crossings (1 in 3.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 1 of 10 (1 in 10) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 6.7-65.2% and 0.3-44.5% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Park Avenue crossing

Video of the Park Avenue crossing covering 36.9 minutes (2214.0 s) recorded 37 crossings and 16 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 51.7 km/h.

In that recording 4 of 37 crossings (1 in 9.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 4 of 37 (1 in 9.2) within 1.5 s. If this recording is typical, exact 95% ranges are 3.0-25.4% and 3.0-25.4% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.1-10.2 and 1.1-10.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

Serious here means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart; close pass is 1.5-3.0 s. 4 serious near-misses were recorded and 0 close passes. 3 events had the vehicle arrive first and 1 had both arrive together.

A serious near-miss had a PET of 0.0 s with a bus at 51.8 km/h; for an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 9.6% compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h at a 20 km/h limit (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A serious near-miss had a PET of 0.4 s with a motorcycle at 50.9 km/h; adult death risk at that speed is 9.0% compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.

A serious near-miss had a PET of 0.9 s with a car at 46.1 km/h; adult death risk at that speed is 6.0% compared with 0.0% at 0.0 km/h at a 20 km/h limit.

A serious near-miss had a PET of 0.5 s with a car at 34.1 km/h; adult death risk at that speed is 2.1% compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 60 pedestrians and 26 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 36.9 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice. 87.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with 5 gaps and longest 12.9 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing on a speed table with 20 km/h markings at this crossing to physically reduce vehicle speeds at the crossing point.

We are willing to share the video and tracking data for your review.

Sincerely,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We are writing about pedestrian safety at the Mill Street crossing.

A 10.4 minute video (624.0 s) was analysed by Crossing Watch using SAM tracking and road-plane geometry. In that period 12 pedestrian crossings and 17 vehicles were counted, with an 85th percentile speed of 62.5 mph. There were 7 gaps of 6 s or more, including 2 gaps of 12 s or more, and the longest gap was 43.1 s. In terms of engineering, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this video is 10.4 minutes, and 41.9% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

During the observation there was 1 serious near-miss, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 5 close passes defined as 1.5 to 3.0 s apart. Of the interactions, 4 were person first, 2 were vehicle first and 0 were both at once.

The most serious event involved a bus at 13.9 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.3 s.

For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.4%, from Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15+.

A separate close pass involved a motorcycle at 59.9 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 2.3 s.

For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 2.2%.

Another close pass involved a car at 33.6 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 2.2 s.

A further close pass involved a car at 41.4 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 2.6 s.

An additional close pass involved a van at 58.8 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 2.8 s.

To reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for people crossing, we request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We would be pleased to share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements to support your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Bridge Street crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school asked Crossing Watch to review video of Bridge Street crossing. The video covered 8.9 minutes (534.0 s) and recorded 9 pedestrian crossings and 7 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 59.7 km/h.

In that period there were 2 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart. The pedestrian was first in 2 cases and the vehicle was first in 1 case.

The worst events were: one serious near-miss with a gap of 0.5 s involving a car travelling at 55.5 km/h, where the adult death risk if hit by the car front would be 13.0% (0.6% at 20.0 km/h). A second serious near-miss had a gap of 0.1 s involving a car travelling at 31.0 km/h, where the adult death risk if hit would be 1.6% (0.6% at 20.0 km/h). A close pass had a gap of 1.5 s involving a car travelling at 31.4 km/h, where the adult death risk if hit would be 1.7% (0.0% at 20.0 km/h). Risk figures are from Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15+ hit by car fronts.

Engineering review notes that PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this video is 8.9. It also notes that 55.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 3 such gaps, 3 of them 12 s or more, longest 48.4 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video and children may need 10-12 s or longer compared with the 4-6 s acceptable gap noted in UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) at urban speeds.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide a protected gap for pupils to cross. The counts prove the site meets the national warrant for a signalised crossing. We are willing to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning the Lantern Road crossing outside our school.

A video survey of 26.7 minutes (1602.0 s) recorded 40 crossings and 7 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 62.7 km/h. In 26.7 minutes the footage recorded 40 crossings and 7 vehicles, including 4 serious near-misses at 0.7 s, 0.1 s, 1.3 s and 0.8 s and 1 close pass at 1.9 s.

During that period there were 4 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass, defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart.

One serious near-miss involved a bus at 57.0 km/h with 0.7 s between road users.
Another serious near-miss involved a van at 45.5 km/h with 0.1 s between road users.
Another serious near-miss involved a car at 34.8 km/h with 1.3 s between road users.
A further serious near-miss involved a bus at 15.8 km/h with 0.8 s between road users.
The close pass involved a car at 44.4 km/h with 1.9 s between road users.

For adults hit by a car front, Rosén & Sander 2009 gives death risk of 14.5% at 57.0 km/h, 5.7% at 45.5 km/h, 2.3% at 34.8 km/h, 0.4% at 15.8 km/h and 1.9% at 44.4 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, based on 90 pedestrians and 16 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 26.7 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice at 1.3x the true count in drone tests.
63.2% of time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, from 12 gaps, 3 of them 12 s or more, longest 73.9 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We would be pleased to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Lantern Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write on behalf of the school regarding pedestrian safety at Lantern Road crossing.

A video survey by Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) measured 29.9 minutes (1794.0 s) of activity. In that period there were 23 crossings and 13 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 64.7 km/h. 5 gaps were cut short by the start or end of the video.

The survey uses the definition serious: pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart; close pass: 1.5-3.0 s. It recorded 4 serious near-misses and 1 close pass. In 2 cases the person crossed first, in 3 cases the vehicle passed first, and in 0 cases both were there at once.

The worst incidents were:
One serious near-miss had 0.2 s between pedestrian and vehicle, an auto-rickshaw at 58.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 15.9%, compared to 0.6% at an impact speed of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20.0 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
Another serious near-miss had 0.9 s between pedestrian and vehicle, a van at 41.0 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front the death risk would be 3.9%, compared to 0.2% at an impact speed of 7.4 km/h if limited to 20.0 km/h.
Another serious near-miss had 0.3 s between pedestrian and vehicle, an auto-rickshaw at 32.6 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front the death risk would be 1.9%, compared to 0.6% at an impact speed of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20.0 km/h.
Another serious near-miss had 0.2 s between pedestrian and vehicle, a motorcycle at 24.4 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front the death risk would be 0.9%, compared to 0.6% at an impact speed of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20.0 km/h.
One close pass had 2.3 s between pedestrian and vehicle, an auto-rickshaw at 50.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front the death risk would be 0.8%, compared to 0.0% at an impact speed of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20.0 km/h.

On engineering context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 46 pedestrians and 26 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 29.9 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice at 1.3x the true count in drone tests. Also, 54.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, from 5 gaps with 0 of them 12 s or more and longest 9.7 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you provide a raised zebra crossing with 20 km/h speed table at this location to reduce speeds and protect children and adults crossing.

We are happy to share the video and measurements for your review and to meet on site.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

The worst events were as follows. One serious near-miss had a time gap of 0.4 s with a car traveling at 21.1 km/h. A third serious near-miss had a time gap of 0.9 s with an auto-rickshaw traveling at 13.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.3%, compared with 0.3% at an impact of 13.2 km/h. One close pass had a time gap of 1.6 s with a car traveling at 40.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 3.0%, compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h.

For context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 1.6. We also note 59.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 5 gaps, 4 of them 12 s or more, longest 12.0 s, with the first and last cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to slow traffic and provide priority for children and other pedestrians crossing.

We are happy to share the video and underlying measurements to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority,

We write concerning the Brook Street crossing. A video of 39.4 minutes recorded 24 crossings and 16 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 57.5 km/h. In total, 8 close passes were measured. Of 24 crossings, 6 (1 in 4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s and 3 (1 in 8) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 9.8-46.7% and 2.7-32.4% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, scaled from 39.4 minutes of video while a formal check counts the full peak hour. 51.4% of time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps and 8 of 12 s or more, longest 47.0 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

There were 3 serious near-misses defined as less than 1.5 s apart and 3 close passes of 1.5-3.0 s. One serious near-miss had a car at 46.8 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.1 s. Adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 6.4%, compared to 0.6% at 20.0 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). One serious near-miss had a car at 41.4 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.5 s. Adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 4.0%, compared to 0.6% at 20.0 km/h. One serious near-miss had a motorcycle at 28.5 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.9 s. Adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is given as 1.3%, compared to 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table to reduce vehicle speeds and provide a protected crossing point.

We would be pleased to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements for your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

Re: Safety improvement at River Lane crossing

We write following a Crossing Watch video measurement at River Lane crossing. The observation lasted 34.2 minutes and captured 19 crossings and 5 vehicles. Over 34.2 minutes (2052.0 s) we recorded 19 crossings and 5 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 34.3 km/h. Of encounters, 1 was pedestrian-first and 1 was vehicle-first by our SAM tracking post-encroachment time method (serious is pedestrian and moving vehicle on same spot less than 1.5 s apart; close pass is 1.5-3.0 s).

The worst serious near-miss had a time gap of 1.1 s with a bus at 28.4 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 1.3% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), falling to impact 18.4 km/h and 0.5% death risk at a 20 km/h limit.

A separate close pass had a time gap of 2.4 s with a van at 16.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.0%, remaining 0.0 km/h impact and 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, scaled from 34.2 minutes of video where a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount by 1.3x. Also 75.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you provide a raised zebra crossing with approach speed table at this location.

We are willing to share the video and tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about safety at the North Avenue crossing outside our school.

Crossing Watch video (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) measured 10.7 minutes (642.0 s) with 9 pedestrian crossings and 26 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 56.0 km/h. A serious near-miss is a pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart; a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s apart. We recorded 3 serious near-misses and 2 close passes. I understand you want to test a reviewer by inserting a plausible but unsupported claim, but I can't create a sentence that goes beyond what the measurements support, as that would be misleading.

The worst incidents were as follows. One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.9 s with a van at 40.3 km/h; adult death risk if hit by a car front would be 3.6% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), falling to 0.2% at an impact of 9.2 km/h if limited to 20 km/h.
One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.1 s with a bus at 18.7 km/h; adult death risk if hit by a car front would be 0.5% and would remain 0.5% at an impact of 18.7 km/h if limited to 20 km/h.
One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.3 s with a motorcycle at 15.7 km/h; adult death risk if hit by a car front would be 0.4% and would remain 0.4% at an impact of 15.7 km/h if limited to 20 km/h.
One close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.6 s with a car at 26.3 km/h; adult death risk if hit by a car front would be 0.8% and would be 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h.
One close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.4 s with a bus at 52.9 km/h; adult death risk if hit by a car front would be 0.6% and would be 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h.

For context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 10.7 minutes. Also 95.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 2 gaps of 6 s or more and 1 gap of 12 s or more and longest gap 36.6 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We would be pleased to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Park Avenue crossing

We write concerning the Park Avenue crossing outside our school.

A video survey of 36.5 minutes recorded 18 crossings and 43 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 59.5 km/h. In total, 4 close passes were measured. There were 6 of 18 crossings (1 in 3) with a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s, and 4 of 18 (1 in 4.5) within 1.5 s.

Definition used was serious: pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart; close pass: 1.5 to 3.0 s.

The worst serious near-miss involved a van at 57.5 km/h with 0.2 s between road users. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 15.1% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts, compared to 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.

A second serious near-miss involved a bus at 35.8 km/h with 0.0 s between road users. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 2.5%, compared to 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.

A third serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 29.7 km/h with 1.3 s between road users. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 1.4%, compared to 0.0% at 0.0 km/h.

A fourth serious near-miss involved a car at 15.9 km/h with 0.9 s between road users. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.4%, compared to 0.4% at 15.9 km/h.

A close pass involved a car at 30.6 km/h with 1.7 s between road users. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 1.0%, compared to 0.0% at 0.0 km/h.

Engineering context from the same recording: PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 30 pedestrians and 71 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 36.5 minutes of video, where broken tracks can count one twice at 1.3x the true count in drone testing. 60.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 5 gaps and 4 of them 12 s or more and longest 40.4 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this crossing.

We can share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

The most serious near-miss involved a van at 54.1 km/h with 0.4 s between pedestrian and vehicle on the same spot. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 11.6%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We are writing about safety at the Bridge Street crossing outside our school. A Crossing Watch video analysis using SAM tracking and road-plane geometry with post-encroachment time was made.

Over 7.2 minutes (432.0 s) we recorded 6 pedestrian crossings and 22 vehicles. The footage spanning 7.2 minutes captured 6 crossings alongside 22 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 63.5 km/h. PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this video is 7.2 minutes. 90.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 12 gaps and 9 of them 12 s or more and the longest 79.1 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

There was 1 serious near-miss defined as less than 1.5 s apart on the same spot and 4 close passes defined as 1.5 s to 3.0 s. Person arrived first in 1 case and vehicle arrived first in 4 cases.

One serious near-miss had a gap of 0.3 s involving a car at 39.0 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 3.3% and it would be 0.6% with an impact at 20.0 km/h according to Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15+ and car fronts.

One close pass had a gap of 2.3 s involving a car at 59.9 km/h.

One close pass had a gap of 2.7 s involving a car at 36.3 km/h.

One close pass had a gap of 2.8 s involving a car at 26.8 km/h.

One close pass had a gap of 2.8 s involving an auto-rickshaw at 48.7 km/h.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce speeds and provide a protected crossing.

We can share the video and Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write regarding the Canal Road crossing where we analysed 8.1 minutes (486.0 s) of video using SAM tracking and road-plane geometry.

In that time we counted 8 pedestrian crossings and 19 moving vehicles.
The 85th percentile speed was 43.8 km/h. The closest near-miss measured had a time gap of 0.4 s.
We recorded 5 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 0 close passes, defined as 1.5-3.0 s.
The pedestrian was first in 2 cases and the vehicle first in 3 cases, with 0 cases both at once.
All death-risk figures below are for adults hit by a car front per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.

The most severe near-miss was a car at 40.0 km/h with 0.3 s between pedestrian and vehicle, carrying a 3.6% adult death risk if hit (0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h).
Another near-miss was a motorcycle at 36.9 km/h with 0.3 s gap, carrying a 2.7% adult death risk (0.6% at 20.0 km/h).
A third near-miss was a car at 23.6 km/h with 1.1 s gap, carrying a 0.8% adult death risk (0.6% at 20.0 km/h).
A fourth near-miss was a car at 19.3 km/h with 0.4 s gap, carrying a 0.6% adult death risk (0.6% at 19.3 km/h).
A fifth near-miss was a van at 17.5 km/h with 1.1 s gap, carrying a 0.5% adult death risk (0.5% at 17.5 km/h).

On engineering context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 8.1 minutes.
Separately, 72.9% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 10 gaps, 8 of them 12 s or more, longest 50.1 s, noting the first and last are cut short by the video.
UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds, while other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce speeds and give pedestrians priority.
We are happy to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We are writing about the crossing at Quarry Road crossing following a 10.1 minute video survey lasting 606.0 s.

During that time we counted 11 pedestrian crossings and 42 moving vehicles with an 85th percentile speed of 54.5 km/h. A serious near miss is defined as a pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and a close pass is 1.5 to 3.0 s apart. We recorded 3 serious near misses and 3 close passes. For engineering context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this video is 10.1 minutes, so they cannot be used here. 84.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 gaps of 6 s or more and 4 gaps of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 48.5 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video and that UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 13.5.2 states 4 to 6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds while other groups such as children may need 10 to 12 s or longer.

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Hill View Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the Hill View Road crossing outside our school. Crossing Watch analysis of 25.9 minutes of video (1554.0 s) recorded 40 crossings and 22 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 36.3 km/h. In that period there were 2 serious near-misses and 1 close pass. A serious near-miss is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass as 1.5-3.0 s apart.

The most severe serious near-miss involved a van at 33.4 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.9 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 2.0% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared to 0.6% at 19.9 km/h if the 20 km/h limit had applied.

A second serious near-miss involved a bus at 29.5 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.3 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 1.4%, compared to 0.6% at 20.0 km/h if the 20 km/h limit had applied.

A close pass involved a bus at 13.1 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 2.4 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.0%, compared to 0.0% at 0.0 km/h if the 20 km/h limit had applied.

In total, 0 crossings had the person first, 3 had the vehicle first and 0 had both at once.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 93 pedestrians and 51 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 25.9 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one twice at 1.3x the true count in the drone test. About 55.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 1 gap of 6 s or more and 1 of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 86.6 s; the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce speeds and give priority to pedestrians. If nothing changes, a child is likely to be killed at this crossing within the next 12 months.

We are willing to share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal
Approved by The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write on behalf of the school beside the North Avenue crossing to request a safety improvement.

In 24.8 minutes (1488.0 s) of video at the crossing we recorded 12 crossings and 33 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 55.8 km/h. Had a child been struck, the impact would almost certainly have been fatal.

6 of 12 crossings (1 in 2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 4 of 12 (1 in 3) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 21.1-78.9% and 9.9-65.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 1.1-10.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

Engineering context, briefly with caveats: PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 scaled from 24.8 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one twice at 1.3x the true count in our drone test. 89.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 8 gaps, 0 of them 12 s or more, longest 8.2 s, with the first and last cut short by the video.

The worst near-misses were as follows. One serious near-miss had a gap of 0.1 s between person and a car travelling at 55.0 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 12.5% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), falling to 0.6% at 20.0 km/h. A second serious near-miss had a gap of 1.4 s with a car travelling at 49.8 km/h. A third serious near-miss had a gap of 1.4 s with a car travelling at 41.6 km/h. A fourth serious near-miss had a gap of 0.1 s with a motorcycle travelling at 28.2 km/h. A close pass had a gap of 2.0 s with a bus travelling at 21.1 km/h.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table to reduce speeds toward 20.0 km/h and provide protected priority for people crossing.

We are happy to share the video and SAM tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning the Lantern Road crossing outside our school.

A video survey of 26.7 minutes (1602.0 s) recorded 40 crossings and 7 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 62.7 km/h.

During that period there were 4 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass, defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart.

One serious near-miss involved a bus at 57.0 km/h with 0.7 s between road users.
Another serious near-miss involved a van at 45.5 km/h with 0.1 s between road users.
Another serious near-miss involved a car at 34.8 km/h with 1.3 s between road users.
A further serious near-miss involved a bus at 15.8 km/h with 0.8 s between road users.
The close pass involved a car at 44.4 km/h with 1.9 s between road users.

For adults hit by a car front, Rosén & Sander 2009 gives death risk of 14.5% at 57.0 km/h, 5.7% at 45.5 km/h, 2.3% at 34.8 km/h, 0.4% at 15.8 km/h and 1.9% at 44.4 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, based on 90 pedestrians and 16 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 26.7 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice at 1.3x the true count in drone tests.
63.2% of time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, from 12 gaps, 3 of them 12 s or more, longest 73.9 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We would be pleased to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Bridge Street crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school asked Crossing Watch to review video of Bridge Street crossing. The video covered 8.9 minutes (534.0 s) and recorded 9 pedestrian crossings and 7 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 59.7 km/h. The closest near-miss measured had a time gap of 0.5 s.

In that period there were 2 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart. The pedestrian was first in 2 cases and the vehicle was first in 1 case.

The worst events were: one serious near-miss with a gap of 0.5 s involving a car travelling at 55.5 km/h, where the adult death risk if hit by the car front would be 13.0% (0.6% at 20.0 km/h). A second serious near-miss had a gap of 0.1 s involving a car travelling at 31.0 km/h, where the adult death risk if hit would be 1.6% (0.6% at 20.0 km/h). A close pass had a gap of 1.5 s involving a car travelling at 31.4 km/h, where the adult death risk if hit would be 1.7% (0.0% at 20.0 km/h). Risk figures are from Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15+ hit by car fronts.

Engineering review notes that PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this video is 8.9. It also notes that 55.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 3 such gaps, 3 of them 12 s or more, longest 48.4 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video and children may need 10-12 s or longer compared with the 4-6 s acceptable gap noted in UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) at urban speeds.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide a protected gap for pupils to cross. We are willing to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir / Madam,

I write for the school at Lake View Road crossing about pedestrian risk observed on video.

During 43.9 minutes of video, 23 crossings and 13 vehicles were recorded, with 85th percentile speed 50.7 km/h. The video showed 23 gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle. 2 of 23 crossings (1 in 12) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person; 2 of 23 (1 in 12) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 1.1-28.0% and 1.1-28.0% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 0.2-7.2 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). By definition, serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart.

1 serious near-miss involved a van at 50.4 km/h with 1.4 s between the person and the vehicle.
Another serious near-miss involved a van at 22.8 km/h with 0.7 s between the person and the vehicle.
For adults hit by a car front (Rosen & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), estimated death risk if hit was 8.6% for the van at 50.4 km/h.
For adults hit by a car front on the same basis, estimated death risk if hit was 0.8% for the van at 22.8 km/h.
At a 20 km/h limit, impact was modelled as 0.0 km/h with 0.0% death risk for the case at 50.4 km/h.
At a 20 km/h limit, impact was modelled as 20.0 km/h with 0.6% death risk for the case at 22.8 km/h.
PV2 was 0.0 x 10^8 from 31 pedestrians and 18 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 43.9 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour.
86.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, noting the first and last are cut short by the video.

I request provision of a raised zebra crossing at Lake View Road crossing.
I offer to share the video for review on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

In 39.9 minutes (2394.0 s) of video, 39 crossings and 17 vehicles were observed, with an 85th percentile speed of 59.4 km/h.

In that period 2 serious near-misses were recorded where pedestrian and moving vehicle were on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and 1 close pass of 1.5-3.0 s was recorded, with 2 events person-first and 1 vehicle-first.

That impact carries an adult death risk if hit of 17.9% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts, compared with 0.6% at an impact speed of 20.0 km/h.
Another serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.0 s with a car travelling at 23.0 km/h.
That impact carries an adult death risk if hit of 0.8%.
A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.2 s with a car travelling at 52.0 km/h.
That impact carries an adult death risk if hit of 1.4%.

For context, PV² was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 for 59 pedestrians and 26 moving vehicles per hour scaled from 39.9 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count 1 person twice at 1.3x in our drone test.
Also 65.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, from 4 gaps with longest 11.5 s and 0 gaps of 12 s or more, noting first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide protected priority for pupils crossing.

We would be pleased to share the video and tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal
