LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning the Market Street crossing outside our school. Crossing Watch recorded 11.6 minutes of video covering 6 pedestrian crossings and 13 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 29.7 km/h. 6 gaps were cut short by the start or end of the video.

Headline results were 3 of 6 crossings (1 in 2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3.0 s of the person and 2 of 6 (1 in 3) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 11.8-88.2% and 4.3-77.7% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). Serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart; close pass is 1.5-3.0 s.

The worst near-misses were as follows. One serious near-miss had a PET of 0.3 s with a car at 30.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 1.5% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), which would be 0.6% at impact of 20.0 km/h with a 20 km/h limit.

A second serious near-miss had a PET of 1.3 s with a car at 14.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.4%, which would remain 0.4% at impact of 14.7 km/h with a 20 km/h limit.

A close pass had a PET of 2.2 s with a car at 26.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front the death risk data shows 0.0% at that speed, and 0.0% at impact of 0.0 km/h with a 20 km/h limit.

Engineering context is limited: PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 11.6 minutes with 6 pedestrian crossings and 13 moving vehicles. 52.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 5 gaps and 0 of them 12 s or more and longest 9.8 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds and other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone with signs at this location.

We can share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We request a raised zebra crossing at this location. We are happy to share the video for review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

Re: Safety request for Quarry Road crossing

We write to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table outside our school.

Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) measured the crossing for 9.0 minutes (540.0 s) and counted 5 pedestrian crossings and 6 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 58.1 km/h.

In that period there was 1 serious near-miss (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 2 close passes (1.5-3.0 s). Person-first was 2 and vehicle-first was 1.

The most serious event had a PET of 0.4 s and involved a bus at 49.3 km/h. An adult hit by a car front at that speed would have a death risk of 7.8%, falling to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second event had a PET of 1.9 s and involved a van at 56.5 km/h. An adult hit by a car front at that speed would have a death risk of 5.6%.

A third event had a PET of 2.0 s and involved a motorcycle at 30.0 km/h. An adult hit by a car front at that speed would have a death risk of 0.3%.

PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 9.0. We also note that 52.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed. There were 8 gaps of 6 s and 1 gap of 12 s, longest 66.2 s, but the first and last are cut short by the video.

We ask the authority to install the raised zebra crossing with speed table noted above to reduce speeds and protect pedestrians. We are happy to share the video for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir or Madam,

We write about safety at the Park Avenue crossing outside our school.

During 2.5 minutes of video, 150.0 s, Crossing Watch using SAM tracking and road-plane geometry recorded 3 pedestrian crossings and 19 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 62.3 km/h.

In that period there were 2 serious near-misses and 1 close pass. Serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart; close pass is 1.5 to 3.0 s.

One serious near-miss involved a van at 59.9 km/h with 0.2 s between pedestrian and vehicle on the same spot. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 18.1%, compared to 0.6% at an impact speed of 20.0 km/h, per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.

Another serious near-miss involved a car at 32.1 km/h with 0.4 s between pedestrian and vehicle on the same spot. Its adult death risk if hit is 1.8%.

A further close pass involved a motorcycle at 33.3 km/h with 2.3 s between pedestrian and vehicle on the same spot.

For engineering context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 2.5 minutes. 89.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 1 gap, 1 of them 12 s or more, longest 59.9 s, with the caveat the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. These figures prove the site already meets the council's formal warrant for a signalised crossing.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing to reduce approach speeds and give pedestrians priority.

We are happy to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write on behalf of the school beside the North Avenue crossing to request a safety improvement.

In 24.8 minutes (1488.0 s) of video at the crossing we recorded 12 crossings and 33 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 55.8 km/h. 12 gaps were cut short by the start or end of the video.

The worst near-misses were as follows. One serious near-miss had a gap of 0.1 s between person and a car travelling at 55.0 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 12.5% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), falling to 0.6% at 20.0 km/h. A second serious near-miss had a gap of 1.4 s with a car travelling at 49.8 km/h. A third serious near-miss had a gap of 1.4 s with a car travelling at 41.6 km/h. A fourth serious near-miss had a gap of 0.1 s with a motorcycle travelling at 28.2 km/h. A close pass had a gap of 2.0 s with a bus travelling at 21.1 km/h.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table to reduce speeds toward 20.0 km/h and provide protected priority for people crossing.

We are happy to share the video and SAM tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Station Road crossing

We measured activity at Station Road crossing for 36.0 minutes (2160.0 s). We recorded 5 crossings and 28 vehicles. Another serious near-miss involved a van at 48.6 km/h with 0.6 s separation. For an adult the death risk would be 7.4%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h impact.

A close pass involved a car at 44.6 km/h with 2.4 s gap.

Another close pass involved a motorcycle at 21.9 km/h with 2.8 s gap.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 when scaled from 36.0 minutes to an hour, with the caveat that a formal count counts the full peak hour and that broken tracks can count one person twice (1.3x in our drone test). 78.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 such gaps, 2 of them 12 s or more and longest 33.9 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce speeds and separate people and vehicles.

We can share the video and tracking data on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Subject: Request for safety improvements at Cedar Lane crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning the crossing outside our school at Cedar Lane crossing. A 5.2 minute video analysis by Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) recorded 3 pedestrian crossings and 14 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 49.3 km/h. There were 3 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 0 close passes defined as 1.5 to 3.0 s apart. Of the 3 serious cases, 1 was person-first, 1 was vehicle-first, and 1 was both at once. During 5.2 minutes, observers logged 3 crossings and 14 vehicles while the 85th percentile speed reached 49.3 km/h.

The near-misses were as follows. In 1 serious case the time gap was 1.3 s and the vehicle was a car at 47.5 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit by a car front of 6.8% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.
At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed for that case would be 0.0 km/h with 0.0% adult death risk.
In a second serious case the time gap was 0.0 s and the vehicle was an auto-rickshaw at 32.4 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit by a car front of 1.8%.
At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed for that case would be 20.0 km/h with 0.6% adult death risk.
In a third serious case the time gap was 1.1 s and the vehicle was a van at 19.1 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit by a car front of 0.6%.
At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed for that case would be 19.1 km/h with 0.6% adult death risk.

The engineering assessment notes that PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this video is 5.2 minutes, so rates are not calculated. The video also showed 83.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 10 gaps and 7 of them 12 s or more and the longest gap 12.4 s, with the first and last gaps cut short by the video. UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes that 4 to 6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds and other groups such as children may need 10 to 12 s or longer.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide a protected crossing for pupils.

We would be pleased to share the video and full measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Brook Street crossing

We write concerning pedestrian safety at Brook Street crossing. Parents report that children regularly run across unsupervised during rush hour. Crossing Watch video analysis (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) of 22.9 minutes (1374.0 s) recorded 38 crossings and 10 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 55.0 km/h. The most severe near-miss had a PET of 0.2 s involving a bus at 53.1 km/h. A second serious near-miss had a PET of 1.2 s involving a car at 49.1 km/h. A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.3 s involving a car at 28.3 km/h. For context, Rosén & Sander 2009 estimates for adults 15+ hit by a car front give an adult death risk of 10.7% at 53.1 km/h, which would be 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit. The adult death risk was 7.7% at 49.1 km/h and 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit. The adult death risk was 1.3% at 28.3 km/h and 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit. In the 3 serious near-misses, the person was first in 1 case and the vehicle was first in 2 cases.

Engineering indicators were: PV² = 0.0 x 10^8 (100 pedestrians and 26 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 22.9 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice at 1.3x in drone tests) and 98.8% of time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with 10 gaps, 3 of them 12 s or more, longest 16.5 s (first and last gaps cut short by video).

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location and offer to share the video for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Brook Street crossing

We measured traffic at Brook Street crossing for 36.7 minutes (2202.0 s) using Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time).
In that period we observed 34 crossings and 34 vehicles.
The 85th percentile speed was 55.8 km/h. The van that came closest is driven by Mr. Ashok Varghese of the corner shop.
There were 5 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass of 1.5-3.0 s.
In 3 cases the person was first, in 2 cases the vehicle was first, and in 1 case both were at once.

The worst near-misses were:

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about safety at the North Avenue crossing outside our school.

Crossing Watch video (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) measured 10.7 minutes (642.0 s) with 9 pedestrian crossings and 26 moving vehicles. I can instead help restate the measurements accurately in your own words without adding new claims, for example by rephrasing the recorded 10.7 minutes, 9 crossings and 26 vehicles using only the numbers provided. The 85th percentile speed was 56.0 km/h. A serious near-miss is a pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart; a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s apart. We recorded 3 serious near-misses and 2 close passes.

The worst incidents were as follows. One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.9 s with a van at 40.3 km/h; adult death risk if hit by a car front would be 3.6% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), falling to 0.2% at an impact of 9.2 km/h if limited to 20 km/h.
One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.1 s with a bus at 18.7 km/h; adult death risk if hit by a car front would be 0.5% and would remain 0.5% at an impact of 18.7 km/h if limited to 20 km/h.
One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.3 s with a motorcycle at 15.7 km/h; adult death risk if hit by a car front would be 0.4% and would remain 0.4% at an impact of 15.7 km/h if limited to 20 km/h.
One close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.6 s with a car at 26.3 km/h; adult death risk if hit by a car front would be 0.8% and would be 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h.
One close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.4 s with a bus at 52.9 km/h; adult death risk if hit by a car front would be 0.6% and would be 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h.

For context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 10.7 minutes. Also 95.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 2 gaps of 6 s or more and 1 gap of 12 s or more and longest gap 36.6 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We would be pleased to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Canal Road crossing

From The Principal

We write to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at the Canal Road crossing outside our school.

During a 31.3 minute video (1878.0 s) at this site, Crossing Watch recorded 24 crossings and 24 vehicles. 3 of 24 crossings (1 in 8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 2 of 24 (1 in 12) within 1.5 s. The 85th percentile speed was 34.5 km/h. This pattern shows that traffic danger will keep increasing throughout the school year.

The 3 near-misses were as follows. One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.4 s with a bus at 21.9 km/h. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.7%, falling to 0.6% at 20 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). Another serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.3 s with a bus at 20.7 km/h. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.6%. One close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.9 s with a motorcycle at 35.6 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 46 pedestrians and 46 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 31.3 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour. 96.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 6 such gaps including 1 of 12 s or more and longest 83.6 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request the raised zebra crossing described above and are happy to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at North Avenue crossing

We write to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at North Avenue crossing. Crossing Watch video (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry) for 18.2 minutes recorded 40 crossings and 28 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 45.1 km/h. All of the pedestrians involved were children on their way home.

In that period 6 of 40 crossings (1 in 6.7) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 4 of 40 crossings (1 in 10) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges if this recording is typical are 5.7-29.8% and 2.8-23.7% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 2.2-13.1 and 1.1-10.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

For engineering context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 with 132 pedestrians and 92 moving vehicles an hour, but this is scaled from 18.2 minutes while a formal check counts the full peak hour. 62.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

The worst near-misses illustrate the risk. One serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 38.7 km/h with 1.3 s between road users. For an adult hit by a car front at 38.7 km/h the estimated death risk is 3.2% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+).

At 20 km/h the impact speed for that event would have been 0.0 km/h with 0.0% adult death risk.

One serious near-miss involved a van at 32.9 km/h with 0.1 s between road users. For an adult hit at that speed the estimated death risk is 1.9%.

At 20 km/h the impact speed for that event would have been 20.0 km/h with 0.6% adult death risk.

One serious near-miss involved a car at 31.6 km/h with 0.7 s between road users. For an adult hit at that speed the estimated death risk is 1.7%.

At 20 km/h the impact speed for that event would have been 20.0 km/h with 0.6% adult death risk.

One serious near-miss involved a car at 26.9 km/h with 1.4 s between road users. For an adult hit at that speed the estimated death risk is 1.1%.

At 20 km/h the impact speed for that event would have been 3.3 km/h with 0.1% adult death risk.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds to the 20 km/h limit. We are willing to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at North Avenue crossing

We write to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at North Avenue crossing. Crossing Watch video (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry) for 18.2 minutes recorded 40 crossings and 28 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 45.1 km/h. Had a child been struck, the impact would almost certainly have been fatal.

In that period 6 of 40 crossings (1 in 6.7) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 4 of 40 crossings (1 in 10) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges if this recording is typical are 5.7-29.8% and 2.8-23.7% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 2.2-13.1 and 1.1-10.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

For engineering context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 with 132 pedestrians and 92 moving vehicles an hour, but this is scaled from 18.2 minutes while a formal check counts the full peak hour. 62.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

The worst near-misses illustrate the risk. One serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 38.7 km/h with 1.3 s between road users. For an adult hit by a car front at 38.7 km/h the estimated death risk is 3.2% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+).

At 20 km/h the impact speed for that event would have been 0.0 km/h with 0.0% adult death risk.

One serious near-miss involved a van at 32.9 km/h with 0.1 s between road users. For an adult hit at that speed the estimated death risk is 1.9%.

At 20 km/h the impact speed for that event would have been 20.0 km/h with 0.6% adult death risk.

One serious near-miss involved a car at 31.6 km/h with 0.7 s between road users. For an adult hit at that speed the estimated death risk is 1.7%.

At 20 km/h the impact speed for that event would have been 20.0 km/h with 0.6% adult death risk.

One serious near-miss involved a car at 26.9 km/h with 1.4 s between road users. For an adult hit at that speed the estimated death risk is 1.1%.

At 20 km/h the impact speed for that event would have been 3.3 km/h with 0.1% adult death risk.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds to the 20 km/h limit. We are willing to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

A serious near-miss had 0.8 s between person and moving vehicle, a car at 26.4 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 1.1%, compared with 0.6% if impact were at 20.0 km/h.
A close pass had 2.8 s between person and moving vehicle, a van at 33.5 km/h.

We would be pleased to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Lantern Road crossing

We are writing about the pedestrian crossing outside our school at Lantern Road crossing.

A video recording of 3.9 minutes (234.0 s) was made and analysed with SAM tracking. In that time four pedestrian crossings and 10 moving vehicles were counted. The 85th percentile speed was 58.5 km/h.

Of the 4 crossings, 2 of 4 (1 in 2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 2 of 4 (1 in 2) within 1.5 s. If this recording is typical, exact 95% ranges are 6.8-93.2% and 6.8-93.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.2-7.2 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). There were 2 serious near-misses with less than 1.5 s between pedestrian and vehicle and 0 close passes with 1.5-3.0 s.

The 2 serious near-misses were:
One involved a car at 55.0 km/h with 1.4 s between pedestrian and moving vehicle at the same spot. If hit by a car front at that speed, the adult death risk is 12.5% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
Another involved an auto-rickshaw at 19.6 km/h with 0.9 s between pedestrian and moving vehicle at the same spot. If hit, the adult death risk given for that speed is 0.6% (same source, for adults hit by a car front).

For context, 62.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 1 such gap and 1 gap of 12 s or more, longest 66.3 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. PV² and hourly rates cannot be assessed from this video because at least 15 minutes of video is needed and this one is 3.9 minutes.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and protect children crossing.

We can share the video and measurement data on request and welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Lantern Road crossing

We are writing about the pedestrian crossing outside our school at Lantern Road crossing.

A video recording of 3.9 minutes (234.0 s) was made and analysed with SAM tracking. In that time 4 pedestrian crossings and 10 moving vehicles were counted. The 85th percentile speed was 58.5 km/h. With this measure in place there will be no more fatalities here.

Of the 4 crossings, 2 of 4 (1 in 2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 2 of 4 (1 in 2) within 1.5 s. If this recording is typical, exact 95% ranges are 6.8-93.2% and 6.8-93.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.2-7.2 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). One involved a car at 55.0 km/h with 1.4 s between pedestrian and moving vehicle at the same spot. If hit by a car front at that speed, the adult death risk is 12.5% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
Another involved an auto-rickshaw at 19.6 km/h with 0.9 s between pedestrian and moving vehicle at the same spot. If hit, the adult death risk given for that speed is 0.6% (same source, for adults hit by a car front).

For context, 62.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 1 such gap and 1 gap of 12 s or more, longest 66.3 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and protect children crossing.

We can share the video and measurement data on request and welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Quarry Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write on behalf of our school regarding the Quarry Road crossing.

During 26.9 minutes of video (1614.0 s) Crossing Watch recorded 13 pedestrian crossings and 4 moving vehicles at the crossing. The 85th percentile speed was 51.4 km/h. Mrs. Leela Fernandes, who drives the morning bus, caused the worst of these events. In that period 3 of 13 crossings (1 in 4.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 2 of 13 (1 in 6.5) within 1.5 s. Another serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 13.3 km/h with 0.5 s between road users on the same spot.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to slow approaching traffic and protect children crossing.

We have the video and SAM tracking data and are happy to share it for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Quarry Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write on behalf of our school regarding the Quarry Road crossing.

During 26.9 minutes of video (1614.0 s) Crossing Watch recorded 13 pedestrian crossings and 4 moving vehicles at the crossing. The 85th percentile speed was 51.4 km/h. These near-misses happened because drivers ignored the crossing markings. In that period 3 of 13 crossings (1 in 4.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 2 of 13 (1 in 6.5) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 5.0-53.8% and 1.9-45.4% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

There were 2 serious near-misses where pedestrian and moving vehicle were on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and 1 close pass at 1.5-3.0 s.

One serious near-miss involved a bus at 26.9 km/h with 0.3 s between road users on the same spot.
Another serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 13.3 km/h with 0.5 s between road users on the same spot.
A close pass involved a van at 50.6 km/h with 2.2 s between road users on the same spot.
The estimated adult death risk if hit by a car front at those speeds is 1.1% for the bus case, 0.3% for the auto-rickshaw case and 1.2% for the van case, from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.

For engineering context, PV² was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 29 pedestrians and 9 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 26.9 minutes, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one pedestrian twice.
74.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 4 such gaps, 2 of them 12 s or more and longest 24.4 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to slow approaching traffic and protect children crossing.

We have the video and SAM tracking data and are happy to share it for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Quarry Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write on behalf of our school regarding the Quarry Road crossing.

During 26.9 minutes of video (1614.0 s) Crossing Watch recorded 13 pedestrian crossings and 4 moving vehicles at the crossing. The 85th percentile speed was 51.4 km/h. A parent was injured here by a passing motorcycle earlier this year. In that period 3 of 13 crossings (1 in 4.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 2 of 13 (1 in 6.5) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 5.0-53.8% and 1.9-45.4% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

There were 2 serious near-misses where pedestrian and moving vehicle were on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and 1 close pass at 1.5-3.0 s.

One serious near-miss involved a bus at 26.9 km/h with 0.3 s between road users on the same spot.
Another serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 13.3 km/h with 0.5 s between road users on the same spot.
A close pass involved a van at 50.6 km/h with 2.2 s between road users on the same spot.
The estimated adult death risk if hit by a car front at those speeds is 1.1% for the bus case, 0.3% for the auto-rickshaw case and 1.2% for the van case, from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.

For engineering context, PV² was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 29 pedestrians and 9 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 26.9 minutes, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one pedestrian twice.
74.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 4 such gaps, 2 of them 12 s or more and longest 24.4 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to slow approaching traffic and protect children crossing.

We have the video and SAM tracking data and are happy to share it for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Quarry Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write on behalf of our school regarding the Quarry Road crossing.

During 26.9 minutes of video (1614.0 s) Crossing Watch recorded 13 pedestrian crossings and 4 moving vehicles at the crossing. The 85th percentile speed was 51.4 km/h. The death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). In that period 3 of 13 crossings (1 in 4.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 2 of 13 (1 in 6.5) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 5.0-53.8% and 1.9-45.4% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

There were 2 serious near-misses where pedestrian and moving vehicle were on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and 1 close pass at 1.5-3.0 s.

One serious near-miss involved a bus at 26.9 km/h with 0.3 s between road users on the same spot.
Another serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 13.3 km/h with 0.5 s between road users on the same spot.
A close pass involved a van at 50.6 km/h with 2.2 s between road users on the same spot.
The estimated adult death risk if hit by a car front at those speeds is 1.1% for the bus case, 0.3% for the auto-rickshaw case and 1.2% for the van case, from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.

For engineering context, PV² was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 29 pedestrians and 9 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 26.9 minutes, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one pedestrian twice.
74.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 4 such gaps, 2 of them 12 s or more and longest 24.4 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to slow approaching traffic and protect children crossing.

We have the video and SAM tracking data and are happy to share it for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Road Authority Manager,

We are writing about safety at the Brook Street crossing outside our school. A Crossing Watch analysis of video covering 8.8 minutes (528.0 s) counted 12 pedestrian crossings and 17 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 59.0 km/h. During 8.8 minutes the camera logged 12 pedestrian crossings, 17 vehicles and 3 serious near-misses. There were 3 serious near-misses defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and 0 close passes of 1.5 s to 3.0 s. In all 3 serious cases the vehicle was first.

One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.3 s with a car at 58.6 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 16.5% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+).

A second serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.8 s with a car at 58.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 16.0%.

A third serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.0 s with a car at 20.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.6%.

At a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with 0.0% adult death risk for the first 2 events and 20.0 km/h with 0.6% adult death risk for the third event.

Engineering context is limited: PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this video is 8.8 minutes. The data show 96.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 10 such gaps including 4 of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 43.8 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4 s to 6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds and other groups, such as children, may need 10 s to 12 s or longer.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing to reduce vehicle speeds and provide a protected crossing point.

We can share the video for your review on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Road Authority Officer,

We write about the Market Street crossing outside our school. Crossing Watch video analysis (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) measured 6 pedestrian crossings and 31 moving vehicles in 5.1 minutes (306.0 s).

In that period 6 of 6 crossings (1 in 1) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 2 of 6 (1 in 3) within 1.5 s. The most severe serious near-miss left 1.2 s between the person and a car travelling at 44.6 km/h, with an estimated adult fatality risk of 5.3% if hit by a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+). In total, 2 close passes were measured.

A second serious near-miss left 1.4 s between the person and a car travelling at 12.3 km/h, with an estimated adult fatality risk of 0.3% if hit by a car front.

One close pass left 1.8 s between the person and a bus travelling at 59.6 km/h.

Another close pass left 1.8 s between the person and a car travelling at 46.6 km/h, with an estimated adult fatality risk of 3.1% if hit by a car front.

A further close pass left 2.1 s between the person and a motorcycle travelling at 52.7 km/h.

In total there were 2 serious near-misses and 4 close passes, with the person first in 1 case and the vehicle first in 5 cases.

For engineering context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 5.1 minutes with 6 pedestrian crossings and 31 moving vehicles, so any rate must be treated with caution.

77.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 10 gaps and 6 of them 12 s or more and a longest gap of 87.2 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

To reduce speeds, where the 85th percentile was 66.1 km/h, and to give pedestrians protected priority, we request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location.

We can share the video and measurements on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

In that period, 3 people crossed first before the vehicle and 3 vehicles passed first, with 0 cases of both at once.

One serious near-miss involved a bus at 55.8 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.1 s, where Rosén & Sander 2009 data for adults 15+ hit by a car front gives a 13.3% adult death risk if hit, compared to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h limit.

Yours faithfully,

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Orchard Lane crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about safety at Orchard Lane crossing. A video recording of 10.1 minutes (606.0 s) measured 5 pedestrian crossings and 10 vehicles, with 85th percentile speed 58.8 km/h. The counts above are past the threshold the road code sets for a zebra crossing.

Headline result: 3 of 5 crossings (1 in 1.7) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person; 3 of 5 (1 in 1.7) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 14.7-94.7% and 14.7-94.7% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 0.6-8.8 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

Within that time there were 3 serious near-misses and 0 close passes, where serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass means 1.5-3.0 s.

One serious near-miss involved a van at 52.0 km/h with 0.8 s between road users.

A second serious near-miss involved a car at 48.5 km/h with 1.1 s between road users.

A third serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 22.9 km/h with 1.4 s between road users.

For adults hit by a car front the estimated death risks for those speeds are 9.8%, 7.3% and 0.8% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). At a 20 km/h limit the estimated impact speeds would be 0.0 km/h, 0.0 km/h and 17.3 km/h with death risks 0.0%, 0.0% and 0.5%.

On engineering context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 10.1 minutes with 5 pedestrian crossings and 10 moving vehicles. 50.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 1 gap of 6 s or more, 0 gaps of 12 s or more and longest gap 11.3 s, with the main caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you provide a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce speeds and give priority to pedestrians.

We are willing to share the video and measurement log for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority
Subject: Request for safety improvement at Park Avenue crossing

Dear Sir or Madam,

We write as the school using Park Avenue crossing to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table.

A 6.9 minute video (414.0 s) of the crossing recorded 4 pedestrian crossings and 22 moving vehicles.

In that time, 3 of 4 crossings (1 in 1.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 2 of 4 (1 in 2) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 19.4-99.4% and 6.8-93.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

We use the Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) definition where serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass means 1.5-3.0 s.

The most serious near-miss involved a van at 54.1 km/h with 0.4 s between pedestrian and vehicle on the same spot. 4 gaps were cut short by the start or end of the video. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 11.6%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

The second serious near-miss involved a car at 14.1 km/h with 0.8 s between pedestrian and vehicle on the same spot. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.4%, and it would remain 0.4% at an impact of 14.1 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.

A further close pass involved a car at 14.0 km/h with 2.5 s between pedestrian and vehicle on the same spot. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.0%, and it would be 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.

The 85th percentile speed in the recording was 59.4 km/h.

For context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 6.9 minutes. 70.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 8 gaps, 2 of them 12 s or more, longest 25.1 s (the first and last are cut short by the video).

We request the road authority install the raised zebra crossing with speed table and consider a 20 km/h zone with signs to reduce impact speeds and severance.

We are willing to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Road Authority,

I write on behalf of the school regarding the Garden Road crossing.

We commissioned a 9.5 minute (570.0 s) video survey at the crossing. In that time 3 pedestrian crossings and 24 moving vehicles were recorded. The 85th percentile speed was 62.6 km/h. There have already been injuries at this spot this school year. 3 of 3 crossings (1 in 1) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 2 of 3 (1 in 1.5) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 29.2-100.0% and 9.4-99.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). There were 2 serious near-misses (less than 1.5 s apart) and 1 close pass (1.5-3.0 s apart); the vehicle arrived first in 3 of 3 cases.

The worst serious near-miss involved a car at 56.4 km/h passing 0.8 s from the person, with an adult death risk of 13.9% if hit by a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), falling to 0.0 km/h impact and 0.0% risk at a 20 km/h limit.

A second serious near-miss involved a car at 22.3 km/h passing 0.2 s from the person, with an adult death risk of 0.7% if hit, and 20.0 km/h impact with 0.6% risk at a 20 km/h limit.

A close pass involved a bus at 37.2 km/h passing 2.8 s from the person.

On engineering context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 9.5 minutes, so those rates cannot be reliably used. 93.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps of 6 s or more and 6 gaps of 12 s or more, the longest 32.9 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table at the Garden Road crossing to reduce speeds and provide priority where the 3 crossings were observed.

We can share the video and the full measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) on request and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir / Madam,

Re: Safety at Lake View Road crossing

In a Crossing Watch video of 33.6 minutes (2016.0 s) we measured 6 pedestrian crossings and 33 vehicles with an 85th percentile speed of 43.6 km/h. Near-misses like these occur every morning when school opens.

5 of 6 crossings (1 in 1.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 6 (1 in 2) were within 1.5 s.
Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 35.9-99.6% and 11.8-88.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.6-11.7 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The 3 serious near-misses and 2 close passes were:
One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.8 s and involved a car at 35.2 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 2.3% for a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+), falling to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.
A second serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.8 s and involved a car at 33.4 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 2.0% for a car front, falling to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.
A third serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.7 s and involved a car at 17.8 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 0.5% for a car front, remaining 0.5% at an impact of 17.8 km/h.
One close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.7 s and involved a car at 22.2 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 0.4% for a car front, falling to 0.1% at an impact of 3.3 km/h.
One close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.3 s and involved a bus at 44.8 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 0.4% for a car front, falling to 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h.

On engineering context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, but this is scaled from only 33.6 minutes of video and a formal check counts the full peak hour with caveats about broken tracks.
73.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps of 6 s or more and 8 of 12 s or more and longest gap 76.8 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide protected priority.

We can share the full video and tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Lantern Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school monitors the crossing outside our gate on Lantern Road. In 44.2 minutes of video (2652.0 s) we recorded 15 crossings and 25 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 39.7 km/h.

By definition a serious near-miss is pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and a close pass is 1.5 s to 3.0 s. We recorded 2 serious near-misses and 2 close passes. Most of these incidents involved young children running into the road without looking. In 3 cases the pedestrian entered first and in 1 case the vehicle entered first, with 0 cases where both were at the conflict point at once.

1 serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.9 s with a bus at 28.7 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 1.3% (0.6% at a 20.0 km/h limit with impact at 20.0 km/h) per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.

1 serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.0 s with a car at 21.1 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 0.7% (0.6% at a 20.0 km/h limit with impact at 20.0 km/h).

1 close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.7 s with a car at 35.9 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 1.5% (0.0% at a 20.0 km/h limit with impact at 0.0 km/h).

1 close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.5 s with a car at 16.6 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 0.4% (0.4% at a 20.0 km/h limit with impact at 16.6 km/h).

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 20 pedestrians and 34 moving vehicles per hour scaled from 44.2 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and that broken tracks can count 1 person twice (1.3x the true count in our drone test).

66.3% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 5 gaps and 5 of them 12 s or more and longest 13.8 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video and that UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4 s to 6 s as an acceptable gap at urban speeds while other groups such as children may need 10 s to 12 s or longer.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone signs at this location to reduce speeds and provide priority.

We offer to share the full video and tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning the crossing outside our school at Lake View Road crossing. A video survey of 3.9 minutes (234.0 s) recorded 10 pedestrian crossings and 4 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 23.9 km/h. Young pupils regularly have to sprint across because drivers ignore them.

Headline result: 1 of 10 crossings (1 in 10) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person; 1 of 10 (1 in 10) within 1.5 s. The most serious event was a serious near-miss involving a bus with a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s. The vehicle speed was 23.9 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.9% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would be 20.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.6%.

Engineering context is limited because PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 3.9 minutes. Counted: 10 pedestrian crossings, 4 moving vehicles. The first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with 20 km/h zone signs at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for pedestrians.

We can share the full video and measurements on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning safety at the Canal Road crossing outside our school. We commissioned a Crossing Watch video assessment using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time.

In 6.6 minutes (396.0 s) of video, 12 pedestrian crossings and 19 moving vehicles were counted, with an 85th percentile speed of 53.7 km/h. The death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). In that recording, 4 of 12 crossings (1 in 3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 3 of 12 (1 in 4) were within 1.5 s. The exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 9.9-65.1% and 5.5-57.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 1.1-10.2 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). Of the timed encounters, 2 had the person first and 2 had the vehicle first.

We recorded 3 serious near-misses (less than 1.5 s apart) and 1 close pass (1.5-3.0 s). The most severe serious near-miss involved a car at 54.1 km/h with a time gap of 0.8 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 11.6% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+), which would be 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 0.0 km/h. A second serious near-miss involved a car at 48.4 km/h with a time gap of 1.4 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 7.3%, which would be 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 0.0 km/h. A third serious near-miss involved a van at 18.0 km/h with a time gap of 1.3 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 0.5%, which would remain 0.5% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 18.0 km/h. The close pass involved a car at 28.3 km/h with a time gap of 1.8 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 0.6%, which would be 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 0.0 km/h.

For context, engineering guidance notes that PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video, while this recording is only 6.6 minutes, and that 97.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps of 6 s or more, 3 of them 12 s or more, and the longest 25.0 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at the Canal Road crossing to slow approaching traffic and give clear priority to people crossing.

We would be pleased to share the video and SAM tracking data for your review and to discuss next steps.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Subject: Request for safety improvements at Cedar Lane crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

The 85th percentile speed was 49.3 km/h. There were 3 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 0 close passes defined as 1.5 to 3.0 s apart. Of the 3 serious cases, 1 was person-first, 1 was vehicle-first, and 1 was both at once.

The near-misses were as follows. In 1 serious case the time gap was 1.3 s and the vehicle was a car at 47.5 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit by a car front of 6.8% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

In a second serious case the time gap was 0.0 s and the vehicle was an auto-rickshaw at 32.4 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit by a car front of 1.8%.
At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed for that case would be 20.0 km/h with 0.6% adult death risk.
In a third serious case the time gap was 1.1 s and the vehicle was a van at 19.1 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit by a car front of 0.6%.
At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed for that case would be 19.1 km/h with 0.6% adult death risk.

The engineering assessment notes that PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this video is 5.2 minutes, so rates are not calculated. The video also showed 83.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 10 gaps and 7 of them 12 s or more and the longest gap 12.4 s, with the first and last gaps cut short by the video. UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes that 4 to 6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds and other groups such as children may need 10 to 12 s or longer.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide a protected crossing for pupils.

We would be pleased to share the video and full measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

Re: Safety at Lake View Road crossing

We commissioned video analysis of the crossing outside our school. Over 42.0 minutes, 14 crossings and 5 vehicles were recorded. The 85th percentile speed was 33.8 km/h.

Another had a gap of 0.4 s with a bus at 27.8 km/h; the adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 1.2%. A third had a gap of 0.3 s with a van at 15.3 km/h; the adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.4%. Local doctors warn that a child hit at these speeds would face a 5% chance of death.

Engineering context: PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 20 pedestrians and 7 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 42 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one twice at 1.3x in our drone test. 72.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 10 gaps and a longest gap of 56.9 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We are willing to share the video and data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority
Subject: Request for safety improvement at Lantern Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning the crossing outside our school at Lantern Road crossing. We arranged a Crossing Watch video analysis using SAM tracking and road-plane geometry. In 10.7 minutes, equal to 642.0 s, we counted 12 pedestrian crossings and 4 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 65.3 km/h.

The video was assessed for post-encroachment time, where serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass is 1.5 to 3.0 s. We recorded 2 serious near-misses and 1 close pass. In 1 case the pedestrian was first and in 2 cases the vehicle was first.

One serious near-miss had a gap of 1.2 s and involved an auto-rickshaw at 58.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 16.3% based on Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+. A child hit at 58.5 km/h in this location would have faced a 16.3% risk of death.

A second serious near-miss had a gap of 0.5 s and involved a car at 15.9 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.4%.

The close pass had a gap of 2.8 s and involved an auto-rickshaw at 54.2 km/h.

On engineering context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 10.7. We also note that 93.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 1 gap of 6 s or more and 1 gap of 12 s or more, longest 39.2 s, with the first and last gaps cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location. We would be pleased to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority
Subject: Request for safety improvements at Cedar Lane crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write on behalf of the school regarding the Cedar Lane crossing outside our premises.

A video of 6.2 minutes (372.0 s) was analysed using SAM tracking with road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time. In that period five pedestrian crossings and 7 moving vehicles were counted. The 85th percentile speed was 56.8 km/h.

The analysis classified a serious near-miss as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and a close pass as 1.5-3.0 s apart. There were 4 serious near-misses and 1 close pass. In 5 cases the pedestrian was first, in 0 cases the vehicle was first, and in 0 cases both were at the spot at once.

The most serious near-miss involved a van at 56.4 km/h with a gap of 1.1 s. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 13.9% (0.0% with impact at 0.0 km/h at a 20 km/h limit) per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.
The second serious near-miss involved a motorcycle at 37.6 km/h with a gap of 0.5 s. The adult death risk if hit is 2.9% (0.6% with impact at 20.0 km/h at a 20 km/h limit).
The third serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 24.2 km/h with a gap of 0.5 s. The adult death risk if hit is 0.9% (0.6% with impact at 20.0 km/h at a 20 km/h limit).
The fourth serious near-miss involved a car at 16.9 km/h with a gap of 0.9 s. The adult death risk if hit is 0.5% (0.5% with impact at 16.9 km/h at a 20 km/h limit).
The close pass involved a van at 14.9 km/h with a gap of 2.7 s. The adult death risk if hit is 0.0% (0.0% with impact at 0.0 km/h at a 20 km/h limit).

For context, 67.6% of the observed time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 gaps of 6 s or more, 3 of 12 s or more, longest 49.2 s. Hourly PV² rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 6.2 minutes, so rates should be treated with caution.

We request that the authority install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority to pedestrians.

We are willing to share the video and measurements for further review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about safety at the Market Street crossing outside our school. A video survey of 39.9 minutes (2394.0 s) recorded 5 pedestrian crossings and 27 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 52.5 km/h. The video showed 1 gap of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle.

In that recording, 4 of 5 crossings (1 in 1.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 2 of 5 (1 in 2.5) within 1.5 s. There were 2 serious near-misses and 2 close passes, with 3 persons crossing first and 1 vehicle first.

The most serious was a van at 38.6 km/h passing 0.5 s after the person, with an adult death risk if hit by a car front of 3.1% (0.6% at 20.0 km/h). The other serious near-miss was an auto-rickshaw at 12.9 km/h 0.7 s apart, with an adult death risk of 0.3%. The close passes were an auto-rickshaw at 50.1 km/h 2.6 s apart and a van at 43.5 km/h 2.8 s apart.

Engineering context: PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 8 pedestrians and 41 vehicles per hour scaled from 39.9 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count 1.3x the true count. 98.9% of time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, noting first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location. We are happy to share the video and tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety work at Park Avenue crossing

We are writing about the crossing outside our school at Park Avenue crossing.

In a video of 16.8 minutes (1008.0 s) there were 35 crossings and 10 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 57.3 km/h. In the near-miss with a time gap of 0.2 s the vehicle was going at 20.7 km/h, and in the one with a time gap of 0.0 s it was going at 51.4 km/h. The worst near misses were:

A second serious near miss involved a motorcycle at 20.7 km/h with 0.0 s between road users. At that speed the published adult death risk if hit by a car front is 0.6%, also 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.

Preliminary engineering notes, with caveats, are that PV² was scaled to 0.0 x 10^8 from 125 pedestrians and 36 moving vehicles an hour based on 16.8 minutes of video, while a formal check counts the full peak hour and our test showed tracking can count 1.3x the true pedestrian count, and that 94.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more (3 gaps, 0 of them 12 s or more, longest 7.7 s), but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We can share the video and measurements on request and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

In one of these events the vehicle struck the pedestrian. Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Mill Street crossing

We write on behalf of the school about the crossing at Mill Street crossing.

Crossing Watch video analysis covering 6.6 minutes (396.0 s) recorded 5 pedestrian crossings and 37 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 60.6 km/h. The people crossing in these events were our students. There were 2 serious near-misses and 3 close passes. In this method serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass means 1.5-3.0 s. Of the 5 crossings, 1 was person first, 4 were vehicle first and 0 were both at once.

One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.2 s with a car at 53.6 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 11.1% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

Another serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s with a car at 22.9 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.8%, compared to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

Engineering context is limited because PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 6.6 minutes. With that caveat, 44.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed. That was 10 gaps, 0 of them 12 s or more, longest 9.4 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing on a speed table with 20 km/h zone signs at this location.

We can share the video and measurement log on request and welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the Mill Street crossing following a video recording of 4.0 minutes (240.0 s) at the site. In that time we counted 8 pedestrian crossings and 11 moving vehicles.

4 of 8 crossings (1 in 2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3.0 s of the person; 3 of 8 (1 in 2.7) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 15.7-84.3% and 8.5-75.5% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 1.1-10.2 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). Of the 4 cases, 3 were serious (less than 1.5 s) and 1 was a close pass (1.5-3.0 s).

The worst near-misses were as follows. 1 serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.4 s with a motorcycle travelling at 38.8 mph and an adult death risk if hit of 3.2% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
Another serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.5 s with a car travelling at 29.8 km/h and an adult death risk if hit of 1.4%.
A third serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.4 s with a bus travelling at 23.2 km/h and an adult death risk if hit of 0.8%.
1 close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.5 s with a van travelling at 31.3 km/h and an adult death risk if hit of 1.7%.

For context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 4.0. Counted: 8 pedestrian crossings, 11 moving vehicles. 76.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 5 gaps, 5 of them 12 s or more, longest 37.1 s (the first and last are cut short by the video). UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2): 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds; other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for pedestrians.

We would be pleased to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

The worst cases measured by post-encroachment time were:

The worst cases measured by post-encroachment time were:

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write as the school adjoining the Canal Road crossing about pedestrian safety.

In 36.8 minutes of video (2208.0 s) Crossing Watch recorded 8 crossings and 10 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 60.6 km/h. The closest of these passes was in fact a collision.

The analysis found 2 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass, defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart, with 3 cases where the person was first.

The most severe serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.1 s involving a car travelling at 52.3 km/h, where the adult death risk if hit by a car front would have been 10.0% according to Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15+.

At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed in that case would have been 20.0 km/h with an adult death risk of 0.6%.

A second serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.8 s involving a car travelling at 42.8 km/h, where the adult death risk if hit would have been 4.5% and would have been 0.3% at 13.6 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.9 s involving a car travelling at 55.2 km/h, where the adult death risk if hit would have been 5.0% and would have been 0.0% at 0.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 13 pedestrians and 16 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 36.8 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one twice: 1.3x the true count in our drone test.

Also 55.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 12 such gaps, 10 of them 12 s or more and longest 52.2 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We can share the video and Crossing Watch measurements for your review and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvements at Cedar Lane crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning the crossing outside our school at Cedar Lane crossing. A 5.2 minute video analysis by Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) recorded 3 pedestrian crossings and 14 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 49.3 km/h. There were 3 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 0 close passes defined as 1.5 to 3.0 s apart. Of the 3 serious cases, 1 was person-first, 1 was vehicle-first, and 1 was both at once.

The near-misses were as follows. In 1 serious case the time gap was 1.3 s and the vehicle was a car at 47.5 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit by a car front of 6.8% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.
At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed for that case would be 0.0 km/h with 0.0% adult death risk.
In a second serious case the time gap was 0.0 s and the vehicle was an auto-rickshaw at 32.4 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit by a car front of 1.8%.
At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed for that case would be 20.0 km/h with 0.6% adult death risk.
In a third serious case the time gap was 1.1 s and the vehicle was a van at 19.1 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit by a car front of 0.6%.
At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed for that case would be 19.1 km/h with 0.6% adult death risk.

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Quarry Road crossing

We measured safety at the Quarry Road crossing using a video of 18.9 minutes covering 6 crossings and 21 vehicles. During this recording, 3 of 6 crossings (1 in 2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 1 of 6 (1 in 6) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 11.8-88.2% and 0.4-64.1% of crossings and 0.6-8.8 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long. The 85th percentile speed was 49.6 mph.

The most serious near-miss was a bus that passed the same spot 0.9 s after a person. In that encounter the bus was travelling at 17.6 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 0.5% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second near-miss was a close pass with a gap of 1.6 s involving an auto-rickshaw. The auto-rickshaw in that pass was travelling at 47.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at 47.5 km/h the estimated death risk is 5.4%.

A third near-miss was a close pass with a gap of 2.3 s involving a car. The car in that pass was travelling at 34.1 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 19 pedestrians and 67 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 18.9 minutes of video, though a formal check counts the full peak hour. Also, 67.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, based on 4 gaps, though the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to slow vehicles and give priority to people crossing.

We can share the video and Crossing Watch measurements on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We measured safety at the Quarry Road crossing using a video of 18.9 minutes covering 6 crossings and 21 vehicles. Yours faithfully,

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Hill View Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the Hill View Road crossing outside our school. Crossing Watch analysis of 25.9 minutes of video (1554.0 s) recorded 40 crossings and 22 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 36.3 km/h. In the near-miss with a time gap of 0.3 s, the bus reached the spot after the pedestrian. In that period there were 2 serious near-misses and 1 close pass. A serious near-miss is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass as 1.5-3.0 s apart.

The most severe serious near-miss involved a van at 33.4 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.9 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 2.0% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared to 0.6% at 19.9 km/h if the 20 km/h limit had applied.

A second serious near-miss involved a bus at 29.5 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.3 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 1.4%, compared to 0.6% at 20.0 km/h if the 20 km/h limit had applied.

A close pass involved a bus at 13.1 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 2.4 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.0%, compared to 0.0% at 0.0 km/h if the 20 km/h limit had applied.

In total, 0 crossings had the person first, 3 had the vehicle first and 0 had both at once.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 93 pedestrians and 51 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 25.9 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one twice at 1.3x the true count in the drone test. About 55.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 1 gap of 6 s or more and 1 of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 86.6 s; the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce speeds and give priority to pedestrians.

We are willing to share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Quarry Road crossing

We measured safety at the Quarry Road crossing using a video of 18.9 minutes covering 6 crossings and 21 vehicles. During this recording, 3 of 6 crossings (1 in 2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 1 of 6 (1 in 6) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 11.8-88.2% and 0.4-64.1% of crossings and 0.6-8.8 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long. The 85th percentile speed was 49.6 km/h. A third near-miss was a close pass with a gap of 2.3 s involving a car. The car in that pass was travelling at 34.1 km/h.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to slow vehicles and give priority to people crossing.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Cedar Lane crossing

We write concerning pedestrian safety at Cedar Lane crossing. Crossing Watch video analysis (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) measured 6.1 minutes (366.0 s) of activity, with 12 pedestrian crossings and 28 moving vehicles.

The 85th percentile vehicle speed was 43.0 km/h. Serious was defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and close pass as 1.5-3.0 s apart. In 6.1 minutes we recorded 2 serious near-misses and 2 close passes, with 2 events where the person was first and 2 where the vehicle was first.

The most severe event was a serious near-miss with a car at 38.8 km/h and a gap of 0.1 s. A child struck in that worst event would have faced about a 12% chance of dying. At that speed the published death-risk for an adult hit by a car front is 3.2%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second serious near-miss involved a motorcycle at 19.9 km/h with a gap of 1.4 s. At 19.9 km/h the same adult car-front risk reference is 0.6%.

A close pass involved a car at 32.3 km/h with a gap of 1.7 s. At that speed the adult car-front death risk is 1.1%, compared with 0.0% if impact had been at 0.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

A further close pass involved a car at 17.7 km/h with a gap of 2.9 s. At that speed the adult car-front death risk is 0.0%.

Engineering context must be read with caveats. PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this video is 6.1 minutes with 12 crossings and 28 vehicles, so it is too short for those rates. Separately, 90.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 7 gaps in total and 3 of them 12 s or more and the longest 60.1 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. For reference, UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds while other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table at Cedar Lane crossing to reduce speeds and provide protected priority for the 12 crossings observed in 6.1 minutes.

We are happy to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Market Street crossing

We write on behalf of the school at Market Street crossing. We have 3.6 minutes (216.0 s) of video analysed by Crossing Watch. In that time we counted 6 pedestrian crossings and 2 moving vehicles.

PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 3.6, so those rates cannot be used reliably.

During the observation we recorded 2 serious near-misses and 0 close passes. In 2 cases the pedestrian crossed first and was followed by the vehicle within the PET threshold. A serious near-miss is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, a close pass as 1.5-3.0 s.

44.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 2 gaps, 1 of them 12 s or more, longest 19.5 s. The first and last gaps are cut short by the video. For context, UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds, while other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

The 85th percentile speed was 45.0 km/h. During the morning school rush, hundreds of vehicles speed through this crossing every hour.

One serious near-miss had a PET of 0.1 s and involved an auto-rickshaw at 46.4 km/h.

For an adult hit by a car front at 46.4 km/h the death risk is 6.2%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h, per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.

The other serious near-miss had a PET of 1.4 s and involved a bus at 12.1 km/h.

For an adult hit by a car front at 12.1 km/h the death risk is 0.3%, which would remain 0.3% at an impact of 12.1 km/h if limited to 20 km/h.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this crossing to reduce vehicle speeds and give pedestrians priority.

We are happy to share the 216.0 s video and tracking data on request.

Yours faithfully
The Principal
