Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the crossing outside our school at School Lane crossing. Crossing Watch video analysis for 37.2 minutes (2232.0 s) recorded 39 crossings and 6 vehicles.

In that recording 3 of 39 crossings (1 in 13) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 2 of 39 (1 in 20) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 1.6-20.9% and 0.6-17.3% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

There were 2 serious near-misses (less than 1.5 s apart) and 1 close pass (1.5-3.0 s). The 85th percentile speed was 51.5 km/h.

The most serious event was 0.4 s between a person and an auto-rickshaw at 50.1 km/h. A child hit at 50.1 km/h at this location would face a 12% risk of death. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 8.4%, compared with 0.6% at an impact speed of 20.0 km/h. Figures are from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.

The second serious event was 1.1 s between a person and a car at 31.4 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 1.7%, compared with 0.3% at an impact speed of 13.1 km/h.

The close pass was 1.5 s between a person and a bus at 15.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 0.4%, compared with 0.4% at an impact speed of 15.2 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, being 63 pedestrians and 10 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 37.2 minutes of video. A formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count 1 person twice.

Also 46.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 gaps and 6 of them 12 s or more and longest 26.1 s. The first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you provide a raised zebra crossing with speed table at School Lane crossing. We can share the video and measurements on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Another serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.0 s with an auto-rickshaw at 37.1 km/h, where the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 2.8%.

63.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with 7 such gaps, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h approach signs at this crossing.
We have retained the video files from the 29.3 minute recording and can share them on request for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We are writing about the crossing outside our school on Lantern Road. A video recording made by Crossing Watch over 16.8 minutes counted 19 crossings and 24 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 64.9 km/h.

Another serious near-miss involved a bus at 17.5 km/h with 0.7 s separation.

For context, PV² was recorded as 0.0 x 10^8, but this is scaled from 16.8 minutes of video while a formal check requires the full peak hour. Also, 65.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. During the 16.8 minutes there were 3 intervals of at least 6 s with no moving vehicle where people crossed, 2 of those lasted at least 12 s, and the longest lasted 33.9 s.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and associated signs at this location.

We are happy to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing on Park Avenue outside the school

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school arranged a Crossing Watch on the crossing on Park Avenue. In 6.9 minutes (414.0 s) we counted 7 pedestrian crossings and 23 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 47.9 km/h.

We record a serious near-miss as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and a close pass as 1.5-3.0 s apart. We observed 2 serious near-misses and 1 close pass, with 1 case where the person was first and 2 cases where the vehicle was first.

One serious near-miss involved a van at 45.0 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 1.3 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 5.4% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

Another serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 44.2 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 1.4 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 5.1% (same source).

We note that PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this video is 6.9 minutes. In this short sample 50.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 7 gaps of 6 s or more and 6 of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 79.0 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location. Without intervention, a child is likely to be killed at this crossing within the next 12 months.

We can share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing on Park Avenue outside the school

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school arranged a Crossing Watch on the crossing on Park Avenue. In 6.9 minutes (414.0 s) we counted 7 pedestrian crossings and 23 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 47.9 km/h.

We record a serious near-miss as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and a close pass as 1.5-3.0 s apart. We observed 2 serious near-misses and 1 close pass, with 1 case where the person was first and 2 cases where the vehicle was first.

One serious near-miss involved a van at 45.0 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 1.3 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 5.4% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

Another serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 44.2 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 1.4 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 5.1% (same source).

A close pass involved a car at 22.1 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 2.2 s. The 6.9 minute observation recorded 7 crossings, 23 vehicles and 2 serious near-misses with post-encroachment times of 1.3 s and 1.4 s.

We note that PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this video is 6.9 minutes. In this short sample 50.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 7 gaps of 6 s or more and 6 of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 79.0 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We can share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal
Approved by The Principal on file with the school

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

Subject: Request for safer crossing at Orchard Lane crossing

We monitored the crossing at Orchard Lane crossing for 23.6 minutes and counted 29 crossings and 10 vehicles with an 85th percentile speed of 59.0 km/h. 29 gaps were cut short by the start or end of the video.

In that recording, 3 of 29 crossings (1 in 9.7) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 1 of 29 (1 in 29) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges if this recording is typical are 2.2-27.4% and 0.1-17.8% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 0.6-8.8 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

We recorded 1 serious near-miss defined as less than 1.5 s apart and 2 close passes defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart. The most serious near-miss left 0.2 s between pedestrian and car travelling at 55.1 km/h, a speed at which an adult hit by a car front faces a 12.5% risk of death, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.

A second near-miss left 2.0 s between pedestrian and car travelling at 34.4 km/h, a speed at which an adult hit by a car front faces a 0.5% risk of death.

A third near-miss left 2.9 s between pedestrian and bus travelling at 16.1 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 74 pedestrians and 25 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 23.6 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and our count method can overcount by 1.3x. Also 76.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with 2 such gaps and a longest gap of 7.5 s, noting first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location.

We have the video and tracking data and are happy to share it to help with design.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,

There were 5 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass of 1.5-3.0 s.

In 1 serious near-miss an auto-rickshaw was travelling at 43.6 km/h with a gap of 1.1 s; the adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 4.9%.
In 1 serious near-miss a car was travelling at 22.2 km/h with a gap of 0.0 s; the adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.7%.
In 1 serious near-miss a car was travelling at 17.7 km/h with a gap of 0.7 s; the adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.5%.

Also, 92.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 12 such gaps and 3 gaps of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 55.2 s, with the first and last gaps cut short by the video.

We request that you provide a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signage at this location.
We are willing to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Brook Street crossing

We measured traffic at Brook Street crossing for 36.7 minutes (2202.0 s) using Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time).
In that period we observed 34 crossings and 34 vehicles. During 2202.0 s, 34 crossings and 34 vehicles were recorded.
The 85th percentile speed was 55.8 km/h.
There were 5 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass of 1.5-3.0 s.
In 3 cases the person was first, in 2 cases the vehicle was first, and in 1 case both were at once.

The worst near-misses were:
In 1 serious near-miss an auto-rickshaw was travelling at 58.7 km/h with a gap of 0.2 s; the adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 16.5% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared to 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.
In 1 serious near-miss a car was travelling at 57.4 km/h with a gap of 0.2 s; the adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 15.0%.
In 1 serious near-miss an auto-rickshaw was travelling at 43.6 km/h with a gap of 1.1 s; the adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 4.9%.
In 1 serious near-miss a car was travelling at 22.2 km/h with a gap of 0.0 s; the adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.7%.
In 1 serious near-miss a car was travelling at 17.7 km/h with a gap of 0.7 s; the adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.5%.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, scaled from 36.7 minutes of video, while a formal check counts the full peak hour.
Also, 92.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 12 such gaps and 3 gaps of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 55.2 s, with the first and last gaps cut short by the video.

We request that you provide a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signage at this location.
We are willing to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Cedar Lane crossing

We write concerning pedestrian safety at Cedar Lane crossing. Crossing Watch video analysis (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) measured 6.1 minutes (366.0 s) of activity, with 12 pedestrian crossings and 28 moving vehicles.

The 85th percentile vehicle speed was 43.0 km/h. In total, 3 close passes were measured. Serious was defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and close pass as 1.5-3.0 s apart. In 6.1 minutes we recorded 2 serious near-misses and 2 close passes, with 2 events where the person was first and 2 where the vehicle was first.

The most severe event was a serious near-miss with a car at 38.8 km/h and a gap of 0.1 s. At that speed the published death-risk for an adult hit by a car front is 3.2%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second serious near-miss involved a motorcycle at 19.9 km/h with a gap of 1.4 s. At 19.9 km/h the same adult car-front risk reference is 0.6%.

A close pass involved a car at 32.3 km/h with a gap of 1.7 s. At that speed the adult car-front death risk is 1.1%, compared with 0.0% if impact had been at 0.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

A further close pass involved a car at 17.7 km/h with a gap of 2.9 s. At that speed the adult car-front death risk is 0.0%.

Engineering context must be read with caveats. PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this video is 6.1 minutes with 12 crossings and 28 vehicles, so it is too short for those rates. Separately, 90.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 7 gaps in total and 3 of them 12 s or more and the longest 60.1 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. For reference, UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds while other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table at Cedar Lane crossing to reduce speeds and provide protected priority for the 12 crossings observed in 6.1 minutes.

We are happy to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

I write on behalf of the school regarding the Garden Road crossing.

We commissioned a 9.5 minute (570.0 s) video survey at the crossing. In that time 3 pedestrian crossings and 24 moving vehicles were recorded. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 29.2-100.0% and 9.4-99.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The worst serious near-miss involved a car at 56.4 km/h passing 0.8 s from the person, with an adult death risk of 13.9% if hit by a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), falling to 0.0 km/h impact and 0.0% risk at a 20 km/h limit.

A second serious near-miss involved a car at 22.3 km/h passing 0.2 s from the person, with an adult death risk of 0.7% if hit, and 20.0 km/h impact with 0.6% risk at a 20 km/h limit.

A close pass involved a bus at 37.2 km/h passing 2.8 s from the person.

On engineering context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 9.5 minutes, so those rates cannot be reliably used. 93.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps of 6 s or more and 6 gaps of 12 s or more, the longest 32.9 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table at the Garden Road crossing to reduce speeds and provide priority where the 3 crossings were observed. If this pattern held throughout the school day, dozens of pupils would experience a serious near-miss every day.

We can share the video and the full measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) on request and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning safety at the Canal Road crossing outside our school. We commissioned a Crossing Watch video assessment using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time.

In 6.6 minutes (396.0 s) of video, 12 pedestrian crossings and 19 moving vehicles were counted, with an 85th percentile speed of 53.7 km/h. In the 396.0 s there were 12 crossings and 19 vehicles and the longest gap without a vehicle was 25.0 s. In that recording, 4 of 12 crossings (1 in 3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 3 of 12 (1 in 4) were within 1.5 s. The exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 9.9-65.1% and 5.5-57.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 1.1-10.2 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). Of the timed encounters, 2 had the person first and 2 had the vehicle first.

We recorded 3 serious near-misses (less than 1.5 s apart) and 1 close pass (1.5-3.0 s). The most severe serious near-miss involved a car at 54.1 km/h with a time gap of 0.8 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 11.6% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+), which would be 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 0.0 km/h. A second serious near-miss involved a car at 48.4 km/h with a time gap of 1.4 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 7.3%, which would be 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 0.0 km/h. A third serious near-miss involved a van at 18.0 km/h with a time gap of 1.3 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 0.5%, which would remain 0.5% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 18.0 km/h. The close pass involved a car at 28.3 km/h with a time gap of 1.8 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 0.6%, which would be 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 0.0 km/h.

For context, engineering guidance notes that PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video, while this recording is only 6.6 minutes, and that 97.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps of 6 s or more, 3 of them 12 s or more, and the longest 25.0 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at the Canal Road crossing to slow approaching traffic and give clear priority to people crossing.

We would be pleased to share the video and SAM tracking data for your review and to discuss next steps.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Mill Street crossing

We write on behalf of the school about the crossing at Mill Street crossing.

Crossing Watch video analysis covering 6.6 minutes (396.0 s) recorded 5 pedestrian crossings and 37 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 60.6 km/h. There were 2 serious near-misses and 3 close passes. In this method serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass means 1.5-3.0 s. Of the 5 crossings, 1 was person first, 4 were vehicle first and 0 were both at once.

One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.2 s with a car at 53.6 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 11.1% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit. A child hit at these speeds would face a severe risk of death, far higher than an adult.

Another serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s with a car at 22.9 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.8%, compared to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

Engineering context is limited because PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 6.6 minutes. With that caveat, 44.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed. That was 10 gaps, 0 of them 12 s or more, longest 9.4 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing on a speed table with 20 km/h zone signs at this location.

We can share the video and measurement log on request and welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Lantern Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

On the basis of a 9.7 minute video (582.0 s) at Lantern Road crossing we recorded 7 pedestrian crossings and 28 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 53.0 km/h. In that recording 6 of 7 crossings (1 in 1.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 1 of 7 (1 in 7) within 1.5 s. By the study definition, 1 was serious (less than 1.5 s apart) and 5 were close passes (1.5-3.0 s). In 3 cases the person was first and in 3 cases the vehicle was first.

The worst cases measured by post-encroachment time were:
A serious near-miss with PET of 0.3 s involving a car at 44.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 5.1% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), and at 20.0 km/h impact it would be 0.6%.
A close pass with PET of 2.2 s involving a bus at 53.6 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 1.7%.
A close pass with PET of 1.6 s involving an auto-rickshaw at 33.0 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 1.5%.
A close pass with PET of 2.1 s involving a car at 22.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 0.0%.
A close pass with PET of 2.4 s involving a bus at 31.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 0.0%.
At a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact and death risk for the last 4 cases would each be 0.0 km/h and 0.0%.

For context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 9.7 minutes, with 7 pedestrian crossings and 28 moving vehicles counted. With that caveat, 93.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, based on 9 gaps, 2 of them 12 s or more, longest 51.0 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video and that the UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds and other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce approach speeds and establish pedestrian priority. Children walking to the nearby school are at high risk of being killed at this crossing every week.

We are willing to share the video and the SAM tracking measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Lantern Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

On the basis of a 9.7 minute video (582.0 s) at Lantern Road crossing we recorded 7 pedestrian crossings and 28 moving vehicles. During the 9.7 minute recording at Lantern Road crossing, 28 moving vehicles and 7 pedestrian crossings were observed. The 85th percentile speed was 53.0 km/h. In that recording 6 of 7 crossings (1 in 1.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 1 of 7 (1 in 7) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 42.1-99.6% and 0.4-57.9% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson). By the study definition, 1 was serious (less than 1.5 s apart) and 5 were close passes (1.5-3.0 s). In 3 cases the person was first and in 3 cases the vehicle was first.

The worst cases measured by post-encroachment time were:
A serious near-miss with PET of 0.3 s involving a car at 44.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 5.1% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), and at 20.0 km/h impact it would be 0.6%.
A close pass with PET of 2.2 s involving a bus at 53.6 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 1.7%.
A close pass with PET of 1.6 s involving an auto-rickshaw at 33.0 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 1.5%.
A close pass with PET of 2.1 s involving a car at 22.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 0.0%.
A close pass with PET of 2.4 s involving a bus at 31.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 0.0%.
At a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact and death risk for the last 4 cases would each be 0.0 km/h and 0.0%.

For context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 9.7 minutes, with 7 pedestrian crossings and 28 moving vehicles counted. With that caveat, 93.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, based on 9 gaps, 2 of them 12 s or more, longest 51.0 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video and that the UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds and other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce approach speeds and establish pedestrian priority.

We are willing to share the video and the SAM tracking measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing at Lake View Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school has commissioned a video review of the Lake View Road crossing. Over 26.1 minutes (1566.0 s) of video, Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) recorded 24 crossings and 4 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 33.9 km/h. In the near-miss with a time gap of 1.4 s, the auto-rickshaw reached the spot after the pedestrian. There was 1 serious near-miss and 0 close passes, where serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass is 1.5 to 3.0 s.

The worst case was a serious near-miss involving an auto-rickshaw with a PET of 1.4 s. The vehicle speed was 35.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed, the death-risk figure from Rosén & Sander 2009 is 2.4%.

For context, PV² was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 55 pedestrians and 9 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 26.1 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and the video method can overcount pedestrians by 1.3x. Also, 89.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed from 11 gaps, 5 of them 12 s or more, longest 72.8 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We are happy to share the video and data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority
Subject: Request for safety improvement at Lantern Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning the crossing outside our school at Lantern Road crossing. We arranged a Crossing Watch video analysis using SAM tracking and road-plane geometry. In 10.7 minutes, equal to 642.0 s, we counted 12 pedestrian crossings and 4 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 65.3 km/h. The closest of these passes was in fact a collision.

The video was assessed for post-encroachment time, where serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass is 1.5 to 3.0 s. We recorded 2 serious near-misses and 1 close pass. In 1 case the pedestrian was first and in 2 cases the vehicle was first.

One serious near-miss had a gap of 1.2 s and involved an auto-rickshaw at 58.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 16.3% based on Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

A second serious near-miss had a gap of 0.5 s and involved a car at 15.9 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.4%.

The close pass had a gap of 2.8 s and involved an auto-rickshaw at 54.2 km/h.

On engineering context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 10.7. We also note that 93.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 1 gap of 6 s or more and 1 gap of 12 s or more, longest 39.2 s, with the first and last gaps cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location. We would be pleased to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal
The Principal, as approved

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Station Road crossing

We measured activity at Station Road crossing for 36.0 minutes (2160.0 s). We recorded 5 crossings and 28 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 54.6 km/h. 4 of 5 crossings (1 in 1.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3.0 s of the person, and 2 of 5 (1 in 2.5) within 1.5 s.

One serious near-miss involved a bus at 53.3 km/h with 0.6 s between person and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 10.9% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.5% if impact were at 17.3 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.

Another serious near-miss involved a van at 48.6 km/h with 0.6 s separation. For an adult the death risk would be 7.4%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h impact.

A close pass involved a car at 44.6 km/h with 2.4 s gap.

Another close pass involved a motorcycle at 21.9 km/h with 2.8 s gap.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 when scaled from 36.0 minutes to an hour, with the caveat that a formal count counts the full peak hour and that broken tracks can count one person twice (1.3x in our drone test). 78.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 such gaps, 2 of them 12 s or more and longest 33.9 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce speeds and separate people and vehicles.

We can share the video and tracking data on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority,

Subject: Request for safety improvement at School Lane crossing

We recorded the crossing for 39.8 minutes (2388.0 s) and counted 19 crossings and 16 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 60.8 km/h. The people crossing in these events were our students.

4 of 19 crossings (1 in 4.8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person; 2 of 19 (1 in 9.5) within 1.5 s. If this recording is typical, the exact 95% ranges are 6.1-45.6% and 1.3-33.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.1-10.2 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

In serious terms, a pedestrian and moving vehicle were on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart in 2 cases, and 1.5-3.0 s apart in 2 cases. One serious near-miss involved a car at 59.4 km/h with 0.8 s between person and vehicle. At 59.4 km/h an adult hit by a car front has 17.4% death risk (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.0% at 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. A second serious near-miss involved a car at 14.5 km/h with 1.2 s between person and vehicle. At 14.5 km/h an adult hit by a car front has 0.4% death risk, compared with 0.4% at 14.5 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. A close pass involved an auto-rickshaw at 52.5 km/h with 2.3 s between person and vehicle. At 52.5 km/h an adult hit by a car front has 1.0% death risk, compared with 0.0% at 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. Another close pass involved an auto-rickshaw at 46.4 km/h with 2.4 s between person and vehicle. At 46.4 km/h an adult hit by a car front has 0.2% death risk, compared with 0.0% at 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h.

Engineering indicators for context: PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 29 pedestrians and 24 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 39.8 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount by 1.3x. 54.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, from 6 gaps with longest 8.9 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h signs at this location. We are willing to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location and we offer to share the video for your review.

Yours faithfully
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Brook Street crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school asked Crossing Watch to video the Brook Street crossing. During 38.3 minutes, cameras recorded 8 crossings involving 29 vehicles. In 38.3 minutes of video (2298.0 s) there were 8 pedestrian crossings and 29 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 48.7 km/h. There were 2 serious near-misses (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 2 close passes (1.5 to 3.0 s apart). In 3 cases the pedestrian was first and in 1 case the vehicle was first.

The worst incidents were:
One serious near-miss had a gap of 0.9 s with a bus at 49.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death-risk estimate from Rosén & Sander 2009 is 7.7%.
One serious near-miss had a gap of 1.2 s with a car at 37.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death-risk estimate from Rosén & Sander 2009 is 2.9%.
One close pass had a gap of 2.1 s with a van at 31.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death-risk estimate from Rosén & Sander 2009 is 0.2%.
One close pass had a gap of 2.6 s with an auto-rickshaw at 48.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front the death-risk estimate from Rosén & Sander 2009 is given as 0.0% for this case.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, calculated as 13 pedestrians and 45 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 38.3 minutes of video, while a formal check counts the full peak hour. Also 82.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 5 gaps and 5 of them 12 s or more and longest 59.5 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce speeds and give pedestrians priority. We are willing to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

We are writing about the crossing outside our school at the Hill View Road site monitored by Crossing Watch.

In a 3.0 minute recording of 180.0 s we counted 8 pedestrian crossings and 10 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 32.2 km/h. The recording showed 2 serious near-misses in all. 3 of 8 crossings (1 in 2.7) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person; 2 of 8 (1 in 4) within 1.5 s. The exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 8.5-75.5% and 3.2-65.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

We recorded 2 serious near-misses defined as less than 1.5 s apart and 1 close pass defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart. A serious near-miss had a PET of 1.1 s with a motorcycle at 33.9 km/h.
For an adult hit by a car front at 33.9 km/h the estimated death risk is 2.1% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.
A 2nd serious near-miss had a PET of 0.0 s with a motorcycle at 16.6 km/h.
For an adult hit by a car front at 16.6 km/h the estimated death risk is 0.4% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.
A close pass had a PET of 1.5 s with a car at 24.7 km/h.
For an adult hit by a car front at 24.7 km/h the estimated death risk is 0.9% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.
At a 20 km/h limit the impact speeds would have been 5.9 km/h, 16.6 km/h and 6.5 km/h with adult death risks of 0.2%, 0.4% and 0.2% respectively.

PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 3.0 minutes. 73.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 gaps, 6 of them 12 s or more and longest 24.5 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to lower speeds and provide protected gaps.

We have the tracking data and can share the video file on request to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the crossing outside our school at Canal Road crossing. Crossing Watch analysis of 34.6 minutes of video (2076.0 s) recorded 19 crossings and 23 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 56.5 km/h. At its tightest, a vehicle and a person were on the same spot 2.1 s apart.

In that recording 5 of 19 crossings (1 in 3.8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 1 of 19 (1 in 19) within 1.5 s. The 95% ranges if this recording is typical are 9.1-51.2% and 0.1-26.0% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.6-11.7 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

There was 1 serious near-miss and 4 close passes as defined by PET under 1.5 s and 1.5-3.0 s.

The serious near-miss had a PET of 0.9 s with a bus at 21.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk was 0.7%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.

A close pass had a PET of 2.0 s with a van at 55.2 km/h.

A close pass had a PET of 2.1 s with a bus at 49.3 km/h.

A close pass had a PET of 2.3 s with a car at 32.6 km/h.

A close pass had a PET of 2.4 s with a van at 39.5 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 when scaled from 34.6 minutes, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and that broken tracks can double-count by 1.3x. Also 93.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 8 gaps of 12 s or more and longest gap 53.8 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. We are not stating that any standard is met.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing to reduce approach speeds and give priority to pedestrians at this location.

We can share the video and tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school on River Lane

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write to request a safer crossing outside our school.

We observed the crossing for 31.5 minutes and recorded 11 crossings and 8 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 49.9 km/h. The video showed 1 gap of 12 s or more with no moving vehicle.

We use the definition that a serious near-miss is a pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and a close pass is 1.5 to 3.0 s apart. In that period there were 0 serious near-misses and 1 close pass.

The worst event was a close pass with a gap of 2.7 s between pedestrian and vehicle. The vehicle involved was a car travelling at 47.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 0.0% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, based on 21 pedestrians and 15 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 31.5 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and that broken tracks can overcount by 1.3x in our drone test. 45.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 7 gaps of 6 s or more including 1 gap of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 83.0 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and protect people crossing.

We are willing to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at River Lane crossing

We write regarding the River Lane crossing outside our school. Crossing Watch recorded 35 crossings and 6 moving vehicles in 16.6 minutes (996.0 s) of video using SAM tracking and road-plane geometry.

6 of 35 crossings (1 in 5.8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person; 2 of 35 (1 in 18) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 6.6-33.6% and 0.7-19.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 2.2-13.1 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

There were 2 serious near-misses (post-encroachment time less than 1.5 s) and 4 close passes (1.5-3.0 s).
One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.6 s with an auto-rickshaw travelling at 33.8 km/h. Adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 2.1% per Rosen & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts, falling to 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.
One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.2 s with a car travelling at 32.9 km/h. Adult death risk if hit at that speed is 1.9%, falling to 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.
One close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.8 s with a car travelling at 56.4 km/h. Adult death risk if hit at that speed is 7.2%.

The 85th percentile speed was 54.6 km/h.
67.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 4 gaps, 2 of them 12 s or more, longest 54.8 s. The first and last are cut short by the video.
PV2 was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 127 pedestrians and 22 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 16.6 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table to reduce vehicle speeds toward 20 km/h where adult death risk is lower. We are willing to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the crossing outside our school on Bridge Street.

A 3.8 minute recording (228.0 s) counted 10 pedestrian crossings and 24 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 28.8 km/h. 80.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more. In that time, 3 of 10 crossings (1 in 3.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 2 of 10 (1 in 5) within 1.5 s.

There were 2 serious near-misses where pedestrian and moving vehicle were on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and 1 close pass where they were 1.5-3.0 s apart. 1 serious near-miss involved a car at 29.5 km/h with a gap of 0.8 s. Another serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 18.0 km/h with a gap of 0.4 s. A close pass involved a bus at 17.1 km/h with a gap of 2.2 s. For an adult hit by a car front at 29.5 km/h the death risk is 1.4%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.

Assessment of PV² hourly rates needs at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 3.8 minutes. During the recording 80.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 7 gaps, 5 of them 12 s or more, longest 16.8 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing to slow traffic and protect people crossing.

We are happy to share the video for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at the Bridge Street crossing

Our school arranged Crossing Watch measurements at the Bridge Street crossing made by SAM tracking with road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time. In 29.3 minutes (1758.0 s) of video, 12 crossings and 29 vehicles were recorded, with an 85th percentile speed of 56.5 km/h. The recording showed 1 serious near-miss in all.

4 of 12 crossings (1 in 3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person; 2 of 12 (1 in 6) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 9.9-65.1% and 2.1-48.4% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 1.1-10.2 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The 2 serious near-misses included one with a post-encroachment time of 1.0 s with an auto-rickshaw at 52.8 km/h, where the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 10.5% from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.
Another serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.0 s with an auto-rickshaw at 37.1 km/h, where the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 2.8%.
A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.8 s with a car at 25.8 km/h, where the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 0.4%.
A further close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.9 s with a motorcycle at 21.5 km/h, where the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 0.2%.

For context, PV2 was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 25 pedestrians and 59 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 29.3 minutes of video, but a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one twice at 1.3x the true count in our drone test.
63.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with 7 such gaps, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h approach signs at this crossing.
We have retained the video files from the 29.3 minute recording and can share them on request for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write regarding the Canal Road crossing where we analysed 8.1 minutes (486.0 s) of video using SAM tracking and road-plane geometry.

In that time we counted 8 pedestrian crossings and 19 moving vehicles.
The 85th percentile speed was 43.8 km/h. Most drivers were exceeding the posted 30 km/h speed limit.
We recorded 5 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 0 close passes, defined as 1.5-3.0 s.
The pedestrian was first in 2 cases and the vehicle first in 3 cases, with 0 cases both at once.
All death-risk figures below are for adults hit by a car front per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.

The most severe near-miss was a car at 40.0 km/h with 0.3 s between pedestrian and vehicle, carrying a 3.6% adult death risk if hit (0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h).
Another near-miss was a motorcycle at 36.9 km/h with 0.3 s gap, carrying a 2.7% adult death risk (0.6% at 20.0 km/h).
A third near-miss was a car at 23.6 km/h with 1.1 s gap, carrying a 0.8% adult death risk (0.6% at 20.0 km/h).
A fourth near-miss was a car at 19.3 km/h with 0.4 s gap, carrying a 0.6% adult death risk (0.6% at 19.3 km/h).
A fifth near-miss was a van at 17.5 km/h with 1.1 s gap, carrying a 0.5% adult death risk (0.5% at 17.5 km/h).

On engineering context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 8.1 minutes.
Separately, 72.9% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 10 gaps, 8 of them 12 s or more, longest 50.1 s, noting the first and last are cut short by the video.
UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds, while other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce speeds and give pedestrians priority.
We are happy to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority
Subject: Request for safer crossing outside school on River Lane

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write regarding the River Lane crossing outside our school. Crossing Watch recorded 25 crossings in 36.0 minutes with 10 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 56.9 km/h. In the near-miss with a time gap of 0.1 s, the bus reached the spot before the pedestrian.

In that period 2 of 25 crossings (1 in 12) were serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 2 of 25 (1 in 12) were within 3 s. Exact 95% ranges if this recording is typical are 1.0-26.0% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The most severe was a bus at 52.9 km/h passing 0.1 s after a person. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 10.6% from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.

The second serious near-miss was a van at 22.9 km/h passing 1.3 s after a person. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.8%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, scaled from 36.0 minutes of video while a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one twice. Also, 62.4% of time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 3 such gaps and longest 81.8 s, though the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for pupils crossing.

We have the video and tracking data and are happy to share them for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for raised zebra crossing at Canal Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning safety at Canal Road crossing outside our school.

A video survey of 10.8 minutes (648.0 s) recorded 7 pedestrian crossings and 10 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 58.5 km/h.

In that time 2 of 7 crossings (1 in 3.5) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 2 of 7 (1 in 3.5) within 1.5 s.

There were 2 serious near-misses where pedestrian and moving vehicle were on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart.

The 1st serious near-miss had a gap of 1.3 s with a bus at 55.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 12.7% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 0.0 km/h.

The 2nd serious near-miss had a gap of 0.1 s with a car at 54.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 11.7%, compared with 0.6% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 20.0 km/h.

For context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 10.8 minutes.

50.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 10 gaps of 6 s or more, 8 of them 12 s or more and longest 15.5 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. During the 10.8 minutes there were 7 crossings, 10 vehicles, and 10 gaps of at least 6 s with 8 of those at least 12 s and the longest at 15.5 s.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with 20 km/h zone signs to reduce vehicle speeds and protect children crossing.

We are willing to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Lantern Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write on behalf of the school regarding pedestrian safety at Lantern Road crossing.

A video survey by Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) measured 29.9 minutes (1794.0 s) of activity. In that period there were 23 crossings and 13 vehicles. That 29.9 minutes included 4 serious near-misses and 1 close pass. The 85th percentile speed was 64.7 km/h.

The survey uses the definition serious: pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart; close pass: 1.5-3.0 s. It recorded 4 serious near-misses and 1 close pass. In 2 cases the person crossed first, in 3 cases the vehicle passed first, and in 0 cases both were there at once.

The worst incidents were:
One serious near-miss had 0.2 s between pedestrian and vehicle, an auto-rickshaw at 58.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 15.9%, compared to 0.6% at an impact speed of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20.0 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
Another serious near-miss had 0.9 s between pedestrian and vehicle, a van at 41.0 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front the death risk would be 3.9%, compared to 0.2% at an impact speed of 7.4 km/h if limited to 20.0 km/h.
Another serious near-miss had 0.3 s between pedestrian and vehicle, an auto-rickshaw at 32.6 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front the death risk would be 1.9%, compared to 0.6% at an impact speed of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20.0 km/h.
Another serious near-miss had 0.2 s between pedestrian and vehicle, a motorcycle at 24.4 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front the death risk would be 0.9%, compared to 0.6% at an impact speed of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20.0 km/h.
One close pass had 2.3 s between pedestrian and vehicle, an auto-rickshaw at 50.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front the death risk would be 0.8%, compared to 0.0% at an impact speed of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20.0 km/h.

On engineering context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 46 pedestrians and 26 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 29.9 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice at 1.3x the true count in drone tests. Also, 54.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, from 5 gaps with 0 of them 12 s or more and longest 9.7 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you provide a raised zebra crossing with 20 km/h speed table at this location to reduce speeds and protect children and adults crossing.

We are happy to share the video and measurements for your review and to meet on site.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,

LETTER:
Dear Road Authority Officer,

We write about the Market Street crossing outside our school. Crossing Watch video analysis (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) measured 6 pedestrian crossings and 31 moving vehicles in 5.1 minutes (306.0 s).

In that period 6 of 6 crossings (1 in 1) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 2 of 6 (1 in 3) within 1.5 s. The most severe serious near-miss left 1.2 s between the person and a car travelling at 44.6 km/h, with an estimated adult fatality risk of 5.3% if hit by a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+). The people crossing in these events were our students.

A second serious near-miss left 1.4 s between the person and a car travelling at 12.3 km/h, with an estimated adult fatality risk of 0.3% if hit by a car front.

One close pass left 1.8 s between the person and a bus travelling at 59.6 km/h.

Another close pass left 1.8 s between the person and a car travelling at 46.6 km/h, with an estimated adult fatality risk of 3.1% if hit by a car front.

A further close pass left 2.1 s between the person and a motorcycle travelling at 52.7 km/h.

In total there were 2 serious near-misses and 4 close passes, with the person first in 1 case and the vehicle first in 5 cases.

For engineering context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 5.1 minutes with 6 pedestrian crossings and 31 moving vehicles, so any rate must be treated with caution.

77.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 10 gaps and 6 of them 12 s or more and a longest gap of 87.2 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

To reduce speeds, where the 85th percentile was 66.1 km/h, and to give pedestrians protected priority, we request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location.

We can share the video and measurements on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 9.9-65.1% and 5.5-57.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.1-10.2 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The video found 3 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart. The worst serious near-miss was 1.2 s apart involving an auto-rickshaw at 47.4 km/h. A second serious near-miss was 0.2 s apart involving a van at 44.0 km/h. A third serious near-miss was 0.4 s apart involving an auto-rickshaw at 13.1 km/h. The close pass was 1.9 s apart involving a car at 50.1 km/h.
For adults hit by a car front, Rosén and Sander 2009 gives an adult death risk if hit of 6.7% for the 47.4 km/h case, 5.0% for the 44.0 km/h case, 0.3% for the 13.1 km/h case, and 3.2% for the 50.1 km/h case. For context, PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 11.1 minutes. The recording also shows 66.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 such gaps and 3 of them 12 s or more and a longest gap of 33.6 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h markings at this location.

We are willing to share the video and measurement files for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school asked for a short video survey at River Lane crossing. The recording lasted 6.8 minutes (408.0 s). In that time 9 pedestrian crossings and 32 moving vehicles were counted. The 85th percentile speed was 30.4 km/h. 4 of 9 crossings (1 in 2.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 4 of 9 crossings (1 in 2.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 13.7-78.8% and 13.7-78.8% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.1-10.2 and 1.1-10.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

For engineering context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 6.8. Counted: 9 pedestrian crossings, 32 moving vehicles. 91.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 11 gaps, 10 of them 12 s or more, longest 86.0 s, with the first and last gaps cut short by the video. UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds and other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

The 4 serious near-misses (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) included a car at 28.4 km/h with a gap of 1.2 s. For that car the estimated death risk if an adult is hit by a car front is 1.3%, compared with 0.4% at an impact of 14.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h.

All death-risk figures are from Rosén & Sander 2009, for adults 15+ hit by car fronts.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at River Lane crossing.

We can share the video and the Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) measurements on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

From the Head of the School, Ring Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We request that you make the crossing outside our school safer by installing a raised zebra crossing with speed table.

Crossing Watch made measurements from video of the crossing using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time. The video covered 6.7 minutes (402.0 s). There were 3 serious near-misses and 1 close pass. Serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart. Close pass is 1.5 to 3.0 s. Of the interactions, 3 were person first, 1 was vehicle first and 0 were both at once.

The worst incidents were as follows. A bus at 55.2 km/h had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 12.6% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.0%.
A car at 37.3 km/h had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 2.8%. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.0%.

On engineering context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video. This video is 6.7 minutes with 6 pedestrian crossings and 23 moving vehicles, so PV² cannot be assessed. 44.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed. There were 5 such gaps, 4 of them 12 s or more, longest 47.1 s. The first and last gaps are cut short by the video. The UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4 to 6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds, while other groups, such as children, may need 10 to 12 s or longer.

We ask you to install the raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location and to consider a 20 km/h zone with signs. We are ready to share the video and the measurements to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the crossing outside our school on River Lane crossing.

Measurements from Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) over 17.7 minutes (1062.0 s) recorded 13 crossings and 19 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 55.5 km/h. In total, 4 close passes were measured.

The worst cases were:
The 1st serious near-miss involved a motorcycle at 47.5 km/h with 1.0 s between pedestrian and vehicle. The adult death risk if hit by a car front was 6.8 % (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), with 0.0 km/h impact and 0.0 % risk at a 20 km/h limit.
The 2nd serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 43.7 km/h with 0.3 s between. The adult death risk if hit by a car front was 4.9 %, with 20.0 km/h impact and 0.6 % risk at a 20 km/h limit.

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school on Station Road

We write following a Crossing Watch measurement at the Station Road crossing over 24.2 minutes (1452.0 s). In that time 38 crossings and 8 vehicles were recorded, the 85th percentile speed was 44.1 km/h, there were 8 gaps of 6 s or more and 7 gaps of 12 s or more with the longest gap 53.4 s, and 89.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more. 38 gaps were cut short by the start or end of the video. 6 of 38 crossings (1 in 6.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 5 of 38 (1 in 7.6) within 1.5 s; exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 6.0-31.3% and 4.4-28.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 1.6-11.7 people in a recording this long (Poisson). Of the 6 events within 3 s, 4 were person first and 2 were vehicle first, with 5 serious near-misses less than 1.5 s apart and 1 close pass 1.5-3.0 s apart as defined.

The 5 serious near-misses were as follows. One involved a bus at 44.5 km/h with 1.0 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 5.2% death risk (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved a car at 39.5 km/h with 1.2 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 3.4% death risk, compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved an auto-rickshaw at 37.6 km/h with 0.3 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 2.9% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved an auto-rickshaw at 27.9 km/h with 0.7 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 1.2% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved a car at 21.4 km/h with 0.5 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 0.7% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h.

The engineering note recorded PV² as 0.0 x 10^8 from 94 pedestrians and 20 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 24.2 minutes, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice (1.3x in our drone test). It also recorded that 89.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location to slow traffic to 20 km/h and protect those crossing. We will share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements on request and welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school on Station Road

We write following a Crossing Watch measurement at the Station Road crossing over 24.2 minutes (1452.0 s). In that time 38 crossings and 8 vehicles were recorded, the 85th percentile speed was 44.1 km/h, there were 8 gaps of 6 s or more and 7 gaps of 12 s or more with the longest gap 53.4 s, and 89.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more. The video showed 38 gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle. 6 of 38 crossings (1 in 6.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 5 of 38 (1 in 7.6) within 1.5 s; exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 6.0-31.3% and 4.4-28.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 1.6-11.7 people in a recording this long (Poisson). Of the 6 events within 3 s, 4 were person first and 2 were vehicle first, with 5 serious near-misses less than 1.5 s apart and 1 close pass 1.5-3.0 s apart as defined.

The 5 serious near-misses were as follows. One involved a bus at 44.5 km/h with 1.0 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 5.2% death risk (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved a car at 39.5 km/h with 1.2 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 3.4% death risk, compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved an auto-rickshaw at 37.6 km/h with 0.3 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 2.9% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved an auto-rickshaw at 27.9 km/h with 0.7 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 1.2% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved a car at 21.4 km/h with 0.5 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 0.7% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h.

The engineering note recorded PV² as 0.0 x 10^8 from 94 pedestrians and 20 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 24.2 minutes, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice (1.3x in our drone test). It also recorded that 89.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location to slow traffic to 20 km/h and protect those crossing. We will share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements on request and welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

We write concerning the crossing on River Lane outside our school. We monitored the crossing by video for 24.7 minutes (1482.0 s) and counted 14 pedestrian crossings and 16 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 46.9 km/h. In total, 5 close passes were measured.

We recorded 1 serious near-miss defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and 1 close pass defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart, with 2 cases where the vehicle arrived first, 0 where the person arrived first and 0 where both arrived at once.

The serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.9 s and involved a car travelling at 41.4 km/h.
For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 4.0%, compared with 0.2% if impact were at 5.8 km/h under a 20 km/h limit (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

The close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.1 s and involved a bus travelling at 30.5 km/h.
For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 0.1%, compared with 0.0% if impact were at 0.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

For context, engineering estimates scale to 34 pedestrians and 39 vehicles an hour to give PV² = 0.0 x 10^8, but a formal check counts the full peak hour and our method can overcount pedestrians by 1.3x due to broken tracks, scaled from 24.7 minutes of video.
84.9% of the observed time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 8 gaps, 5 of them 12 s or more, longest 35.3 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce approach speeds and give priority to those crossing.

We are happy to share the video and tracking data for your review and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Station Road crossing

We write as the school using the crossing outside our gate. Crossing Watch video covering 25.6 minutes (1536.0 s) recorded 8 pedestrian crossings and 35 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 57.9 km/h. The video showed 11 gaps of 12 s or more with no moving vehicle.

The analysis found 4 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 2 close passes defined as 1.5 s to 3.0 s apart. Of the 8 potential conflicts, 4 had the person first, 2 had the vehicle first, and 0 had both at once.

The worst near-misses were:
- 1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.5 s with an auto-rickshaw at 59.9 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 18.1%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
- 1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.6 s with a van at 51.1 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 9.1%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 19.1 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
- 1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.9 s with a bus at 40.7 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 3.8%, compared with 0.2% at an impact of 8.1 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
- 1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.5 s with a car at 30.1 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 1.5%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
- 1 close pass had a gap of 2.2 s with a car at 51.9 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 1.4%, compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
All death-risk figures are from Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults aged 15+ hit by car fronts.

For context, the video gives PV² of 0.0 x 10^8 from 19 pedestrians and 82 vehicles per hour, with the caveat that this is scaled from 25.6 minutes not a full peak hour and our test shows broken tracks can overcount pedestrians by 1.3x. Also, 62.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 11 such gaps including 3 of 12 s or more and longest 74.2 s, with the caveat that first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and give priority to pedestrians.

We have the video and Crossing Watch data and are happy to share them for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Canal Road crossing

We write from the school served by Canal Road crossing. A 30.2 minute video recording (1812.0 s) recorded 40 pedestrian crossings and 35 vehicles at the site.
5 of 40 crossings (1 in 8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 4 of 40 (1 in 10) were within 1.5 s, defined as serious.
The 85th percentile speed was 64.4 km/h.
The worst serious near-miss involved a motorcycle at 59.6 km/h with 0.1 s between person and vehicle on the same spot; if hit by a car front at that speed the risk of death for an adult is 17.8%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h, source Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.
A second serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 34.5 km/h with 1.1 s between person and vehicle; the adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 2.2%.
A third serious near-miss involved a bus at 18.7 km/h with 0.0 s between person and vehicle; the adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.5%.
A fourth serious near-miss involved a car at 14.1 km/h with 0.7 s between person and vehicle; the adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.4%.
A close pass involved an auto-rickshaw at 48.0 km/h with 2.1 s between person and vehicle; the adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 1.4%.
For engineering context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 79 pedestrians and 70 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 30.2 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and the pedestrian count method can overcount. 43.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, based on 1 gap with longest 8.2 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.
We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this crossing to reduce speeds and provide priority for people crossing. A child hit at these speeds would have faced a far higher chance of dying, making immediate intervention essential.
We are willing to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

We write regarding the safety of the crossing outside our school on Market Street.

We arranged a video-based Crossing Watch for 36.4 minutes (2184.0 s). In that time 35 crossings and 39 vehicles were observed. 6 of 35 crossings (1 in 5.8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 35 crossings (1 in 12) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 6.6-33.6% and 1.8-23.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile speed was 57.4 km/h. The closest near-miss measured had a time gap of 1.0 s.

By definition a serious near-miss is less than 1.5 s apart and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s apart.
One serious near-miss had a PET of 0.7 s with a car at 57.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 14.9% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+).
A second serious near-miss had a PET of 1.0 s with a van at 47.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 6.6%.
A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.5 s with a car at 39.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 3.3%.
A close pass had a PET of 1.8 s with a car at 21.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.3%.
A further close pass had a PET of 2.7 s with a van at 59.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front the recorded death risk is 0.0%.
At a 20 km/h limit the modelled adult death risks for these events would fall to 0.0%, 0.0%, 0.6%, 0.0% and 0.0% respectively.

In engineering terms, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, from 58 pedestrians and 64 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 36.4 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour. 69.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 10 such gaps, 1 of them 12 s or more and the longest 56.1 s; the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

Given these measurements we request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We are willing to share the video and tracking data for your review and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

We write regarding the safety of the crossing outside our school on Market Street.

We arranged a video-based Crossing Watch for 36.4 minutes (2184.0 s). In that time 35 crossings and 39 vehicles were observed. 6 of 35 crossings (1 in 5.8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 35 crossings (1 in 12) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 6.6-33.6% and 1.8-23.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile speed was 57.4 km/h. 69.4% of the time was inside gaps of 12 s or more.

By definition a serious near-miss is less than 1.5 s apart and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s apart.
One serious near-miss had a PET of 0.7 s with a car at 57.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 14.9% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+).
A second serious near-miss had a PET of 1.0 s with a van at 47.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 6.6%.
A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.5 s with a car at 39.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 3.3%.
A close pass had a PET of 1.8 s with a car at 21.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.3%.
A further close pass had a PET of 2.7 s with a van at 59.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front the recorded death risk is 0.0%.
At a 20 km/h limit the modelled adult death risks for these events would fall to 0.0%, 0.0%, 0.6%, 0.0% and 0.0% respectively.

In engineering terms, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, from 58 pedestrians and 64 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 36.4 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour. 69.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 10 such gaps, 1 of them 12 s or more and the longest 56.1 s; the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

Given these measurements we request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We are willing to share the video and tracking data for your review and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal
