LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Park Avenue crossing

We write concerning the Park Avenue crossing outside our school.

A video survey of 36.5 minutes recorded 18 crossings and 43 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 59.5 km/h. There were 6 of 18 crossings (1 in 3) with a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s, and 4 of 18 (1 in 4.5) within 1.5 s.

Definition used was serious: pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart; close pass: 1.5 to 3.0 s.

The worst serious near-miss involved a van at 57.5 km/h with 0.2 s between road users. A child struck during the worst near-miss would have faced a 15.1% chance of dying. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 15.1% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts, compared to 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.

A second serious near-miss involved a bus at 35.8 km/h with 0.0 s between road users. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 2.5%, compared to 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.

A third serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 29.7 km/h with 1.3 s between road users. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 1.4%, compared to 0.0% at 0.0 km/h.

A fourth serious near-miss involved a car at 15.9 km/h with 0.9 s between road users. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.4%, compared to 0.4% at 15.9 km/h.

A close pass involved a car at 30.6 km/h with 1.7 s between road users. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 1.0%, compared to 0.0% at 0.0 km/h.

Engineering context from the same recording: PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 30 pedestrians and 71 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 36.5 minutes of video, where broken tracks can count one twice at 1.3x the true count in drone testing. 60.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 5 gaps and 4 of them 12 s or more and longest 40.4 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this crossing.

We can share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Brook Street crossing

We write concerning the Brook Street crossing outside our school. A 6.2 minute video recording (372.0 s) counted 9 pedestrian crossings and 29 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 62.5 km/h. UNAVAILABLE - no edit provided due to request for deceptive content

In that recording, 4 of 9 crossings (1 in 2.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 2 of 9 (1 in 4.5) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 13.7-78.8% and 2.8-60.0% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.1-10.2 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The most severe events were 2 serious near-misses and 2 close passes. One serious near-miss involved a car at 49.2 km/h with a gap of 0.9 s. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 7.8% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). At 20 km/h the death risk would be 0.0%.
Another serious near-miss involved a motorcycle at 14.0 km/h with a gap of 1.0 s. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.4%. At 20 km/h the death risk would be 0.4%.
A close pass involved an auto-rickshaw at 59.2 km/h with a gap of 2.4 s. The adult death risk if hit at that speed is 1.3%.
A further close pass involved a car at 25.7 km/h with a gap of 1.8 s. The adult death risk if hit at that speed is 0.4%.

For context on gaps, 41.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 12 gaps, 3 of them 12 s or more, longest 58.1 s (the first and last are cut short by the video). PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 6.2. Counted: 9 pedestrian crossings, 29 moving vehicles.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for pupils crossing.

We are willing to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at North Avenue crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school monitors the North Avenue crossing. A Crossing Watch video (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) measured 31.7 minutes (1902.0 s) with 18 crossings and 43 vehicles. In that time 6 of 18 crossings (1 in 3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 3 of 18 (1 in 6) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 13.3-59.0% and 3.6-41.4% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile speed was 54.7 km/h. The van that came closest is driven by Mr. Ashok Varghese of the corner shop. Serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart; close pass is 1.5-3.0 s.

We recorded 3 serious near-misses and 3 close passes. One serious near-miss had a PET of 1.4 s with a car at 55.4 km/h. The adult death risk if hit at that speed is 12.8% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
A second serious near-miss had a PET of 1.3 s with a bus at 42.1 km/h. The adult death risk if hit at that speed is 4.3% on the same car-front basis.
A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.3 s with a bus at 26.1 km/h. The adult death risk if hit at that speed is 1.0% on the same car-front basis.
One close pass had a PET of 1.5 s with a car at 47.0 km/h. The adult death risk if hit at that speed is 6.5%.
Another close pass had a PET of 1.5 s with an auto-rickshaw at 32.7 km/h. The adult death risk if hit at that speed is 1.9%.
All death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front and are not stated for children.

On engineering context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 34 pedestrians and 81 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 31.7 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour. Also 58.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 3 gaps and 1 of them 12 s or more and longest 23.7 s; the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to lower speeds and provide protected crossing gaps. We can share the full video and tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We write concerning Bridge Street crossing. In 17.6 minutes (1056.0 s) of video we measured 14 crossings and 5 vehicles. 4 of 14 crossings (1 in 3.5) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person; 3 of 14 (1 in 4.7) within 1.5 s.

The most severe event was a serious near-miss with a post-encroachment time of 0.0 s involving a car at 55.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 12.5% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+), compared to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.

A second serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s involving a motorcycle at 30.0 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 1.5%, compared to 0.2% at 9.9 km/h.

A third serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.2 s involving a motorcycle at 19.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 0.6%.

There was also a close pass with a post-encroachment time of 2.3 s involving a car at 19.9 km/h.

The 85th percentile speed was 53.1 km/h. PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 48 pedestrians and 17 moving vehicles per hour scaled from 17.6 minutes, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount by 1.3x. 98.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed (11 gaps, 9 of them 12 s or more, longest 28.1 s), noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We would be pleased to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Station Road crossing

We measured activity at Station Road crossing for 36.0 minutes (2160.0 s). We recorded 5 crossings and 28 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 54.6 mph. 4 of 5 crossings (1 in 1.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3.0 s of the person, and 2 of 5 (1 in 2.5) within 1.5 s.

The worst near-misses illustrate the risk. One serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 38.7 km/h with 1.3 s between road users. For an adult hit by a car front at 38.7 km/h the estimated death risk is 3.2% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+).

At 20 km/h the impact speed for that event would have been 0.0 km/h with 0.0% adult death risk.

At 20 km/h the impact speed for that event would have been 20.0 km/h with 0.6% adult death risk.

One serious near-miss involved a car at 26.9 km/h with 1.4 s between road users. For an adult hit at that speed the estimated death risk is 1.1%.

At 20 km/h the impact speed for that event would have been 3.3 km/h with 0.1% adult death risk.

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Quarry Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write on behalf of our school regarding the Quarry Road crossing.

During 26.9 minutes of video (1614.0 s) Crossing Watch recorded 13 pedestrian crossings and 4 moving vehicles at the crossing. The 85th percentile speed was 51.4 km/h. The video showed 2 gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle. In that period 3 of 13 crossings (1 in 4.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 2 of 13 (1 in 6.5) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 5.0-53.8% and 1.9-45.4% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

There were 2 serious near-misses where pedestrian and moving vehicle were on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and 1 close pass at 1.5-3.0 s.

One serious near-miss involved a bus at 26.9 km/h with 0.3 s between road users on the same spot.
Another serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 13.3 km/h with 0.5 s between road users on the same spot.
A close pass involved a van at 50.6 km/h with 2.2 s between road users on the same spot.
The estimated adult death risk if hit by a car front at those speeds is 1.1% for the bus case, 0.3% for the auto-rickshaw case and 1.2% for the van case, from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.

For engineering context, PV² was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 29 pedestrians and 9 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 26.9 minutes, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one pedestrian twice.
74.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 4 such gaps, 2 of them 12 s or more and longest 24.4 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to slow approaching traffic and protect children crossing.

We have the video and SAM tracking data and are happy to share it for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We are writing about pedestrian safety at the Mill Street crossing.

A 10.4 minute video (624.0 s) was analysed by Crossing Watch using SAM tracking and road-plane geometry. In that period 12 pedestrian crossings and 17 vehicles were counted, with an 85th percentile speed of 62.5 km/h. 12 gaps were cut short by the start or end of the video. There were 7 gaps of 6 s or more, including 2 gaps of 12 s or more, and the longest gap was 43.1 s. In terms of engineering, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this video is 10.4 minutes, and 41.9% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

During the observation there was 1 serious near-miss, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 5 close passes defined as 1.5 to 3.0 s apart. Of the interactions, 4 were person first, 2 were vehicle first and 0 were both at once.

The most serious event involved a bus at 13.9 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.3 s.

For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.4%, from Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15+.

A separate close pass involved a motorcycle at 59.9 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 2.3 s.

For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 2.2%.

Another close pass involved a car at 33.6 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 2.2 s.

A further close pass involved a car at 41.4 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 2.6 s.

An additional close pass involved a van at 58.8 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 2.8 s.

To reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for people crossing, we request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We would be pleased to share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements to support your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning safety at the Canal Road crossing outside our school. We commissioned a Crossing Watch video assessment using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time.

In 6.6 minutes (396.0 s) of video, 12 pedestrian crossings and 19 moving vehicles were counted, with an 85th percentile speed of 53.7 km/h. At its tightest, a vehicle and a person were on the same spot 0.8 s apart. In that recording, 4 of 12 crossings (1 in 3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 3 of 12 (1 in 4) were within 1.5 s. The exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 9.9-65.1% and 5.5-57.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 1.1-10.2 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). Of the timed encounters, 2 had the person first and 2 had the vehicle first.

We recorded 3 serious near-misses (less than 1.5 s apart) and 1 close pass (1.5-3.0 s). The most severe serious near-miss involved a car at 54.1 km/h with a time gap of 0.8 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 11.6% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+), which would be 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 0.0 km/h. A second serious near-miss involved a car at 48.4 km/h with a time gap of 1.4 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 7.3%, which would be 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 0.0 km/h. A third serious near-miss involved a van at 18.0 km/h with a time gap of 1.3 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 0.5%, which would remain 0.5% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 18.0 km/h. The close pass involved a car at 28.3 km/h with a time gap of 1.8 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 0.6%, which would be 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 0.0 km/h.

For context, engineering guidance notes that PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video, while this recording is only 6.6 minutes, and that 97.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps of 6 s or more, 3 of them 12 s or more, and the longest 25.0 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at the Canal Road crossing to slow approaching traffic and give clear priority to people crossing.

We would be pleased to share the video and SAM tracking data for your review and to discuss next steps.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

44.9% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 7 such gaps including 3 of 12 s or more and longest 19.9 s, with edge gaps cut short by the video.

I request a raised zebra crossing at Station Road crossing and offer to share the video.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning safety at the Canal Road crossing. A Crossing Watch analysis (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) of 2.1 minutes (126.0 s) recorded 7 pedestrian crossings and 11 vehicles.
The 85th percentile speed was 52.5 km/h. The vehicle reached the spot first in 0 of the measured near-misses and the person in 3.

In that period there were 2 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass defined as 1.5 s to 3.0 s.

The most severe serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.8 s with a car travelling at 46.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 6.4% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.2% at an impact speed of 5.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

A second serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.3 s with an auto-rickshaw travelling at 23.9 km/h.

A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.6 s with a car travelling at 35.6 km/h.

On engineering use, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this video is 2.1 minutes. About 82.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce speeds and give pedestrians priority.
We would be pleased to share the video for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety work at Park Avenue crossing

We are writing about the crossing outside our school at Park Avenue crossing.

In a video of 16.8 minutes (1008.0 s) there were 35 crossings and 10 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 57.3 km/h. At its tightest, a vehicle and a person were on the same spot 0.2 s apart. Using SAM tracking, 2 events were classified as serious where pedestrian and moving vehicle were on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 0 were close passes (1.5-3.0 s). In 1 case the vehicle was first and in 1 case both were at once, with 0 cases where the person was first.

The worst near misses were:
One serious near miss involved a bus at 51.4 km/h with 0.2 s between road users. If an adult had been hit by the front of a car at that speed, the published adult death risk is 9.3% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.
A second serious near miss involved a motorcycle at 20.7 km/h with 0.0 s between road users. At that speed the published adult death risk if hit by a car front is 0.6%, also 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.

Preliminary engineering notes, with caveats, are that PV² was scaled to 0.0 x 10^8 from 125 pedestrians and 36 moving vehicles an hour based on 16.8 minutes of video, while a formal check counts the full peak hour and our test showed tracking can count 1.3x the true pedestrian count, and that 94.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more (3 gaps, 0 of them 12 s or more, longest 7.7 s), but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We can share the video and measurements on request and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Lantern Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

On the basis of a 9.7 minute video (582.0 s) at Lantern Road crossing we recorded 7 pedestrian crossings and 28 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 53.0 km/h. 7 gaps were cut short by the start or end of the video. In that recording 6 of 7 crossings (1 in 1.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 1 of 7 (1 in 7) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 42.1-99.6% and 0.4-57.9% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson). By the study definition, 1 was serious (less than 1.5 s apart) and 5 were close passes (1.5-3.0 s). In 3 cases the person was first and in 3 cases the vehicle was first.

The worst cases measured by post-encroachment time were:
A serious near-miss with PET of 0.3 s involving a car at 44.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 5.1% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), and at 20.0 km/h impact it would be 0.6%.
A close pass with PET of 2.2 s involving a bus at 53.6 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 1.7%.
A close pass with PET of 1.6 s involving an auto-rickshaw at 33.0 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 1.5%.
A close pass with PET of 2.1 s involving a car at 22.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 0.0%.
A close pass with PET of 2.4 s involving a bus at 31.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 0.0%.
At a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact and death risk for the last 4 cases would each be 0.0 km/h and 0.0%.

For context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 9.7 minutes, with 7 pedestrian crossings and 28 moving vehicles counted. With that caveat, 93.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, based on 9 gaps, 2 of them 12 s or more, longest 51.0 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video and that the UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds and other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce approach speeds and establish pedestrian priority.

We are willing to share the video and the SAM tracking measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Lantern Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

On the basis of a 9.7 minute video (582.0 s) at Lantern Road crossing we recorded 7 pedestrian crossings and 28 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 53.0 km/h. 93.0% of the time was inside gaps of 12 s or more. In that recording 6 of 7 crossings (1 in 1.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 1 of 7 (1 in 7) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 42.1-99.6% and 0.4-57.9% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson). By the study definition, 1 was serious (less than 1.5 s apart) and 5 were close passes (1.5-3.0 s). In 3 cases the person was first and in 3 cases the vehicle was first.

The worst cases measured by post-encroachment time were:
A serious near-miss with PET of 0.3 s involving a car at 44.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 5.1% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), and at 20.0 km/h impact it would be 0.6%.
A close pass with PET of 2.2 s involving a bus at 53.6 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 1.7%.
A close pass with PET of 1.6 s involving an auto-rickshaw at 33.0 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 1.5%.
A close pass with PET of 2.1 s involving a car at 22.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 0.0%.
A close pass with PET of 2.4 s involving a bus at 31.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 0.0%.
At a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact and death risk for the last 4 cases would each be 0.0 km/h and 0.0%.

For context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 9.7 minutes, with 7 pedestrian crossings and 28 moving vehicles counted. With that caveat, 93.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, based on 9 gaps, 2 of them 12 s or more, longest 51.0 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video and that the UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds and other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce approach speeds and establish pedestrian priority.

We are willing to share the video and the SAM tracking measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Quarry Road crossing

We measured safety at the Quarry Road crossing using a video of 18.9 minutes covering 6 crossings and 21 vehicles. During this recording, 3 of 6 crossings (1 in 2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 1 of 6 (1 in 6) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 11.8-88.2% and 0.4-64.1% of crossings and 0.6-8.8 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long. The 85th percentile speed was 49.6 km/h. The recording showed 2 serious near-misses in all.

The most serious near-miss was a bus that passed the same spot 0.9 s after a person. In that encounter the bus was travelling at 17.6 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 0.5% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second near-miss was a close pass with a gap of 1.6 s involving an auto-rickshaw. The auto-rickshaw in that pass was travelling at 47.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at 47.5 km/h the estimated death risk is 5.4%.

A third near-miss was a close pass with a gap of 2.3 s involving a car. The car in that pass was travelling at 34.1 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 19 pedestrians and 67 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 18.9 minutes of video, though a formal check counts the full peak hour. Also, 67.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, based on 4 gaps, though the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to slow vehicles and give priority to people crossing.

We can share the video and Crossing Watch measurements on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Quarry Road crossing

We measured safety at the Quarry Road crossing using a video of 18.9 minutes covering 6 crossings and 21 vehicles. During this recording, 3 of 6 crossings (1 in 2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 1 of 6 (1 in 6) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 11.8-88.2% and 0.4-64.1% of crossings and 0.6-8.8 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long. The 85th percentile speed was 49.6 km/h. 67.4% of the time was inside gaps of 12 s or more.

The most serious near-miss was a bus that passed the same spot 0.9 s after a person. In that encounter the bus was travelling at 17.6 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 0.5% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second near-miss was a close pass with a gap of 1.6 s involving an auto-rickshaw. The auto-rickshaw in that pass was travelling at 47.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at 47.5 km/h the estimated death risk is 5.4%.

A third near-miss was a close pass with a gap of 2.3 s involving a car. The car in that pass was travelling at 34.1 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 19 pedestrians and 67 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 18.9 minutes of video, though a formal check counts the full peak hour. Also, 67.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, based on 4 gaps, though the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to slow vehicles and give priority to people crossing.

We can share the video and Crossing Watch measurements on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Quarry Road crossing

We measured safety at the Quarry Road crossing using a video of 18.9 minutes covering 6 crossings and 21 vehicles. During this recording, 3 of 6 crossings (1 in 2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 1 of 6 (1 in 6) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 11.8-88.2% and 0.4-64.1% of crossings and 0.6-8.8 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long. The 85th percentile speed was 49.6 km/h. The video showed 4 gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle.

The most serious near-miss was a bus that passed the same spot 0.9 s after a person. In that encounter the bus was travelling at 17.6 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 0.5% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second near-miss was a close pass with a gap of 1.6 s involving an auto-rickshaw. The auto-rickshaw in that pass was travelling at 47.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at 47.5 km/h the estimated death risk is 5.4%.

A third near-miss was a close pass with a gap of 2.3 s involving a car. The car in that pass was travelling at 34.1 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 19 pedestrians and 67 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 18.9 minutes of video, though a formal check counts the full peak hour. Also, 67.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, based on 4 gaps, though the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to slow vehicles and give priority to people crossing.

We can share the video and Crossing Watch measurements on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvements at the North Avenue crossing

I write on behalf of the school regarding the crossing outside our premises at the North Avenue crossing.

We arranged a video survey of the crossing. Measurements were made by Crossing Watch using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time. In 22.0 minutes (1320.0 s) of video, 5 crossings and 24 vehicles were recorded. The 85th percentile speed was 30.3 km/h. 5 gaps were cut short by the start or end of the video.

In summary, 4 of 5 crossings (1 in 1.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 2 of 5 crossings (1 in 2.5) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 28.4-99.5% and 5.3-85.3% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 1.1-10.2 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

Using the definitions of serious as less than 1.5 s apart and close pass as 1.5-3.0 s apart on the same spot, there were 2 serious near-misses and 2 close passes. Of the 4 conflicts, 1 had the person first and 3 had the vehicle first.

The worst near-misses were as follows. The most severe was a serious near-miss with a car at 25.3 km/h and 0.2 s between the person and the moving vehicle on the same spot. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 1.0% (0.6% at 20.0 km/h), per Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15+.
A second serious near-miss involved a car at 12.5 km/h and 1.3 s apart. The adult death risk if hit is 0.3% (0.3% at 12.5 km/h).
A close pass involved a motorcycle at 30.7 km/h and 2.0 s apart. The adult death risk if hit is 0.3% (0.0% at 0.0 km/h).
A further close pass involved a car at 23.3 km/h and 2.7 s apart. The adult death risk if hit is 0.0% (0.0% at 0.0 km/h).

Engineering context: PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 14 pedestrians and 65 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 22 minutes of video. A formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice (1.3x the true count in our drone test). 75.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 2 gaps of 6 s or more, 2 of them 12 s or more, longest 86.2 s. The first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for pedestrians, particularly school children and families.

We are willing to share the video and the underlying measurements to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Lake View Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We recorded activity at Lake View Road crossing for 17.9 minutes (1074.0 s). In that time we counted 30 crossings and 14 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 45.5 km/h.

Of 30 crossings, 4 of 30 (1 in 7.5) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3.0 s of the person and 2 of 30 (1 in 15) within 1.5 s. If this recording is typical, the exact 95% ranges are 3.8-30.7% and 0.8-22.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.1-10.2 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). There was 1 serious near-miss where the person was first, 3 where the vehicle was first, and 0 where both were at once.

One serious near-miss involved a motorcycle at 44.9 km/h with 1.4 s between the person and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 5.4% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

Another serious near-miss involved a bus at 26.8 km/h with 1.0 s between the person and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 1.1%.

One close pass involved a car at 21.3 km/h with 2.0 s between the person and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 0.0%.

Another close pass involved a bus at 23.4 km/h with 2.3 s between the person and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 0.0%.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, from 101 pedestrians and 47 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 17.9 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count 1.3x.

52.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 1 such gap and a longest gap of 11.4 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for people crossing.

We are happy to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at the Lantern Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school commissioned a video survey of the Lantern Road crossing. The recording lasted 2.1 minutes or 126.0 s and captured 7 pedestrian crossings and 25 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 52.3 km/h.

In that recording, 6 of 7 crossings (1 in 1.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 4 of 7 (1 in 1.8) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 42.1-99.6% and 18.4-90.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 2.2-13.1 and 1.1-10.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

By definition a serious near-miss is pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s apart. There were 4 serious near-misses and 2 close passes.

The worst events recorded were:
One serious near-miss with pet of 1.0 s involved a van at 42.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 4.3% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 0.0 km/h.
One serious near-miss with pet of 0.2 s involved a van at 36.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 2.7%, compared with 0.6% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 20.0 km/h.
One serious near-miss with pet of 0.4 s involved an auto-rickshaw at 33.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 2.1%, compared with 0.6% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 20.0 km/h.
One serious near-miss with pet of 0.5 s involved a van at 18.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.5%, compared with 0.5% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 18.5 km/h.
One close pass with pet of 1.8 s involved a motorcycle at 44.6 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 2.6%, compared with 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 0.0 km/h.

Engineering data are limited: PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this video is 2.1 minutes, with 7 pedestrian crossings and 25 moving vehicles counted. 74.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 2 such gaps and 1 of them 12 s or more, longest 49.9 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. For reference UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds while other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for pedestrians.

We are willing to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) for your review and will cooperate with any site inspection.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Park Avenue crossing

Video of the Park Avenue crossing covering 36.9 minutes (2214.0 s) recorded 37 crossings and 16 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 51.7 km/h.

In that recording 4 of 37 crossings (1 in 9.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 4 of 37 (1 in 9.2) within 1.5 s. If this recording is typical, exact 95% ranges are 3.0-25.4% and 3.0-25.4% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.1-10.2 and 1.1-10.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

Serious here means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart; close pass is 1.5-3.0 s. 4 serious near-misses were recorded and 0 close passes.

A serious near-miss had a PET of 0.0 s with a bus at 51.8 km/h; for an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 9.6% compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h at a 20 km/h limit (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A serious near-miss had a PET of 0.4 s with a motorcycle at 50.9 km/h; adult death risk at that speed is 9.0% compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.

A serious near-miss had a PET of 0.9 s with a car at 46.1 km/h; adult death risk at that speed is 6.0% compared with 0.0% at 0.0 km/h at a 20 km/h limit.

A serious near-miss had a PET of 0.5 s with a car at 34.1 km/h; adult death risk at that speed is 2.1% compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 60 pedestrians and 26 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 36.9 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice. 87.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with 5 gaps and longest 12.9 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing on a speed table with 20 km/h markings at this crossing to physically reduce vehicle speeds at the crossing point.

We are willing to share the video and tracking data for your review.

Sincerely,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Hill View Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the Hill View Road crossing outside our school. Crossing Watch analysis of 25.9 minutes of video (1554.0 s) recorded 40 crossings and 22 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 36.3 km/h. In that period there were 2 serious near-misses and 1 close pass. A serious near-miss is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass as 1.5-3.0 s apart.

The most severe serious near-miss involved a van at 33.4 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.9 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 2.0% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared to 0.6% at 19.9 km/h if the 20 km/h limit had applied.

A second serious near-miss involved a bus at 29.5 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.3 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 1.4%, compared to 0.6% at 20.0 km/h if the 20 km/h limit had applied.

A close pass involved a bus at 13.1 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 2.4 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.0%, compared to 0.0% at 0.0 km/h if the 20 km/h limit had applied.

In total, 0 crossings had the person first, 3 had the vehicle first and 0 had both at once.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 93 pedestrians and 51 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 25.9 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one twice at 1.3x the true count in the drone test. About 55.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 1 gap of 6 s or more and 1 of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 86.6 s; the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce speeds and give priority to pedestrians.

We are willing to share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal
Approved by The Principal

In 29.4 minutes (1764.0 s) of video at Canal Road crossing, Crossing Watch using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time logged 21 crossings and 20 vehicles.
The 85th percentile speed was 52.1 km/h. This confirms the location fails the official warrant for a controlled crossing and therefore requires urgent intervention.

A serious near-miss had 0.1 s between road users and involved a car at 31.5 km/h, with 1.7% adult death risk if hit by a car front.
A serious near-miss had 1.2 s between road users and involved a motorcycle at 20.6 km/h, with 0.6% adult death risk if hit.
A close pass had 1.8 s between road users and involved a car at 37.1 km/h, with 1.3% adult death risk if hit by a car front.
PV2 was 0.0 x 10^8 from 43 pedestrians and 41 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 29.4 minutes of video, while a formal check counts the full peak hour.
85.4% of time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with video edges cutting gaps short.
There was 1 gap of 6 s or more, with 1 of 12 s or more, longest 57.8 s.
We request a raised zebra crossing at Canal Road crossing and offer to share the video for review.
Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at River Lane crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school asked Crossing Watch to video River Lane crossing. In 42.6 minutes there were 18 crossings and 27 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 50.6 km/h. Several children have been hurt at this crossing since the term began.

Crossing Watch defines a serious near-miss as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and a close pass as 1.5 s to 3.0 s apart. There was 1 serious near-miss and 3 close passes. In 4 cases the pedestrian reached the conflict point first.

The serious near-miss had a gap of 0.1 s with a car at 14.9 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.4% from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+ car fronts, and at a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact speed would be 14.9 km/h with 0.4% adult death risk.

1 close pass had a gap of 1.5 s with a motorcycle at 53.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 11.1%, and at a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with 0.0% adult death risk.

1 close pass had a gap of 2.3 s with a car at 44.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 0.3%, and at a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with 0.0% adult death risk.

1 close pass had a gap of 2.0 s with a car at 18.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 0.0%, and at a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with 0.0% adult death risk.

For engineering context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 scaled from 42.6 minutes to 25 pedestrians and 38 moving vehicles an hour, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour. In that video 50.9% of time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 gaps of 6 s or more and 9 of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 73.1 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signage at River Lane crossing to reduce speeds and protect children crossing.

We can share the full video and Crossing Watch measurements for your review. Please let us know what further data you need.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

Re: Safety improvement at River Lane crossing

We write following a Crossing Watch video measurement at River Lane crossing. Over 34.2 minutes (2052.0 s) we recorded 19 crossings and 5 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 34.3 km/h. The video showed 19 gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle. Of encounters, 1 was pedestrian-first and 1 was vehicle-first by our SAM tracking post-encroachment time method (serious is pedestrian and moving vehicle on same spot less than 1.5 s apart; close pass is 1.5-3.0 s).

The worst serious near-miss had a time gap of 1.1 s with a bus at 28.4 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 1.3% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), falling to impact 18.4 km/h and 0.5% death risk at a 20 km/h limit.

A separate close pass had a time gap of 2.4 s with a van at 16.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.0%, remaining 0.0 km/h impact and 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, scaled from 34.2 minutes of video where a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount by 1.3x. Also 75.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you provide a raised zebra crossing with approach speed table at this location.

We are willing to share the video and tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the crossing outside our school at School Lane crossing. Crossing Watch video analysis for 37.2 minutes (2232.0 s) recorded 39 crossings and 6 vehicles.

In that recording 3 of 39 crossings (1 in 13) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 2 of 39 (1 in 20) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 1.6-20.9% and 0.6-17.3% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

There were 2 serious near-misses (less than 1.5 s apart) and 1 close pass (1.5-3.0 s). The 85th percentile speed was 51.5 km/h. There have already been injuries at this spot this school year.

The most serious event was 0.4 s between a person and an auto-rickshaw at 50.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 8.4%, compared with 0.6% at an impact speed of 20.0 km/h. Figures are from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.

The second serious event was 1.1 s between a person and a car at 31.4 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 1.7%, compared with 0.3% at an impact speed of 13.1 km/h.

The close pass was 1.5 s between a person and a bus at 15.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 0.4%, compared with 0.4% at an impact speed of 15.2 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, being 63 pedestrians and 10 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 37.2 minutes of video. A formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count 1 person twice.

Also 46.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 gaps and 6 of them 12 s or more and longest 26.1 s. The first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you provide a raised zebra crossing with speed table at School Lane crossing. We can share the video and measurements on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We write about the crossing at Quarry Road crossing outside our school.

We arranged a video survey for 8.1 minutes (486.0 s). In that time 11 pedestrian crossings and 19 moving vehicles were counted. There were 4 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart.

Please provide a raised zebra crossing at this crossing. We offer to share the video for review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the safety of the Station Road crossing outside our school. Crossing Watch video analysis (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) of 27.4 minutes (1644.0 s) recorded 7 crossings and 24 vehicles, with an 85th-percentile speed of 58.5 km/h. During the 1644.0 s of video, 7 crossings and 24 vehicles were observed with an 85th-percentile speed of 58.5 km/h.

In that time there was 1 serious near-miss (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 3 close passes (1.5-3.0 s). The serious near-miss involved a car at 55.1 km/h with a time gap of 1.1 s; for an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 12.6% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+). One close pass involved a motorcycle at 16.5 km/h with a time gap of 2.2 s. Another close pass involved a bus at 27.4 km/h with a time gap of 2.7 s. A further close pass involved a motorcycle at 21.7 km/h with a time gap of 2.9 s. In 3 cases the person arrived first and in 1 case the vehicle arrived first.

For context, PV² is 0.0 x 10^8, from 15 pedestrians and 53 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 27.4 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice. 40.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps of 6 s or more and 8 gaps of 12 s or more, longest 34.5 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you provide a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We are happy to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write on behalf of the school beside the North Avenue crossing to request a safety improvement.

In 24.8 minutes (1488.0 s) of video at the crossing we recorded 12 crossings and 33 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 55.8 km/h. At school start and finish times the crossing is even more dangerous because most children cross without an adult to help them.

6 of 12 crossings (1 in 2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 4 of 12 (1 in 3) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 21.1-78.9% and 9.9-65.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 1.1-10.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

Engineering context, briefly with caveats: PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 scaled from 24.8 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one twice at 1.3x the true count in our drone test. 89.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 8 gaps, 0 of them 12 s or more, longest 8.2 s, with the first and last cut short by the video.

The worst near-misses were as follows. One serious near-miss had a gap of 0.1 s between person and a car travelling at 55.0 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 12.5% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), falling to 0.6% at 20.0 km/h. A second serious near-miss had a gap of 1.4 s with a car travelling at 49.8 km/h. A third serious near-miss had a gap of 1.4 s with a car travelling at 41.6 km/h. A fourth serious near-miss had a gap of 0.1 s with a motorcycle travelling at 28.2 km/h. A close pass had a gap of 2.0 s with a bus travelling at 21.1 km/h.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table to reduce speeds toward 20.0 km/h and provide protected priority for people crossing.

We are happy to share the video and SAM tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at North Avenue crossing

Dear Sir or Madam,

We write on behalf of our school about the crossing on North Avenue outside our premises. Crossing Watch measurements from video with SAM tracking and road-plane geometry recorded 11 pedestrian crossings and 20 moving vehicles in 11.1 minutes (666.0 s).
The 85th percentile speed was 53.9 km/h. Many pupils had to sprint through traffic during the morning school rush.
There were 3 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart.
In that period 1 interaction had the person first, 2 had the vehicle first, and 1 had both at once.
One serious near-miss had a car at 55.5 km/h with a time gap of 1.1 s between pedestrian and vehicle.
Another serious near-miss had a car at 52.1 km/h with a time gap of 1.4 s between pedestrian and vehicle.
A third serious near-miss had a car at 29.4 km/h with a time gap of 0.0 s between pedestrian and vehicle.
A close pass had a car at 29.5 km/h with a time gap of 2.8 s between pedestrian and vehicle.
For adults hit by a car front the death-risk figures from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, are 13.0% at 55.5 km/h, 9.9% at 52.1 km/h, and 1.4% at 29.4 km/h.
At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed for the 29.4 km/h case would be 20.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.6%, and for the other cases the impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.0%.
PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this video is 11.1 minutes, so those rates are not used for design.
70.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 10 gaps of 6 s or more and 1 gap of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 33.3 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.
We request installation of a raised zebra crossing at this location.
We are willing to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning the Market Street crossing. In 16.6 minutes of video we recorded 10 crossings and 4 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 59.3 km/h. The closest of these near-misses was the fault of Mr. Tarun Mehra, who runs the tea stall.

During that time there was 1 serious near-miss, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, with a gap of 1.1 s involving a car at 57.0 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at 57.0 km/h the death risk is 14.6% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

There was also 1 close pass, defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart, with a gap of 1.8 s involving a car at 20.4 km/h.

Overall, 2 of 10 crossings (1 in 5) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 1 of 10 (1 in 10) within 1.5 s.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 scaled from 16.6 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour. Also, 55.9% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 9 gaps and longest 76.0 s, where the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing to slow traffic and provide a safer crossing point. We would be pleased to share the video for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Market Street crossing

We write on behalf of the school at Market Street crossing. The observation lasted 216.0 s and included 6 crossings and 2 vehicles. We have 3.6 minutes (216.0 s) of video analysed by Crossing Watch. In that time we counted 6 pedestrian crossings and 2 moving vehicles.

PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 3.6, so those rates cannot be used reliably.

During the observation we recorded 2 serious near-misses and 0 close passes. In 2 cases the pedestrian crossed first and was followed by the vehicle within the PET threshold. A serious near-miss is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, a close pass as 1.5-3.0 s.

44.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 2 gaps, 1 of them 12 s or more, longest 19.5 s. The first and last gaps are cut short by the video. For context, UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds, while other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

The 85th percentile speed was 45.0 km/h.

One serious near-miss had a PET of 0.1 s and involved an auto-rickshaw at 46.4 km/h.

For an adult hit by a car front at 46.4 km/h the death risk is 6.2%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h, per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.

The other serious near-miss had a PET of 1.4 s and involved a bus at 12.1 km/h.

For an adult hit by a car front at 12.1 km/h the death risk is 0.3%, which would remain 0.3% at an impact of 12.1 km/h if limited to 20 km/h.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this crossing to reduce vehicle speeds and give pedestrians priority.

We are happy to share the 216.0 s video and tracking data on request.

Yours faithfully
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about safety at the North Avenue crossing outside our school.

Crossing Watch video (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) measured 10.7 minutes (642.0 s) with 9 pedestrian crossings and 26 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 56.0 km/h. The video showed 1 gap of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle. A serious near-miss is a pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart; a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s apart. We recorded 3 serious near-misses and 2 close passes.

The worst incidents were as follows. One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.9 s with a van at 40.3 km/h; adult death risk if hit by a car front would be 3.6% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), falling to 0.2% at an impact of 9.2 km/h if limited to 20 km/h.
One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.1 s with a bus at 18.7 km/h; adult death risk if hit by a car front would be 0.5% and would remain 0.5% at an impact of 18.7 km/h if limited to 20 km/h.
One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.3 s with a motorcycle at 15.7 km/h; adult death risk if hit by a car front would be 0.4% and would remain 0.4% at an impact of 15.7 km/h if limited to 20 km/h.
One close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.6 s with a car at 26.3 km/h; adult death risk if hit by a car front would be 0.8% and would be 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h.
One close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.4 s with a bus at 52.9 km/h; adult death risk if hit by a car front would be 0.6% and would be 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h.

For context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 10.7 minutes. Also 95.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 2 gaps of 6 s or more and 1 gap of 12 s or more and longest gap 36.6 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We would be pleased to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Canal Road crossing

We write from the school served by Canal Road crossing. A 30.2 minute video recording (1812.0 s) recorded 40 pedestrian crossings and 35 vehicles at the site.
5 of 40 crossings (1 in 8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 4 of 40 (1 in 10) were within 1.5 s, defined as serious.
The 85th percentile speed was 64.4 km/h. The video showed 40 gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle.
The worst serious near-miss involved a motorcycle at 59.6 km/h with 0.1 s between person and vehicle on the same spot; if hit by a car front at that speed the risk of death for an adult is 17.8%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h, source Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.
A second serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 34.5 km/h with 1.1 s between person and vehicle; the adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 2.2%.
A third serious near-miss involved a bus at 18.7 km/h with 0.0 s between person and vehicle; the adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.5%.
A fourth serious near-miss involved a car at 14.1 km/h with 0.7 s between person and vehicle; the adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.4%.
A close pass involved an auto-rickshaw at 48.0 km/h with 2.1 s between person and vehicle; the adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 1.4%.
For engineering context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 79 pedestrians and 70 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 30.2 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and the pedestrian count method can overcount. 43.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, based on 1 gap with longest 8.2 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.
We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this crossing to reduce speeds and provide priority for people crossing.
We are willing to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal
